units.la: Serenissimo & Potentissimo Monarchæ CAROLO SECUNDO, Dei Gratia Magnæ Britanniæ Franciæ & Hiberniæ Regi, Fidei Defensori, &c.
units.tr: Most Serene and Most Potent Monarch CHARLES THE SECOND, by the Grace of God King of Great Britain, France and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, etc.

units.la: Serenissime REX,
units.tr: Most Serene KING,

units.la: PRodeat jam sub Tuis Auspiciis Illa Patris Tui Gloriosissimi Imago, Illa quâ magis ad Dei similitudinem quam quà Rex aut Homo accedit. A prodeprodeat vero eo colore peregrino, quo facta omnibus conspectior fiat publica. Ita enim Tu voluisti, ut sic Lingua omnium communi Orbi traderem, in quâ utinam fœliciorem Tibi operam navare licuisset, ut illam Nativam Elegantiam, illam Vim verborum & Lumina, illam admirabilem sermonis structuram exprimerem. Quod cùm fieri (fortasse nec à peritissimis) à me certe non possit, præstat interim ut cum aliqua venustatis injuria magnam partem Europæ alloquatur, quàm intra paucos suæ Gentis clausa apud cæteros omnes conticescat. Sunt enim hîc velut quædam Dei Magnalia quæ spargi expedit humano generi, & in omnium linguis exaudiri: Id pro mea facultate curavi, ut si non sensa Tanti Authoris ornatè, at perspicuè & fidè traderem, imo nec ab ipsa dictione & phrasi (quantum Latini idiomatis ratio permittit) vel minimum recederem. Sacri enim Codicis Religiosum esse decet Interpretem. Et certe proxime ab illo sacro & adorando Codice (qui in has comparationes non cadit) spero non me audacem suturum si dixero nullum inter caeteros mortalium, vel Authore vel Argumento illustriorem, vel, in quo viva magis Pietas & eximie Christiana spiratur.
units.tr: May that image of Your most glorious Father now go forth under Your auspices, the image by which a man or a king comes closer to the likeness of God. It goes forth in that foreign colour, by which it becomes more conspicuous and public to all. For You wished it so, that I should hand it on to the whole world in the common language of all. Would that I had been allowed to serve You better in that language, so that I could express its native elegance, its force and brilliance of words, its admirable structure of style. Since this cannot be done by me (perhaps not even by the most skilled), it is at least better that it address a large part of Europe with some loss of elegance, than that it remain shut up among a few of its own nation and silent to all others. For there are here, as it were, certain magnalia of God, which it is good to spread among mankind and to hear in the tongues of all. I have taken care, so far as my ability allowed, that if I could not render the thoughts of so great an Author elegantly, I would at least render them clearly and faithfully; indeed I have departed in the least possible degree from the very diction and phrasing (as far as the nature of the Latin idiom permits). For it becomes the interpreter of a sacred book to be scrupulous. And certainly, next to that holy and adorable Book (which does not fall into these comparisons), I hope I shall not seem bold if I say that there is no other among mortal writings more illustrious either in author or in subject, or in which living piety and an eminently Christian spirit breathe more.

units.la: Habet verò sanctitas Regia nescio quid ex fortunae suae Majestate sublimius quiddam & augustius, & quae imperium magis obtinet in mentes hominum, & reverentiâ majore excipitur: quare & his maximè instrumentis usus est Deus qui illam partem sacrae paginae ad solennem Dei cultum pertinentem, Psalmos scilicet, & Hymnos, caeteraque
units.tr: Royal holiness, however, has something more lofty and august from the majesty of its fortune, and it holds greater sway over men's minds and is received with greater reverence. Therefore God used these instruments especially for that part of Holy Scripture which pertains to the solemn worship of God, namely the Psalms and Hymns and other

units.la: ejusmodi perpetuis Ecclesiæ vsibus inservitura, transmitterent hominibus & Authoritatem quandam conciliarent. Quid quòd libentius etiam arripiunt homines sic objectam & traditam pietatem. Quod & Libro huic evênit, & erit magis eventurum, quò iam multò diffusior plures sui capaces invenerit.
units.tr: such things, destined for the perpetual uses of the Church, so that they might hand them down to men and lend them a certain authority. Moreover, men seize more willingly such piety when it is set before them and delivered in this way. This has happened to this Book, and will happen more, since by now, having spread much more widely, it has found many capable of it.

units.la: Magnum erat profecto sic meditari sic scribere; multo majus sic vivere, sic mori: ut sit hæc penè nimia dictu pietas exemplo illius superata. Scit hæc illa Orbis Pars miserrima jam & contaminatissima. Utinam hanc maturius intellexissent virtutem, quam jam ferò laudant & admirantur amissam, nec illa opus fuisset dirâ fornace quâ tam eximia Regis pietas exploraretur, ex quâ nos tantùm miseri facti sumus, ille omnium fælicissimus: Cujus illa pars vitæ novissima & ærumnosissima & supremus dies (in quo Hominibus & Angelis spectaculum factus stetit animo excelso & interrito, summum Fidei, Constantiæ, Patientiæ exemplar, superior Malis suis, & tota simul congestâ inferni malitiâ) omnes omnium Triumphos & quicquid est humanæ Gloriæ superavit. Nihil egistis O quot estis hominum! (sed nolo Libro sanctissimo quicquam tetrius præfari, nec quos ille inter preces nominat, maledicere) nihil (inquam) egistis hoc parricidio, nisi quod famam illius & immortalitatem cum æterno vestro probro & scelere coniunxistis. Nemo unquam ab orbe condito tot veris omnium lachrymis, tot sinceris laudibus celebratus est. Nulli unquam Principum in secundisagenti illos fictos plausus vel Metus dedit, vel Adulatio vendidit, quàm bi[?]o verissimos expresse Fuga, Carcer, Theatrum & illa omnium funestissima Securis, quâ obstupefecit Hostes moriens, & cæsus triumphavit.
units.tr: It was indeed a great thing to meditate and write thus; much greater to live thus and to die thus, so that this piety is almost too great to speak of, surpassed by his example. That most wretched and now most polluted part of the world knows this. Would that they had understood this virtue sooner, which they now late praise and admire as lost, and there had been no need for that dreadful furnace by which so exceptional a piety of the King was tested, from which we alone became wretched, while he became the most fortunate of all. His last and most woeful part of life, and his final day, in which, made a spectacle to men and angels, he stood with lofty and fearless mind, the highest model of faith, constancy and patience, superior to his evils and to all the malice of hell gathered together at once, surpassed all the triumphs of all and whatever is human glory. You have accomplished nothing, O how many of you men there are! (but I do not wish to preface this most holy Book with anything more foul, nor to curse those whom he names in his prayers) you have accomplished nothing (I say) by this parricide, except that you have joined his fame and immortality to your eternal shame and crime. No one since the world was made has been celebrated with so many true tears of all, with so many sincere praises. No prince ever prospering received from flattery those feigned applauses, or from fear, as much as the most true ones expressed by flight, prison, the stage, and that most dismal of all axes, by which he, dying, astounded his enemies, and, slain, triumphed.

units.la: Tu interim (Rex Augustissime) vera & viva Patris Effigies (cujus inter summas erat fœlicitates humanas & in adversis solatium Te genuisse; in quo superstite mori non potest) inflammeris maxime hoc mortis illius exemplo non tam in vindictæ cupidinem (in quem alii te extimulent, non Ego) quam in Heroicæ Virtutis & Constantiæ zelum: Hanc vero primum adeas (quam nulla vis tibi invito eripiet) Hæreditariam Pietatem; & quo es in tuos omnes affectu maxime Philostorgo, hunc libru[?] eodem tecum Genitore satum amplestere; Dic sapientiæ soror mea es, & prudentiam affinem voca; hanc tu consule, hanc frequens meditare, hanc imbibe penitus & in Animam tuam transfunde. Vides in Te omnium conjectos oculos, in Te omnium Bonorum spes sitas, ex Te omnium vitas pendere, quas jamdiu multi tædio projecissent, nisi ut essent quas tibi impenderent. Magnum onus incumbit, magna urget procella, magna expectatio. Major omnium quam quæ unquam superiùs, Virtutum necessitas: An sit Regnum amplius in Britannia futurum, an Religio, an Homines, an Deus, ex tuâ Virtute, Tuâ Fortunâ dependet,Immo, sola potius ex Deo Fortuna: cujus opem quo magis hîc necessariam agnoscis, præsentaneam requiris, eò magis ma-gisque (quod jam facis) omni pietatis officio promereris; & illa quæ in Te large sparsit Bonitatis,Prudentiæ, Temperantiæ, Justitiæ, & omnis Regiæ Virtutis semina foveas, augeas, & in fructum maturés, ut tibi Deus placatus & propitius quod detraxit Patri Tuo felicitatis humanæ, Tibi adjiciat, & omnes illius ærumnas conduplicatis in te beneficiis compenset, & appelleris Ille Restaurator, quem te unicè optant omnes & spe-rant futurum, & ardentissimis precibus expetit
units.tr: You meanwhile, most august King, the true and living image of your Father (among whose highest human felicities, and whose consolation in adversity, was to have begotten you; in whom, though he is gone, he cannot die), be inflamed especially by this example of his death, not so much with a desire for vengeance (to which others may urge you, not I) as with zeal for heroic virtue and constancy. First embrace this hereditary piety, which no force will snatch from you against your will; and with the affection you bear to all your own most of all, embrace this book, begotten with you of the same Father. Say, "Wisdom is my sister," and call prudence kin; consult her, meditate on her frequently, imbibe her deeply and pour her into your soul. You see the eyes of all turned upon you, the hopes of all good men set upon you, the lives of all hanging upon you, which many would long since have cast away in weariness, had they not something to devote them to. A great burden rests on you, a great storm presses, a great expectation: a greater necessity of virtues than ever before. Whether the kingdom is to remain in Britain, whether religion, whether men, whether God, depends on your virtue and your fortune, or rather on fortune from God alone. The more you recognise that his help is here necessary, and seek it as near at hand, the more and more you deserve it by every office of piety (as you already do). May you foster, increase and bring to ripe fruit those seeds of goodness, prudence, temperance, justice and every royal virtue which God has scattered widely in you, so that God, placated and propitious, may add to you what he took from your Father of human felicity, and may compensate all his troubles with benefits doubled upon you; and that you may be called that Restorer whom all desire you alone to be, hope you will be, and seek with most ardent prayers.

units.la: ΕΙΚΩΝ ΒΑΣΙΛΙΚΗ. I. De indictione Parlamenti, ab ipso Rege.
units.tr: Εἰκὼν Βασιλική [Eikon Basilike]. I. On the summoning of Parliament by the King himself.

units.la: Proxima hæc Comitia indixi non aliorum magis suasu, & rerum mearum necessitate, quàm meo proprio judicio, & sponte adductus, ut qui semper exististimaverim Parlamenta rite habita, tùm Coronæ meæ saluberrima, tùm in Populum gratissima. Et licet haud excidisset animo, quas scintillas olim in his Conventibus nonnullorum intemperies, suscitaverat, (quos propterea, ut eas restinguerem, per hos aliquot annos intermisi) tamen cùm certo jam apud me statuissem, æquis omnium & sobriis desideriis satisfacere, & si qua essent in Regno vel Ecclesia publica Gravamina, levare, sperabam hoc candore animi mei, & illorum æquitate conspirante, occurrí posse omnibus incommodis, quæ ex errore nostri mutuo, oriri potuissent. Quanquam enim illud subvereror, vix vitari etiamnum posse affectus quorundam & præjudicia, quæ rebus aliquanto officerent, tamen integrum meipsum custodire certus haud dubitabam rationum pondere, quicquid in lance adversa factiosum, deprimere.
units.tr: I called this coming assembly not so much at the urging of others or from the necessity of my affairs as by my own judgment and of my own accord, since I have always held that Parliaments, when properly conducted, are most salutary for my Crown and most welcome to the People. Although the sparks which the excesses of some in these assemblies once kindled had not slipped from my mind (which is why I suspended them for these last few years, to quench those sparks), yet since I had now firmly resolved to satisfy the fair and sober desires of all, and to relieve whatever public grievances there were in the Kingdom or the Church, I hoped that by the candour of my mind and their fairness working together, all the troubles that might arise from our mutual error could be met. For although I feared that the feelings and prejudices of some, which would somewhat hinder affairs, could hardly yet be avoided, I was certain that I would keep myself unimpaired, and I did not doubt that by the weight of reasons I would press down whatever was factious on the opposing scale.

units.la: Permolestum erat sane audire, quibus Partium studiis & Popular Impetu Deputatorum Electiones agebantur, sperans tamen gravitate & prudentia Optimæ Partis, temperari posse cæterorum fervorem, zelumque quanquam Boni animi, tamen promptum nimis ire præcipitem, restrictum fore & præfinitum iis limitibus, queis conservandæ, & sanandæ Reipublicæ utilissime inserviret, nemini magis quam mihi Conventus erat iste optabilis. Conscius siempe[?] integri cordis mei, affectusque in populi bonum & justa desideria, propensissimi, oblectabar hac maxime fiduciâ firmam postea inter nos concordiam & nexum nasciturum.
units.tr: It was truly very distressing to hear with what party zeal and popular impetus the elections of the Deputies were being conducted. Yet, hoping that the fervour of the others could be tempered by the gravity and prudence of the better part, and that their zeal, though well-meant, yet too ready and headlong, would be restrained and confined within those limits by which it might most usefully serve to preserve and heal the Commonwealth, no one desired this Assembly more than I did. Conscious of the sincerity of my heart and of my strongest inclination towards the good of the people and their just desires, I took my delight above all in this hope, that a firm concord and bond would afterwards arise between us.

units.la: Enimvero remotis suspicionibus, ē[?] re mea erat maxime, & liberorum meorum, ut amorem & commoda populi mei omni modo procurare, & tueri contenderem. Quæ mihi unica videtur in hoc mundo restare felicitas, ad quam Iusti Monarchæ adspiret ambitio; in qua Honos scilicet Illius & Salus proxime à Deo consistit. Nec difficulter admodum passurus eram, minui in quibusdam Prærogativam meam, cum tantillâ jactura subditorum affectibus pensata, nihil perderem.
units.tr: Indeed, setting suspicions aside, it was above all in my interest, and in that of my children, to strive to promote and protect by every means the love and welfare of my people. This seems to me the only happiness remaining in this world, to which the ambition of a just Monarch aspires, and in which his honour and safety, under God, chiefly consist. Nor would I have found it very hard to allow some of my Prerogative to be diminished, since I would lose nothing that is outweighed by the affection of my subjects at so small a cost.

units.la: Demereri quidem decreveram, non amicos meos solum, sed inimicos quoque: superatis corum[?] desideriis qui factiosissime in me animabantur, modo æquum quid petere & moderatum simularent.
units.tr: I had indeed resolved to deserve well not only of my friends but also of my enemies: once their desires were met, I would overcome even those who raged most factiously against me, provided they pretended to ask for something fair and moderate.

units.la: Iras vero & odia, quæ Ἀφέριτα[?] quorundam aut Remissio, in Civili & Ecclesiastica administratione, in Regimen nostrum derivaverat, iis volui legibus expiare, & in futurum provisionibus, quæ non solum secus admissa corrigerent, sed imperfectius instituta, si quid mancum esset, supplerent. Nemini enim mortalium concedo, ut majori me zelo agatur ad stabiliendam Religionem, Veritatemque illius & Ordinem, & Unitatem conservandam, gnarus scilicet, nullas Civium Dissensiones faces perniciosius jactari, quam quæ privatis Factionibus Religionem prætexunt.
units.tr: But the angers and hatreds which the [obscure] of some, or their remission, had derived against our rule in civil and ecclesiastical administration, I wished to expiate by such laws, and for the future by provisions which would not only correct what had been admitted amiss, but would also supply whatever was lacking in things imperfectly instituted. For I concede to no mortal that I am moved by greater zeal to establish Religion, its truth and order, and to preserve unity, knowing well that no firebrands of civil dissension are hurled more destructively than those which pretend religion as a cover for private factions.

units.la: Constitueram vero, quæ plena & liberâ consultatione in Parlamento adhibitâ, manifeste explorarentur perperam fieri, reformare: iis vero omnibus, quorum Conscientia mea & Ratio æquitati suffragabatur, rogationibus annuere. Atque utinam intra hos me limites tenuissem, nec judicium meum passus fuissem in quibusdam rebus, Importunitate aliorum potius, quam argumentis obrui. Haud prodidissem me hac fiducia eorum insidiis, quibus diu ansam in me quærentibus, vires tantum hactenus, & occasio ad nocendum defuerant.
units.tr: I had, however, resolved to reform whatever was clearly found to have been done wrongly, after full and free deliberation in Parliament, and to assent to all those bills which my conscience and reason approved as just. Would that I had kept myself within these limits, and had not allowed my judgment, in some matters, to be overborne by the importunity of others rather than by arguments! I would not have betrayed myself by this confidence to their snares, since they had long sought an occasion against me and had until now lacked only the strength and opportunity to do harm.

units.la: Sed maturis jam factis peccatis nostris, obstandum non erat amplius Divinæ Iustitiæ, quo minus Gloriam illam suam ex adversis nostris repeteret, quâ illum in secundis fraudavimus.
units.tr: But since our sins had now ripened, Divine Justice could no longer be resisted, so that it might recover from our adversities that glory which we had robbed it of in prosperity.

units.la: Tu enim Domine satis clare demonstrasti futuræ Reformationis consilia, non semper Iustitiæ tuæ satisfacere, nec priorum delictorum ultionem obstruere.
units.tr: For you, Lord, have shown clearly enough that plans for future Reformation do not always satisfy your Justice, nor block the punishment of earlier offences.

units.la: Oppresserunt spes nostras peccata nostra; Tu nos docuisti, Domine, veniam a tua Misericordia, sperare, non ex nostro emendandi Proposito.
units.tr: Our sins have overwhelmed our hopes; you have taught us, Lord, to hope for pardon from your Mercy, not from our purpose of amendment.

units.la: Cum vindicaveris Gloriam tuam Iudiciis tuis, simulque ostenderis, quo periculo tibi displicemus, placandi in posterum fiducia: restituet ut speramus Misericordia tua illas Benedictiones, quas tam prave abutentibus abstulisti.
units.tr: When you have vindicated your Glory by your Judgments, and at the same time have shown how greatly we displease you, the confidence of appeasing you in future: your Mercy will, as we hope, restore those Blessings which you took away from us who abused them so badly.

units.la: Quia non mature satis piguit de peccatis nostris, fecisti, ut jam pigeat de remediis immaturis.
units.tr: Because we were not sorry enough, or soon enough, for our sins, you have now made us grieve over hasty remedies.

units.la: Non tamen me pænitet hunc Conventum indixisse, quia feci Domine recto corde, ad Gloriam tuam præcipuè & salutem populi attento.
units.tr: Yet I do not repent of having summoned this Assembly, because I have done so, Lord, with an upright heart, attentive above all to your Glory and the welfare of the people.

units.la: Quæ consecutæ sunt calamitates in me & Regna mea, tuæ sunt in nos Iracundiæ effectus justissimi, qui tamen demum dispensantes ita tuâ misericordiâ, proficere nobis possunt in futuram benedictionem, & meliores in fruendo nobis animos præstare.
units.tr: The calamities which have followed upon me and my Kingdoms are the most just effects of your anger against us; yet, at length dispensing them in your mercy, they can profit us for future blessing, and make our minds better in enjoying you.

units.la: Interim Domine, quanquam plurimis nos solatiis destitueris, dones tamen mihi & populo meo beneficium afflictionum & castigationis tuæ, ut non virga tua minus quam baculo confortemur: jam non plagæ hostiles erunt, sed paterna verbera, cum illa affectus nostros humilitate induceris, eum modum patientiæ, quæ pænitentes filios deceat, simul dederis.
units.tr: Meanwhile, Lord, although you have deprived us of very many comforts, grant to me and to my people the benefit of your afflictions and chastisement, so that we may be comforted no less by your rod than by your staff. Now they will not be hostile blows but fatherly stripes, since by bringing our feelings to humility you have also given that measure of patience which becomes penitent sons.

units.la: Nulla erit causa cur pæniteat malorum, quæ ex hoc Parlamento fluxerunt, cum per illa me & populum meum ad synceram pœnitentiam perduxeris.
units.tr: There will be no cause to regret the evils which have flowed from this Parliament, since by them you have led me and my people to sincere repentance.

units.la: Potior infinitis modis, cum perpessionibus nostris gratia tua, quam pax peccantibus.
units.tr: Your grace, together with our sufferings, is in countless ways better than peace for sinners.

units.la: O tu qui suprema es Bonitas & Sapientia, qui dominaris in omnia consilia nostra, dominare etiam in corda, & quo graviora jam patimur à tua Iustitia, eo meliores nos exhibeat tua misericordia.
units.tr: O you who are supreme Goodness and Wisdom, who rule over all our counsels, rule also over our hearts; and the more grievously we now suffer from your Justice, let your Mercy make us the better.

units.la: Fac Domine, ut quemadmodum ob peccata nostra in venenum cesserunt Antidota, ita gratia tua transmutante, in Antidota jam cedat venenum. Et sicut peccata pacis nostræ, bellum hoc infœlicissimum perstruxerunt, ita bello hoc denuo ad beatam[?] pacem præparemur. Ut quanquam plenum molestiarum sit mihi in terris regnum, fruar regno pacis in corde meo, & illo postea cœlesti, quod Christi sanguine acquisitum, Servatoris mei gratia, servo tuo peccatori imperties.
units.tr: Lord, grant that as, on account of our sins, antidotes have turned into poison, so by your transforming grace poison may now turn into antidotes. And as our sins have built up this most unhappy war against our peace, so by this war may we be prepared again for a blessed peace; so that, although my kingdom on earth is full of troubles, I may enjoy the kingdom of peace in my heart, and afterwards that heavenly kingdom, which, acquired by Christ's blood, you bestow by the grace of my Saviour upon your sinful servant.

units.la: 2. De morte Comitis Straffordiæ.
units.tr: 2. On the death of the Earl of Strafford.

units.la: INtuebar in Comitęm Straffordiæ, ut virum nobilem, summis negotiis parem, eumque qui metu potius Principem, quam pudore deterreret, ne illum Publicæ rei præficeret.
units.tr: I looked upon the Earl of Strafford as a noble man, equal to the greatest affairs, and one whom fear rather than shame would have deterred from setting him over the public business.

units.la: Hinc enim forsan nasci in illo poterat majora audendi fiducia; quâ deinde in magnos Errores[?], & plurimorum inimicitias laberetur. Quas haud dubiò affatim contraxit, dum in Celso Orbe moventi, claroq; & vivido fulgore, multos invidos halitus instar Solis excitaret, qui populari odio densati, nubem quandam & tenebras vel clarissimis meritis & innocentiæ offunderent.
units.tr: For from this perhaps there could arise in him a greater confidence in daring, by which he would then slide into great errors and into the enmity of many. These he undoubtedly drew upon himself in abundance, since, moving in a lofty sphere with a clear and vivid brilliance, he stirred up many envious breaths, like the sun, which, thickened by popular hatred, would cast a certain cloud and darkness over even his most distinguished merits and innocence.

units.la: Ego vero quanquam judicio meo omnia illius non probem, quæ Ille forsan actus potius necessitate temporum, & Populi illius Moribus, quàm ulla proprii ingenii asperitate, & insolentia admisit, nunquam tamen exploratum habui tam grave illius Crimen, ut capitali supplicio mactandum malitiæ inimicorum exponerem.
units.tr: I, indeed, although in my judgement I do not approve of all the things he did, which he perhaps admitted more from the necessity of the times and the manners of that people than from any harshness or arrogance of his own nature, nevertheless never held his crime to be so grave that I would expose him to the malice of his enemies to be slaughtered by capital punishment.

units.la: Nunquam sane tam difficili Temporum Statu conflictabar, quam in infælicis illius Comitis discrimine, cum inter actus Conscientiæ meæ fluctuans, & necessitatem (ut quidam ajebant) importunis populi mei flagitationibus auscultandi, obtemperavi eorum consilio, qui (in me animo ut opinor benevolo) suadebant, ut tutiora in præsens, quàm quæ justiora sunt visa, eligerem, atque adeo Externæ inter homines Pacis, internam Conscientiæ Rectitudinem coram Deo post ponerem.
units.tr: I was never struggling in so difficult a state of affairs as in the peril of that unhappy Earl, when, wavering between the dictates of my conscience and the necessity (as some said) of yielding to the importunate demands of my people, I followed the counsel of those who (well-disposed towards me, I think) urged me to choose what seemed safer for the present rather than what seemed more just, and so to put the inward uprightness of conscience before God behind outward peace among men.

units.la: Tantum verò abest, ut vel inficias eam, vel dissimulem nimiam[?] illam Facilitatem, quâ me flecti passus sum (nunquam enim integrè assentiebar) in mortem illius, quem nullâ lege convictum judicabam, ut nullum unquam conscientiæ morsum ægriùs tulerim: quod ia in argumentum poenitentiae meae, sæpe plurimo cum dolore, coram Deo & hominibus testatus sum, ut vitium pravæFragilitatis, quâ me cum ostendi, in quem plus metus hominum, quam Dei timor pollebat: cujus Nomine[?] & Loco in terris indignus est, qui actu tam insignis injustitiæ, quem nulla possunt pensare vel Publica commoda, damnum aliquod Politicum declinat.
units.tr: Far indeed am I from either denying or disguising that excessive facility by which I allowed myself to be bent (for I never fully assented) towards the death of a man whom I judged convicted by no law, so that I have never borne any bite of conscience more painfully. For this reason I have often testified, with much grief, before God and men, to my repentance, and to the vice of my wicked frailty, by which I showed myself one in whom the fear of men had more power than the fear of God. He is unworthy of his name and of his place on earth who, by an act of such notorious injustice, which no public advantage can outweigh, avoids some political loss.

units.la: Misera sane transactio! accepta in conscientiis plaga, mederi malis Rei-publicæ, & excitatâ in pectore nostro tempestate, æstus populares, & querelas compescere.
units.tr: A wretched transaction indeed! A wound taken in the conscience, in order to heal the ills of the commonwealth, and, a storm being stirred in our breast, to quell the popular tumults and complaints.

units.la: Nec fefellit eventus Dei justitiam; & quæ consecuta sunt tristissima satis mundo declarârunt, quam fallax est illud satius unum interire vel innoxium, quam populi ofsensam, vel ruinam accersere. Nihil enim mihi atrocius evenisset, si asserta Straffordii Innocentia, & justissimis Conscientiæ dictatis obtemperans, legem illam Damnatoriam obfirmare recusassem, quàm quæ postea minore cum solatio perpessus sum Ipse, & Populus meus, postquam ingratis quorundam obtestationibus tam crudelem gratiam indulsissem. Quin & illud etiam observavi, eos qui Authores mihi erant suis consiliis, ut sententiam illam ratam facerem, nullam aliam mercedem Gratiosi Officii, quàm Direptiones, Vexationes, & omne genus contumeliæ ab illo ipso, quem captabant populo retulisse: illo solum minimè omnium læso qui id sedulò ei suadebat ne refragranti conscientiæ assenti-rer. Deus illis & mihi turpem hanc præcipitationem tantæ rei ignoscat.
units.tr: Nor did the outcome deceive regarding the justice of God; and the most sorrowful events that followed have declared to the world well enough how false is that saying, that it is better that one innocent man perish than that the offence or ruin of the people be brought on. For nothing more atrocious would have befallen me, had I, asserting Strafford's innocence and obeying the most just dictates of conscience, refused to ratify that condemning law, than what I afterwards suffered myself, with less consolation, along with my people, after I had granted so cruel a favour to the ungrateful entreaties of certain men. Indeed I also observed this: those who were my advisers, urging me to make that sentence valid, had received no other reward for their service to favour than plunder, harassment, and every kind of insult from that very people whom they were courting; and he, least of all, was harmed who most diligently urged me not to assent against the resisting conscience. May God pardon both them and me this shameful haste in so great a matter.

units.la: Culpæ interim meæ propriæ, tam plenè conscius, eò libentius Iudicia ampleætor, quæ mihi, visum est Deo, infligere, tanquam media illius (uti spero) misericordiâ sanctificata, quò facilius de ista (mihi enim proculdubiò sic erat) iniquitate resipiscam, simulq; admoneor, optimam in Politicis normam esse, Unicam Iustitiam cæteris omnibus commodis potiorem habere, & pacem Conscientiæ salute Regnorum.
units.tr: Meanwhile, being so fully conscious of my own fault, I embrace more willingly the judgements which it has pleased God to inflict on me, as means sanctified by his mercy (as I hope), so that I may more readily repent of that iniquity (for so it was to me without doubt), and at the same time I am reminded that the best rule in politics is to hold justice alone above all other advantages, and that the peace of conscience is the safety of kingdoms.

units.la: Nec quicquam magis deinceps firmavit animum meum adversus aliorum violentias (qui iisdem me artibus adorti sunt) ne in Acta consentirem conscientiæ meæ adversantia, quàm acres illæ punctura & stimuli, quæ ob rem Straffordianam usque adhuc hærebant.
units.tr: Nor did anything more firmly strengthen my mind against the violence of others (who assailed me with the same arts) so that I would not consent in acts contrary to my conscience, than those sharp pricks and goads which, on account of Strafford, have clung to me even until now.

units.la: Neque hæc ideo, quòd animus fuisset illum postea negotiis adhibere, renitente præsertim Parlamento: illud unicè mihi optassem, nullatenus affinem fuisse culpæ illius mortis, de cujus innocentia nemini melius quàm mihi constabat.
units.tr: Nor is this because I had wished to employ him in affairs afterwards, especially when Parliament resisted: I would have wished only this, that I had in no way been connected with the guilt of that death, of whose innocence no one was more certain than I.

units.la: Imo neque ipsa ea Crimina illi objecta, post longam & æquam disceptationem ita perspicua erant, ut Majori parti utriusque Confessus de illis quid certi liqueret (Superiori præcipue Magnatum) quorum vix tertia pars aderat, cùm in illam Legem discederent. Quin & in ipsa Domo Inferiori plurimi homines nobiles, per se prompti satis Straffordii dignitatem, & potentiam minuere, nondum tamen de commissō ejus in Leges persuasi, capitale in eum sententiam ferre non audebant: qui mox ob suffragiorum suorum integritatem, affixis in publico & quasi proscriptis Nominibus vulgi odio & furori objiciebantur; crescente ita in immensum audaciā Vociferantium Iustitiam, (id est, quicquid ipsis collibuisset) à me & illis faciendum, vt credibile sit multos perterrefactos magis quam de aequitate sententiae persuasos condemnantium calculis accessisse.
units.tr: Indeed, even the very crimes objected to him were not, after a long and fair debate, so clear that anything certain was evident to the greater part of either assembly (especially to the Upper House of the nobles, of whom scarcely a third part was present when they went over to that law). Moreover, even in the Lower House, many noble men, though ready enough of themselves to diminish Strafford's dignity and power, yet not persuaded of his guilt against the laws, did not dare to pass a capital sentence against him. Soon afterwards, because of the integrity of their votes, their names were posted in public, as if proscribed, and they were exposed to the hatred and fury of the crowd; and so the boldness of those shouting for justice (that is, whatever they themselves pleased) to be done by me and by them grew immensely, so that it is credible that many who voted for condemnation were moved by terror rather than persuaded of the equity of the sentence.

units.la: Sed & Scitum[?] illud posterius, quo istius praecedendi[?] cassabatur Authoritas, ne deinceps in exemplum traheretur, satis mundo declarat, tactos fuisse aliquo sensu etiam hostes illius infensissimos, conscios scilicet quam rigidè cum illo actum fuisset, & quod postea in seipsis experiri noluissent.
units.tr: But that later decree also, by which the authority of that preceding measure was cancelled, lest it be drawn into a precedent in future, declares sufficiently to the world that even his most bitter enemies were touched by some feeling, namely, conscious of how harshly he had been treated, and of what they themselves would not have wished to experience afterwards.

units.la: Hunc interim mærorem meum, & teneritudinem animi, quòd in unius hominis sanguinem injustè latæ sententiæ, eique sub legis formulâ, & speciosis coloribus adumbratæ, & vitandi publici mali necessitate expressæ, invitus tamen, utcunque, Deum testor, acquieverim, spero testimonio mihi fore in posteros coram Deo & hominibus, quàm abhorream à reatu & onere immensi illius sanguinis, in exitiali hoc bello profusi, (quem imponunt mihi nonnulli, ut seipsos liberent) qui multo minùs extimescam meam vitam perdere, quàm vel uni cuipiam[?] perinjuriam admere.
units.tr: Meanwhile this grief of mine, and tenderness of spirit, that I have acquiesced, however unwillingly, in a sentence unjustly passed against the blood of one man, and shadowed under the form of law and specious colours, and extorted by the necessity of avoiding public evil (I call God to witness), I hope will be a testimony to me before God and men in future, of how much I abhor the guilt and burden of that immense blood, shed in this deadly war (which some men lay upon me, so that they may free themselves), I who fear far less to lose my own life than to do the least injury to anyone at all.

units.la: 6 Tu vero Domine infinitæ misericordiæ, ignosce mihi hoc crimen pravæ Obsequentiæ, quod me gravius premit, quam quenquam alium, cum nec inimam[?] invidiæ contra illum, aut Malitiæ tentationem habuerim, & quo eram loco constitutus, eo ut servare debuerim, ut consensum meum saltem in perniciem illius denegassem.
units.tr: 6 You indeed, Lord of infinite mercy, forgive me this crime of wicked compliance, which weighs on me more heavily than on anyone else, since I had neither any spite against him nor any temptation of malice, and since, from the place in which I was set, I ought to have kept, so as at least to have denied my consent to his destruction.

units.la: Iniquitatem meam cognosco, & peccatum meum contra me est semper.
units.tr: I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.

units.la: Libera me de sanguinibus Deus Deus salutis meæ, & exaltabit lingua mea justitiam tuam.
units.tr: Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God, the God of my salvation, and my tongue shall exalt your righteousness.

units.la: Tibi soli peccavi, & malum coram te feci: vidisti enim contradictionem intra cor meum & manum.
units.tr: Against you only have I sinned, and done evil in your sight: for you have seen the contradiction within my heart and hand.

units.la: Ne tamen projicias me à facie tua: Asperges me sanguine Redemptoris mei, & mundabor! lavabis me pretiosâ hac effusione, & super nivem dealbabor.
units.tr: Do not, however, cast me away from your face: sprinkle me with the blood of my Redeemer, and I shall be cleansed! Wash me with this precious outpouring, and I shall be made whiter than snow.

units.la: Fac ut discam Justitiam è Judiciis tuis mecamque[?] in tua Justitia fragilitatem agnoscam: dum auscultabam suadentibus, unius sanguine fuso, futuris malis occurrere, tu mihi & Regnis meis propter hoc & alia peccata, magnas, diuturnas, graves ærumnas infixisti.
units.tr: Make me learn justice from your judgements, and let me acknowledge my frailty in your justice: while I listened to those urging that by the shedding of one man's blood the evils to come be met, you, for this and other sins, have laid upon me and upon my kingdoms great, lasting, and grievous afflictions.

units.la: Fac ut Justitiam, quæ voluntas tua est, anteponam omnibus adversis clamoribus quæis[?] iniqua hominis voluntas revelatur. Satis est, semel me ab illis expugnatum, ut tibi displicendo iis placerem. O nunquam amplius permittas, me quâcunque ratione * Politicâ[?] adversari rationi conscientiæ meæ, quod est atrociter peccare contra Te Deum Rationis, & conscientiarum nostrarum Judicem.
units.tr: Make me prefer justice, which is your will, to all the hostile clamours by which man's unjust will is revealed. It is enough that I was once overcome by them, so as to please them by displeasing you. O never again permit me, by any political consideration whatever, to oppose the reason of my conscience, for that is to sin grievously against you, God of Reason and Judge of our consciences.

units.la: Quantiscunque tibi (Domine) aliis rebus me privare placuerit, redde mihi lætitiam salutaris tui & me spiritu principali tuo sustineas, qui voluntatem meam subjicit nemini, nisi luci illi Rationis Iustitiæ, Religionis, quæ lucet in corde meo. Ecce enim veritatem dilexisti in intimis, & in exterioribus expressionibus Integritatem.
units.tr: Whatever other things, Lord, it may please you to deprive me of, restore to me the joy of your salvation, and sustain me with your princely spirit, which subjects my will to no one except to that light of Reason, of Justice, of Religion, which shines in my heart. For behold, you have loved truth in the inward parts, and integrity in the outward expressions.

units.la: Exaudi Domine vocem Filii tui, & servatoris mei sanguinis, loquentis meliora: Sic Auditui meo & populi dabis gaudium & lætitiam, & exultabunt ossa humiliata.
units.tr: Hear, Lord, the voice of your Son and my Saviour, speaking better things: so you will give joy and gladness to my hearing and to the people, and the humbled bones will rejoice.

units.la: 3. De ingressu Regis in Confessum Inferiorē.
units.tr: 3. The King's Entry into the Lower House

units.la: Adiisse me Domum Inferiorem, ut Quinque Membra. Ordinis illius in jus [illegible, ~8 letters] adversarii mei, illud erat quod odiose exagitabant adversarii mei, & acerbissimis calumniis insectabantur.
units.tr: I had gone to the Lower House to bring the Five Members of that Order to justice, and this was the point my adversaries bitterly harped on and attacked with the most vicious slanders.

units.la: Verum est, eos qui nullarum partium erant, suspicionibus & metu haud leviter perculsos, imo plurimos etiam Meorum hoc facto offensos, quasi impetu magis, quam ratione suscepto, nec eâ prudentiâ gubernato, quæ in tam lubrico tempore necessaria fuisset.
units.tr: It is true that those who belonged to neither party were not lightly shaken by suspicion and fear, and that very many of my own people were offended by the deed, as if it had been undertaken on impulse rather than on reasoned judgment, and not conducted with the prudence that such a slippery time required.

units.la: At ignorabant Hi justas causas meas, & argumenta perspicua, quibus me tam instructum arbitrabar, ut nihil ad criminis evidentiam cujus illos accusabam, præter æquum & liberum forum requirerem.
units.tr: But they did not know my just causes and clear arguments, by which I believed myself so well equipped that I asked for nothing beyond a fair and open tribunal to establish the crime of which I accused them.

units.la: Nullâ hîc irritabat offensione, nec vindictæ appetitu contra ipsos privatim nisi in quantum me certo deprehendisse existimarem quàm nefaria Consilia injissent, & quàm illicitis Federibus ad turbanda mihi Regna se obstrinxissent:quorum omnium ut fidem facerem, minimum abfuit ne Chirographa eorum producerem, qui tumultus sequentes excitassent.
units.tr: I was not moved here by any offence, nor by a desire for private revenge against them, except insofar as I thought I had clearly discovered how wicked the plans they had devised were, and with what unlawful covenants they had bound themselves to disturb my kingdoms. To make all this credible, I came very close to producing the signed documents of those who had stirred up the tumults that followed.

units.la: Secus visum est Providentiæ. Non tamen deerant argumenta efficacia ad excitandas suspiciones in Principis animo, qui non stupidè vecors omnem curam publicæ tranquillitatis abjecerat: cui ut consulerem, postulando ut in quinque vel sex homines æquo & legitimo judicio inquireretur, (quod Deum testor, unicus mihi finis erat) quid inde pejus evenisset si obtinuissem quod volui,quàm, ut vel illis sontibus deprehensis, asserta esset causa mea, & Regni mei; vel patefactâ ipsorum innocentiâ, suspiciones meæ omnes abstergerentur, quas, ut nullâ malitiâ ortas, ita Ratio non permisit suffocari.
units.tr: Providence decided otherwise. Yet there were no lack of effective arguments to arouse suspicion in the mind of the Prince, who had not, in a stupid and reckless way, cast off all care for public peace. To meet this, I asked that five or six men be inquired into by a fair and lawful judgment (God is my witness that this was my sole aim). What would have turned out worse, had I obtained what I wanted, than this: either, with those guilty men detected, my cause and that of my kingdom would have been vindicated; or, with their innocence revealed, all my suspicions would have been wiped away, which, having arisen from no malice, reason did not permit to be stifled.

units.la: In quas flammas odiorum hæc scintilla (quam omni modo extinguere conabar) brevi tempore eruperit, nimis notum mundo est.
units.tr: How quickly this spark of hatred, which I tried to extinguish by every means, burst into flames, is too well known to the world.

units.la: Quod verè nonnulli calumniabantur, quasi per vim grassari in Domum Inferiorem, & Privilegia invadere destinassem, erat omnium salsissimum; cùm Deum testor, nec in mentem tale quicquam venisset, nec qui mecum tunc erant, ulla facti vel dicti mei significatione quid ejusmodi colligere potuissent.
units.tr: Some truly slandered that I intended to rush violently into the Lower House and seize its privileges. This was the most absurd of all, for I call God to witness that nothing of the kind ever entered my mind, nor could those who were with me then have gathered anything of the sort from any deed or word of mine.

units.la: Visos esse in comitatu meo aliquot Nobiles, ut haud insolens erat Majestati Regiae, & in turbidis temporibus, praesidium, ita nec numero aequabant ordinariam Stipatorum cohortem, si tumultus accidisset, longe impares futuri discrimini. Neque erant illi magis adventu meo perterriti, quam ipse parum securus ab eorum petulantiis, si nullos mecum adduxissem, qui reverentiam mei aliquam imprimerent. Imbuebantur enim tunc homines iis de me sinistris opinionibus, quas postea omni factorum verborumque acerbitate declararunt.
units.tr: Some nobles were seen in my retinue. This was not unusual for the royal majesty in troubled times, as a safeguard; yet their number did not match the ordinary company of attendants, and if a tumult had broken out they would have been far unequal to the danger. Nor were they more alarmed by my coming than I myself was uneasy about their insolence, had I brought no one with me to command some respect for me. For men were then steeped in such sinister opinions about me, which they afterwards declared by every bitterness of deed and word.

units.la: Omnino sic se res habet. Istos homines, & eorum sequaces suspiciebat vulgus attonitum tanquam Legum & Immunitatum suarum Patronor[?] me longe potiores, atque adeo digniores, quos suo invicem patrocinio propugnarent. Deo illos relinquo & ipsorum conscientiis, ad quae severa Tribunalia (si quid tale in me machinati fuerint) nullus erit suffugii locus, nec praesenti impunitate, aut popularibus vindiciis liberari.
units.tr: Altogether, this is how matters stood. The bewildered crowd looked up to these men and their followers as the patrons of its laws and liberties, far more suitable, and therefore more worthy, to defend one another with their patronage. I leave them to God and to their own consciences. If they have plotted anything of the sort against me, there will be no place of refuge for them before severe tribunals, nor will they be freed by present impunity or by popular vindications.

units.la: Ad haec interim, obstructa humana Justitia, una homini Christiano provocatio est, arham[?] scilicet & praeludium inevitabilis illius judicii quod districte in examen revocabit quę hic perperam vel parum decisa.
units.tr: Meanwhile, with human justice obstructed, there remains for a Christian one appeal, namely that to God's judgment, the prelude to that inevitable judgment which will strictly call into examination whatever has here been wrongly or insufficiently decided.

units.la: Id satagebam, si Deo visum fuisset, ut obviam iretur iis motibus, quos ex improbâ quorundam Sedulitate nisi mature coerceretur necessario secuturos prævidebam, quod & postea evenit cum multorum Millium (dolens. dico) pernicie.
units.tr: This was my concern, if it had pleased God, that those movements be checked which I foresaw would necessarily follow from the wicked zeal of some, unless they were restrained in good time. This indeed came to pass afterwards, to the ruin of many thousands (I say it with grief).

units.la: • Ut vero vim aliquam facerem libertati Ordinum, vel eorum Iustam Authoritatem quoquo modo infirmarem, nulla unquam mihi subiit cogitatio, nec sane opus esse rebar tam asperis auxiliis, stante a me Ratione & Infirmitia : ad quæ potius extrema quam deventum fuisset, omnem pati repulsam æquo animo decreveram.
units.tr: But that I should do any violence to the freedom of the Orders, or in any way weaken their just authority, never entered my thought, nor did I think such harsh aids needed, with reason and my own weakness standing on my side. Rather, I had resolved to bear any rebuff with an even mind rather than resort to extreme measures.

units.la: Tu vero Domine testis mihi es in Cœlis, & in corde meo, si quam violentiam, aut oppressionem adversus innocentes cogitaverim, vel si iniquitas in manibus meis.
units.tr: You, Lord, are my witness in heaven and in my heart, if I have devised any violence or oppression against the innocent, or if iniquity is in my hands.

units.la: Tunc persequatur inimicus animam meam, & conculcet in terra vitam meam, & gloriam meam in pulverem deducat.
units.tr: Then let the enemy pursue my soul, and trample my life into the earth, and bring my glory down into the dust.

units.la: Tu qui non juxta intuitum hominis judicas, sed ultra omnes populares apparentias perspicax, corda Scrutaris ac uris[?] renes, illuminans abscondita tenebrarum, libere agas.
units.tr: You who do not judge by the sight of man, but, seeing far beyond all popular appearances, search the hearts and the reins and reveal the hidden things of darkness, act freely.

units.la: Ne mihi meæ afflictiones, (quod prudentes & pii nunquam faciunt) imputentur mihi in argumentum peccati hac in re: haud magis quam eorum impunitas in testimonium Innocentiæ apud bonos valebit. Sed ignosce quod male fecerint, etiamsi in hoc mundo fuerit illis impune.
units.tr: Let my afflictions not be imputed to me as an argument of sin in this matter (which the prudent and godly never do), any more than their impunity will count as testimony of innocence among good people. But forgive them that they have done evil, even though they have gone unpunished in this world.

units.la: Protege servum tuum ab occultis conspirationibus, & aperta violentia sanguinariorum, & perversorum hominum, secundum simplicitatem cordis & innocentiam manuum hac in re.
units.tr: Protect your servant from secret conspiracies and the open violence of bloodthirsty and perverse men, according to the simplicity of my heart and the innocence of my hands in this matter.

units.la: Iudica Domine causam meam, & sustine Iudicium meum; tu qui sedes super Thronum, qui judicas justitiam, ut servus tuus lætetur semper in salutari tuo.
units.tr: Judge, Lord, my cause, and uphold my judgment; you who sit upon the throne and judge righteousness, so that your servant may always rejoice in your salvation.

units.la: De Insolentia Tumultuum.
units.tr: On the Insolence of the Tumults.

units.la: Nihil unquam existimabam (peccatis nostris exceptis) certum magis præsagium earum quæ insecutæ sunt calamitatum, quàm Tumultus illos Londinenses, & Westmonasterienses, statim à primo fere Parlamenti Conventu auspicantes, qui non ut æstus quidam, & procellæ maris (quibus suus tamen terror non deest) sed velut Terræ motus, (quo nil extat horribilius) fundamenta ipsa convellere, & subruere minabantur.
units.tr: I never thought, sins of our own apart, that there was a surer omen of the calamities which followed than those Tumults of the Londoners and Westminster men, which began almost from the very first meeting of Parliament. They did not come like some surge and storm of the sea, which has its own terror, but like an earthquake, than which nothing is more dreadful, and threatened to shake and overthrow the very foundations.

units.la: Quemadmodum vero in coercendis his Maris furoribus clarissimè se demonstrat Divina Potentia, ita non minus manifestat se Deus in compescendo populo, quem cum insano Confluxu & clamoribus, omnes Legum fines & authoritatis repagula trans-ilire, permiserit, nullum certius indicium est, Deum vehementer esse toti Genti infensum.
units.tr: Just as the Divine power shows itself most clearly in restraining the fury of the sea, so God makes his displeasure no less plain when he allows a people to leap over every limit of law and every barrier of authority in a mad crowd and with shouting. There is no surer sign that God is deeply angry with the whole nation.

units.la: Eo vero insolentiæ creverunt illi nostri Tumultus ut nec ipsi utriusque Ordinis Confessus Libertati vel Honori parcerent, nulla omnino reverentia deterriti, ne illos minis, & probris insectarentur, pulsatis etiam quibusdam, & ferociter perculsis, prout illis plus minusve grati erant. Neque hic stetit eorum furor, sed ad Me usque perrexit & Aulam meam agresti quadam audacia, dictisque & factis contumeliosissimis.
units.tr: Those tumults of ours grew so insolent that they spared neither the Liberty nor the Honour of either House. Restrained by no reverence at all, they assailed members with threats and insults, beating some and striking others savagely, according as they were more or less pleasing to them. Nor did their fury stop there. It pressed on even to me, and to my court, with rustic boldness and with the most insulting words and deeds.

units.la: Neque brevis hic Paroxysmus, aut conquassatio statim desitura; sed quotidiana planè febris, auctis indies in majus fervoribus & qui mitigari jam amplius nec remitti poterant.
units.tr: This was not a brief fit or a shaking that would soon cease. It was a daily fever, with the heat increasing day by day to a height that could no longer be softened or abated.

units.la: Primum ergo Præsidium implorabant adversus illos Terrores, quos ipsi sibi & aliis fecerant: nihil enim erat revera quod prudentes & cordatos viros magis terrebat, quam illa infimæ & rusticæ plebis tumultuaria coactio, quæ hanc ab illis disciplinam hauserat, ut comitiis primo supplicarent, deinde illa ipsa protegerent, mox etiam & præscriberent, postremò imperitarent, & dominarentur.
units.tr: At first they begged protection against those terrors which they had themselves created, both for themselves and for others. There was in truth nothing that frightened prudent and sensible men more than the tumultuous coercion of that base and rustic mob. It had learned this discipline from its leaders: first to petition the assembly, then to protect those very men, soon to dictate to them, and at last to command and lord it over them.

units.la: Per hos scilicet Tumultus, omnes Parlamenti obices (id est omnis suffragandi libertas, candidèque & æquanimiter disceptandi ratio) unâ operâ tollendi. Hi Domum utramque expurgare, & putrida (ut vocabant) Membra ejicere. Hi præfractas conscientias, quæ expedire se liberè volebant, perdomare penitus & subigere: hi omnes Factiones, seditiones Schismata, & quicquid adversus Ecclesiasticam aut civilem Politiam rogabatur, eò usque propugnare, dum prævaleret: denique quisquis animo volvebat perniciem Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ; obstetricari hi erant paratissimi; quorum impetus & vesana præcipitatio, nec maturitatem consiliorum expectabat, nec actiones fætandi tempora, nec cum ordinem gravitatem, deliberationem, quæ Parlamentum maximè decebat; sed barbara quadam immanitate, quasi rupto utero, abortiva quæcunque Decreta qualia Ducibus eorum placuissent, exscindere omninò festinabat.
units.tr: By these tumults, of course, every obstacle to Parliament was to be removed at one stroke: that is, all freedom to vote and all honest and calm method of debate. Through them the two Houses were to be purged and their "rotten members," as they called them, cast out. Through them consciences which wished to speak freely were to be wholly broken and subdued. Through them all factions, seditions and schisms, and whatever was contrived against the ecclesiastical or civil polity, were to be defended for as long as they prevailed. In short, whoever in his mind planned the ruin of Church and Commonwealth found these men most ready to act as midwives. Their violent and frenzied haste waited neither for the maturity of counsels nor for the time to bring forth actions, nor did it respect the order, gravity and deliberation which befit Parliament most. Rather, with a savage monstrosity, as if the womb had burst, they hastened to cut out by abortion whatever Decrees had pleased their leaders.

units.la: Tam portentosa certè, & detestanda omnia, ut vel sobrium quemvis hominem puderet vehementer, pigeretque, cùm his non tantùm veniam dari, sed insigniter applaudi cerneret, adhortantibus nonnullis, & in pejus instigatibus.
units.tr: All these things were so monstrous and detestable that any sober man would be deeply ashamed and grieved to see such people not merely pardoned but openly applauded, with some urging them on and inciting them to worse.

units.la: Herclè careret potius Vir Bonns illo quod tantopere expetebat Bono publico quàm tam improbis mediis procuratum vellet. Sed inter Dei præscriptum & impotentes hominum affectus rara admodum concordia est. Gaudent similibus sui instrumentis violenta consilia: & qui ad privatos suos fines intentiores sunt, difficulter se circumscribunt Dei mediis. Ingeret semper aliquid Violentia, quantumvis Ratione repugnante.
units.tr: By Hercules, a good man would rather go without that public good which they desired so eagerly than wish it to be procured by such wicked means. But there is very little agreement between what God prescribes and the unbridled passions of men. Violent counsels delight in instruments like themselves, and those who are too eager for their private ends scarcely keep within God's means. Violence will always bring something about, however much it is opposed by reason.

units.la: Qui autem fuerint Demagogi isti, & Turbarum Patroni, qui accersebant ultro hos homines, & blanditiis suis stimulabant, denique gubernabant eorum, & moderabantur clamores. Plurimi sunt adhuc in vivis nimis confesii, quàm ut dissimulent. Deus suo tempore patefaciet, quàm in idoneahec[?] Media fuerint ad suum finem assequendum.
units.tr: Who these demagogues were, and the patrons of the uproar who summoned these men of their own accord, who spurred them on with their flattery and finally guided and controlled their shouting, many are still alive and too well known to conceal it. God will reveal in his own time how unfit those means were for attaining their end.

units.la: Verùm, ut haud quaquam[?] mirandum est, iratum Mare furere, cum vehementibus ventis agitatur; ita nec vulgus etiam insolescere ab ejusmodi hominibus inflammatum, qui existimatione aliqua ingenii & pietatis praecipuè commendantur.
units.tr: But just as it is no wonder that the angry sea rages when it is stirred by violent winds, so it is no wonder that the common people grow insolent when inflamed by men of this kind, who are especially commended for some reputation of talent and piety.

units.la: Iam quod maximè formidabilem fecit hanc ferociam, id erat, quod cum plurimi de hoc graviter conquesti essent, Nonnulli ex ipsorum ordine, me etiam per Internuncios frequenter expostulante, nil remedii efficacis obtineri potuisset, reprimendo huic malo idoneum, quod jam passim in omnes spargi & latissimè dominari videbatur.
units.tr: What made this fierceness most to be feared was this: although many had complained of it bitterly, and some of their own order had often remonstrated with them through messengers (and I too had protested), no effective remedy could be obtained that would check this evil, which now seemed to spread everywhere and to rule very widely.

units.la: Is erat stupor quorundam, ut nil inde incommodi metuerent. Ea aliorum petulantia, ut virorum se multo praestantiorum contumeliis & injuriis gauderent, suam gnari[?] Securitatem in vulgi palpo constare, ita sensum omnem amiserant non meae solum, sed & Suae Honestatis simul & Incolumitatis, unde nunquam impetrari potuit vel unum ab illis Edictum, quo vel Examini subjicerentur, nedum supplicio, aut nota ulla afficerentur Turbines isti & incendiarii qui pâssim undique volitabant Pol[?]entiam suam jastantes, & turbam quoties usus fuit, colligebant. Quos interim hæc facientes, nonnulli à quibus plus sapientiæ expectasses ut amicos suos agnoscebant zelum & industriam collaudantes eorum scilicet, quiDiabolo simillimi circumibant quærentes quem potissimum fallerent & devorarent.
units.tr: There was a kind of stupor among some, so that they feared no harm from it. Others were so wanton that they rejoiced in the insults and injuries done to men far better than themselves. Knowing that their own safety rested on flattering the mob, they lost all sense not only of my honour but also of their own honour and safety together. For this reason it was never possible to obtain from them a single Edict by which those whirlwinds and firebrands, who flew about everywhere, boasting of their power, and gathered crowds whenever they wished, might be subjected to examination, let alone punished or marked with any censure. Meanwhile some men from whom one might have expected more wisdom acknowledged them as friends, praising the zeal and industry of such people, who were very like the Devil, walking about, seeking whom they might devour.

units.la: Fateor me cum tam pertinacem eorum obsurdescentiam comperissem, ut nec Episcoporum Declaratio qui primas illas Infolentias & vim experti erant, nec quod ab aliis Proceribus & viris Honoratis, tum à Me ipso remonstratum fuerat, haud quicquam prosiceret ad sedandos hosTumultus, & incolumitatem præstandam non libertati solum Parlamentariæ, sed & Personis nostris propriis in ipsis urbis platæis: haud jam amplius existimasse obligari me ultra per præsentiam meam Audaciam hanc insignem, & Contemptus irritare: sperans brevi mei subdućtione spatium fore aliquod quo reciprocari posset hic æstus, & in sanam mentem cæteri, ac modestiam suam redirent.
units.tr: I confess that when I found them so obstinately deaf that neither the Declaration of the Bishops, who had first experienced that insolence and violence, nor what other peers and men of rank had pointed out, nor what I myself had remonstrated, did anything at all to quiet these tumults or to secure the safety not only of Parliamentary liberty but also of our own persons in the very streets of the city, I no longer thought myself bound to remain in the city, under the eyes of such notorious audacity, and so to provoke contempt. I hoped that after a short withdrawal of my presence there would be some interval in which this ferment could subside, and the others return to a sound mind and their former modesty.

units.la: Tribuent alii fortasse Tufillanimitati[?] ut quis vulgi minis perterritus Publicam Stationem desereret. At mihi contra videtur non veræ fortitudinis, sed amentis cujusdam audaciæ, ultro se mari irruenti cum certissimo periculo objicere: quin dandum potius spacium dum hæc ferocia subsidat & si quid ruptum fuerit opportune restituatur. Sane vir verè fortis & magni animi mallet iniquis licet conditionibus, numeroque & loco inferior, in aperto campo & recto more .de pugnare, quam inter turbam incognitam fædè colluctari.
units.tr: Some may perhaps ascribe it to pusillanimity that a man, frightened by the threats of the mob, should abandon his public post. But to me it seems not the mark of true courage but of a certain mad boldness to throw oneself, of one's own accord, in the path of a rushing sea with certain danger. Rather, time should be given while this fierceness subsides, and whatever has been broken may be restored at the right moment. Indeed, a man who is truly brave and great of spirit would prefer, even on unfair terms and though inferior in number and position, to fight in an open field and by the rules of battle, rather than to wrestle shamefully among an unknown mob.

units.la: Suspicio erat quibusdam, non paucis etiam affirmantibus me, cum ab Albâ Aulâ discederé Bellum statim meditatum, cum non alia ratione (Deum testor) discesserim quàm ut personam meam & conscientiam à violentia incolumem præstarem. Deus novit me tunc temporis nec de Bello vel minimum cogitasse. Nec credibile est cuiquam sano homini, me, si tale consilium iniissem, tot me Actis superioribus, & quibusdam etiam postea infirmaturum; cum revera, ut omni modo declinarem Bellum, mihi soli in plurimis denegavi. Constat nullos tunc fuisse mihi exercitus ad quos confugerem, nec qui auxilium aut ultionem sponderent.
units.tr: Some suspected, and not a few affirmed, that when I left White Hall I had at once planned war. Yet, God is my witness, I left for no other reason than to keep my person and my conscience safe from violence. God knows that at that time I did not think even slightly of war. Nor is it credible to any sane man that I, if I had formed such a plan, would have denied it so often in my earlier acts and even later on, when in most matters I had refused to do anything of the sort, simply in order to avoid war. It is clear that at that time I had no armies to which I could turn, nor any who would promise help or revenge.

units.la: Quis jam crimini mihi vertat & aliis, si ab assiduis tumultuantium infultibus mature nos subduceremus, incerti, an eos furor & ira eò usque incenderent, ut quos ungulis jam constrictos quasi ludibundi tenebant, non discerperent penitus & devorarent. Numquam herclè abijssem à Domo mea, modò vel æquis conditionibus manere licuisset. Multa pati decreveram & quidem multa pertuleram, haud tamen officii mei arbitrabar Majestatem Loci, & Personæ meæ, tum Uxoris & Liberorum incolumitatem petulantiæ eorum prostituere, qui ferocissimè insultare prompti sunt, cum objecta injuriarum capacia, & idoneum tempus nanscifcantur.
units.tr: Who, then, would blame me or others if we withdrew in good time from the constant assaults of the rioters, uncertain whether their fury and anger would burn so far that they would not, once they had caught us in their claws as if in sport, tear us completely apart and devour us? By Hercules, I would never have left my house if I could have stayed there even on fair terms. I had resolved to suffer much, and indeed I had suffered much. Yet I did not think it my duty to expose the majesty of the place, my own person, and the safety of my wife and children to the wantonness of men who are ready to insult most fiercely whenever they find something open to injury and a suitable time.

units.la: Hos verò omnes Tumultus (quorum, complures jam homines Deo rationem reddiderunt, cæteris adhuc viventibus hæret crimen) tempus jam, & communis multorum reatus ita plane sepelivit, ut jam amplius nolim defodere. Credo tamen summum illum Seditionum & civilium Turbarum Vindicem, illis olim hominibus, & illi Vrbi in pœnarum suarum speculo crimina sua demonstraturum. Fallor, an non eodem quo deliquerint exemplo, sint aliquando plectendi.
units.tr: These Tumults (for which several men have already given account to God, while the guilt still clings to the rest who are living) time and the common guilt of so many have buried so thoroughly that I no longer wish to dig them up. Yet I believe that the supreme avenger of seditions and civil disorders will one day show that city its own crimes in the mirror of its punishments. I may be mistaken, but I doubt whether they ought not to be punished by the same example by which they sinned.

units.la: Equidem si in isto Conventu (prout prima illius Electio, & Constitutio spondebat) pleno & integro Numero confessum fuisset, membris utriusque Ordinis libertate suffragandi permissa (quod Honestas Ratio & Religio postulabat) haud dubitandum est, quin res ita commodè transigi potuissent ut spei & voto Bonorum omnium uberrimè fuisset satisfactum.
units.tr: Indeed, if in that assembly (as its first election and constitution promised) the full and complete number had met, with the members of each order permitted the freedom to vote (which honest reason and religion demanded), there is no doubt that matters could have been settled so suitably that the hope and wish of all good men would have been most richly satisfied.

units.la: Quod enim ad me attinet, statueram Rationi in omnibus auscultare, & quantum capere potuissem, obtemperare: sed velut sues in hortis ordinatim consitis, ita in Publicis Consiliis, sordidæ Turbæ colluvies susque deque miscent [?], & spargunt omnia, & stercoribus suis collutulant.
units.tr: As for me, I had resolved to obey reason in all things and to submit as far as I could. But just as swine in orderly gardens, so the filthy crowd mixes up the public councils, turns everything upside down, and wallows them in its own dung.

units.la: Subit animum aliquando hæc cogitatio; occurri forsan potuisse quæ insecuta sunt malis, si in alium quempiam locum Angliæ quod opporopportunè satis poteram, Parlamentum transtulissem, gratum scilicet futurum in quocunque loco, nullibi verò, tot diversis & pravis Humoribus obnoxium. Sed hæc omnia Deo relinquenda sunt, qui Sapientiæ suæ Gloriam, miserias & stultitias nostras detegendo illustrat.
units.tr: Sometimes this thought comes to my mind: the evils that followed might have been averted if I had transferred Parliament to some other place in England, as I could have done quite conveniently. It would certainly have been agreeable in any place, but nowhere would it have been exposed to so many diverse and perverse humours. Yet all these things must be left to God, who by uncovering our miseries and follies makes his own wisdom shine forth.

units.la: Tu autem Domine refugium mihi & suscep-tor meus ad te confugiam, & in tuto fuero, tu compescis strepitum marium, & fremitum populorum.
units.tr: But you, O Lord, are my refuge and my upholder; to you I flee, and I shall be safe. You quell the roaring of the seas and the tumult of the peoples.

units.la: Flumina Domine intraverunt, torrentes pene absorbuissent animam meam.
units.tr: The floods have come in, O Lord; the torrents have almost swallowed up my soul.

units.la: Intucor[?] peccata mea, & peccata populi mei, (tumultus animarum nostrarum contra Te Domine (ut justam Popularis hujus Diluvii causam, quod ita omnes fidei, modestiae, Legum, Justitiae, Religionis ripas superare & transilire permisisti
units.tr: I look upon my sins and the sins of my people (the tumults of our souls against you, O Lord), as the just cause of this popular deluge, since you have allowed them so to overflow and leap over all the banks of faith, modesty, laws, justice and religion.

units.la: Tu vero qui congregas aquas in locum unum, ut arida appareant, & reverti coegisti aquas quae terram obruebant verbo potentiae tuae. Compesce hanc vulgi Belluam & Eripe me à ferocia, & contradictionibus populi.
units.tr: But you, who gather the waters into one place so that the dry land appears, and who by the word of your power have forced back the waters that were covering the earth, restrain this beast of the mob, and rescue me from the fierceness and opposition of the people.

units.la: Reddemobis[?] precamur libertatem consiliorum, & Parlamentorum fac ut nullo affectu occaecati lucem Rationis, & Religionis intucamur, eamque ordine illo & gravitate sequamur quae homines decet & Christianos, sic nomen tuum laudabimus qui es Deus ordinis & consilii.
units.tr: We beg you to restore freedom to councils and parliaments. Grant that, blinded by no passion, we may look upon the light of reason and religion, and follow it with that order and seriousness which befit men and Christians; so shall we praise your name, you who are the God of order and counsel.

units.la: Quod aut nolit homo, aut nequit reprimere omnipotens tua Justitia & potestas, & velit.
units.tr: What man is unwilling or unable to restrain, your almighty justice and power can restrain, and will.

units.la: Des Domine his qui adhuc in vivis sunt, aquas[?] tu conscios nosti excitandi, vel non coercendi hos motus, tempestivum dolorem & sensum ingentis peccati sui: Pudor illos in hac vita plectat, non in futura supplicia.
units.tr: Grant, O Lord, to those who are still alive, since you alone know how to stir up or not to restrain these movements, timely sorrow and a sense of their great sin. Let shame punish them in this life, so that they need not suffer punishment in the future.

units.la: Præfinias & coerceas impotentiam nostrorum affectuum ratione, errores veritate, seditiones Legibus rite administratis, schismata denique Charitate, ut fiamus sicut tua Ierusalem Civitas in seipsa unita.
units.tr: Forestall and restrain the unruliness of our passions by reason, our errors by truth, our seditions by laws rightly administered, and finally our schisms by charity, so that we may become, as your Jerusalem, a city united within itself.

units.la: Hæc concedas Domine in bono tempore tuo propter Iesum Christum, AMEN.
units.tr: Grant these things, O Lord, in your good time, for the sake of Jesus Christ. AMEN.

units.la: 5. De lege Triennalis Parlamenti, & conti- nuatione illius postea durante utriusque Do- mus placito.
units.tr: 5. Concerning the Triennial Act of Parliament, and its later continuance during the pleasure of both Houses.

units.la: UT jam palam Orbi innotescerent illa prima mea Consilia, quàm paratus essem omnia contribuere, quæ Iustitia; Ratio, Honor, Conscientia permisêre, ut ad felicem exitum perduceretur Parlamentum (in quo nil aliud spectabam, quàm Regnorum meorum Bonum commune) legem illam de Triennalibus Parlamentis confirmavi libens, quod ut lenè & opportunum Pharmacum (si rectè adhibitum) praeveniret malignos humores, ne praepollerent nimium aut invalescerent, modò remedium non esset morbi causa, nullo posteà remedio sanabilis.
units.tr: So that my first intentions might become plainly known to the world, and how ready I was to contribute everything that justice, reason, honour and conscience allowed, in order that Parliament might be brought to a happy outcome (in which I looked for nothing but the common good of my kingdoms), I gladly confirmed the law concerning Triennial Parliaments. I thought it a gentle and opportune remedy (if rightly applied) which would forestall malignant humours, so that they might not grow too strong or gain strength, provided the remedy did not itself become the cause of the disease, to be cured by no remedy afterwards.

units.la: Aroitrabar huic Conventui satis jam negotiorum superesse, quae Triennium hoc integrum (interpositis recessibus) occuparet. Nunquam vero id credidi futurum, ut hinc arriperent occasionem nonnulli plus sibi insuper laboris imponendi, infecta ea denuo faciendo, quae tam benè jam acta repererant. Ea improba est multorum sedulitas, creant sibi potius quàm defit negotium, & malè agere instituunt, quàm nil agant omnino.
units.tr: I judged that this assembly would have enough business to occupy the whole of that triennium (with recesses interposed). Yet I never believed it would come about that some men would seize the occasion to impose on themselves further labour, undoing again those things which they had found so well done. Such is the wicked busyness of many: they create work for themselves rather than lack it, and prefer to do badly rather than to do nothing at all.

units.la: Quum angusta nimis videretur illa prima mea Concessio, quàm ut Timori quorundam caveret, & negotia Publica perficeret, etiam amplius mihi persuaderi passus sum legem illam sancire Illimitati Consessus, durante scilicet Domorum placito, id quod aliis sonabat, perpetuum Parlamentum.
units.tr: Since that first concession of mine seemed too narrow to satisfy the fears of some and to complete the public business, I allowed myself to be persuaded further to sanction by law that the unlimited assembly, namely to continue during the pleasure of the Houses, which to others sounded like a perpetual Parliament.

units.la: Hoc suprema mea fiduciae testimonio, sperabam in aeternum excludere, & quasi pessulo obducto eliminare omnes retro Suspiciones, & futuros Errores: Certè haudquaquam animus erat, meipsum foras ejicere, quàm mihi mercedem nonnulli hujus gratiae retulerunt.
units.tr: By this supreme token of my trust I hoped to shut out for ever, and as if by a bolted bar to exclude, all past suspicions and future errors. Certainly my mind was far from casting myself out of doors; yet some have repaid me for this favour in return.

units.la: Fateor huic simile nunquam factum à Decessoribus meis: aequo tamen interpreti nihil aliud significat, quâ confidentiâ versatus fun inter subditos meos sperans haudquaquam male usuros tanta gratia, qua, ut ostenderem quantum illis considerem, me ipsum in tanto apice praerogativae restrinxeram.
units.tr: I admit that nothing like this had ever been done by my predecessors. Yet a fair interpreter will understand it as nothing more than the confidence with which I dealt with my subjects, hoping that they would by no means misuse so great a favour; and to show how highly I regarded them, I had restricted myself from such a height of prerogative.

units.la: Boni certe subditi aequum haud omnino duxissent, ut deterior esset ideo mea conditio, quia eorum reddideram meliorem: neque revera evenisset, si didicissent nonnulli aequè uti moderate occasionibus bene vel male agendi, ac importune expetere.
units.tr: Surely good subjects would not have thought it fair that my condition should be made the worse for that reason, because I had made theirs the better. Nor would it in fact have happened, had some learned to use occasions of acting well or ill as moderately as they demand them immoderately.

units.la: A continuatione hujus Parlamenti existimabam contineri sic melius posse, & quasi justis suis modis temperari Rempublicam, vim suam legibus, & vigorem reddi, quod, ut accuratissime fieret, neminis magis quàm mei intererat, cum per eas non minus Jura mea Regia, quàm Civium cujusvis conservantur. Ultrà quàm leges mihi tribuunt nil postulo, citrà, neminem credo vel infimae sortis subdi-torum debere accipere.
units.tr: I believed that by the continuance of this Parliament the commonwealth could be better contained in this way, and as if tempered by its just measures, that its power might be given strength and its vigour by laws; and that this should be done as exactly as possible concerned no one more than myself, since by them my royal rights are preserved no less than those of any citizen. I ask for nothing beyond what the laws grant me, and I believe that I ought to accept nothing short of them, nor should anyone of the lowest subjects.

units.la: Sparsa fama à nonnullis & credita, pœnituisse me statim hujus Concessionis, & persuadere mihi alii volebant satis causae fuisse cur id facerem. At neque subito nec facile in eam suspicionem adducebar, ut à viris spectatae famae eam unquam ingratitudinem meruerem, ut quo plura iis donaveram, eò minus mihi cum illis frui liceret, qui vel largissimis concessionibus me haud quicquam immimutum credebam, dùm sic populi mei amorem redimere, & confirmare potuissem [?].
units.tr: A report spread by some and believed was that I had at once repented of this concession, and some wished to persuade me that there was reason enough for my doing so. But I was neither quickly nor easily brought to such a suspicion, that I should have deserved such ingratitude from men of proven reputation, that the more I had given them, the less I should be allowed to enjoy them with those whom I believed were not in the least diminished even by the most generous concessions, so long as I could thus win back and confirm the love of my people.

units.la: De quo neque adhuc despero, posse me Dei Bonitatem incremento illius benedicere, cum majori otio dato minus loci fit futurum prajudiciis, cum jam sensu integro & nullis assectibus obscurato intueantur in illa nostra [?] Regia magis indulta, quam ab amicissimo animo profecta, quæ in hunc tantum sincerum concesseram, ut perpetuam illis hanc fœlicitatem [?], qui in eo jam solum miseri sunt [?] quod oblatis bonis frui ambitione quorundam prohibentur.
units.tr: Nor do I yet despair of this: that God's goodness may bless me with its increase. For when greater leisure has been given, there will be less room for prejudices, since they now look upon those concessions of mine, granted more out of royal indulgence than issuing from a most friendly spirit, with a whole and unclouded sense, unobscured by any passions.
