units.tr: You taught through the wisest of kings that it is a snare to a man to devour what is holy and only afterwards to reconsider his vows.

units.la: Custodi Famulum Tuum usque, ne consentiat in perjuras & sacrilegas rapinas, ne stigma mihi in æternum & exccratio hæreat, tanquam Te & Ecclesiam Tuam spolianti iis omnibus quæ & Munificentia Tua donaverit, & Clementia Tua à Nobis acceperit ut Doctrinæ & Pietatis incitamenta.
units.tr: Keep your servant, lest he consent to perjured and sacrilegious plunder, lest the stigma and the curse cling to me for ever, as to one who despoils you and your Church of all those things which your bounty has given, and which your clemency has received from us as incentives to doctrine and piety.

units.la: Quanquam ærario meo exhausto, & imminutis Redditibus grande æs alienum contraxerim, haud me inde tentari permittas, ut tam profana ratione hæc damna resarciam, ne Carbone ab Altari Tuo id in Throno meo & Conscientia incendii excitetur, quod vix unquam extingui licuerit.
units.tr: Although my treasury is exhausted and my revenues diminished, and I have contracted a great debt, do not permit me to be tempted to make good these losses by so profane a method, lest from your altar a coal be kindled in my throne and conscience, which could scarcely ever be put out.

units.la: Sed nec publici nominis liberatio (quod stultitiæ quorundam vel profusio obligavit) fiat unquam occasio exhauriendi Ecclesiam.
units.tr: But let not the deliverance of the public name (which the folly or profusion of some has bound us to) ever become an occasion for draining the Church.

units.la: Pace nos modo benedixeris, convalescet statim Respublica, Haud vero Ecclesia, his præsertim temporibus, ubi charitas multorum frigida est, & Religio parce sordida.
units.tr: If only you bless us with peace, the commonwealth will recover at once; the Church will not, especially in these times, when the charity of many is cold and religion is scarcely clean.

units.la: Tu Tibi & Ecclesiæ Tuæ ministrantibus, perpetuæ illa externa subsidia, quæ & voluntate piorum Donantium & Legum Iustitia debentur: & his gratiam tuam largiaris, quo hæc possint mereri, & recte uti in Tuam Gloriam, & pauperum levamen, ut induantur Iustitia Sacerdotes tui, & pauperes pane saturentur.
units.tr: You grant to yourself and to your ministering Church those perpetual external supports which are owed both by the will of pious donors and by the justice of the laws. Bestow your grace on these, that they may deserve them and use them rightly, to your glory and the relief of the poor, so that your priests may be clothed with righteousness and the poor may be satisfied with bread.

units.la: Sancta ne dentur porcis, nec canibus panis, circumeant potius Civitatem, fremant ut Canis & murmurent si non fuerint saturati.
units.tr: "Let not the holy things be given to dogs, nor bread to dogs" (cf. Matt. 7.6). Let them rather go about the city, snarling like dogs and grumbling if they are not satisfied.

units.la: Sacras illas offas & frustula, quæ nonnullorum violentia devoravit, nunquam detur illis vel posteris eorum, concoquere. Fiant hæc illis ut vinea Naboth Achabo, fel in ore ipsorum, putredo Nomini, tinea familiis, & conscientia-rum aculeus.
units.tr: Let those sacred morsels and scraps, which the violence of some has devoured, never be given to them or their descendants to digest. Let these things become to them what Naboth's vineyard was to Ahab: gall in their mouth, rot to their name, moth to their families, and a sting to their consciences.

units.la: Divide eorum linguas[?] & corda, qui sic invicem fœderantur contra Ecclesiam, & Regnum: ut insipientia eorum manifesta fiat omnibus, & ultra non proficiant.
units.tr: Divide the tongues and hearts of those who so league themselves together against the Church and the Kingdom, so that their folly may become plain to all and they may prosper no further.

units.la: Sed propitius esto Iustitiæ mcæ[?] (Domine) ut in misericordia Altissimi non commovear.
units.tr: But be merciful to my righteousness, O Lord, so that I may not be moved by the mercy of the Most High.

units.la: 15. De Suspicionibus & Probris in Re-gem jactis, quo Po- pulum in illum conci- tarent.
units.tr: 15. Concerning the suspicions and reproaches cast upon the King, by which they sought to stir up the people against him.

units.la: NI mea propriâ Innocentiâ, & Divinâ ope sublevarer, succumberem in hoc conflictu Malitiæ in me omni arte grassantis, dùm vel falsis Calumniis veritatem opprimere conatur, vel fictis Suspicionibus, id quod solidi defuerat, in hac improba causa supplere.
units.tr: Unless I were sustained by my own innocence and by divine help, I would succumb in this conflict with Malice, which rages against me with every art, while it tries either to crush the truth with false Calumnies, or, by invented Suspicions, to supply in this wicked cause what was lacking in solid proof.

units.la: Revera, quidquid contra me pessimum aperta hostilitate egerunt, præ his leve est: multò enim Coronas libentior, quàm Famam perderem: cùm Existimationem meam & Honorem etiam Regnis meis habeam potiora.
units.tr: Indeed, whatever they have done against me by open hostility is slight compared with these things. For I would rather lose my Crown than my Good Name, since I hold my reputation and honour to be more precious even than my kingdoms.

units.la: Hæc enim cum vita terminantur: illa inclitâ quadam Immortalitate super-sunt sunt mortuo. Cùm Bono Nomine suo, Principes velut aromatis conditi, æterno Posterorum Amori & Gratitudini consecrantur.
units.tr: The former end with life, but the latter survive the dead with a certain illustrious immortality. Princes, embalmed with their good name as with spices, are consecrated to the eternal love and gratitude of posterity.

units.la: Turpes istæ & falsæ Calumniæ, occultæ primò illis Fabricæ erant adversus Populi in Me amorem constructæ, ut cùm his priùs suffossis cuniculis (hostes Illis pariter ac Mihi) existimationem meam labefactassent, fides omnium in me & afsectus quasi (displosâ Machinâ) ster-nerentur.
units.tr: These foul and false Calumnies were at first secret devices built against the people's love for me, so that, by first digging mines (enemies alike to them and to me), they might weaken my reputation, and then the faith and affection of all toward me would be, as it were, laid low when the engine was sprung.

units.la: In quo tamen, Deo gratias, haud ita vehementer afficior Honoris mei proprii jacturâ, quam flagitio illo & gravi periculo quibus animæ populi mei objiciuntur, qui hac semel suspicionum suligine obcæcati, facilè præceps agentur in abrupta quæcunque & atrocia; ubi, tantum abest ut peccatum suum & periculum agnoscant, ut sint hîc ultrò Zelum suum imputaturi, dum illis interim exhibear ita dignus perire, ut ipsi ambiant meri[?], qui me perdant potissimum: tunc se Deum timere maximè arbitrantes, cum Regis omnem reverentiam excusserint.
units.tr: In this, however, thanks be to God, I am not so greatly affected by the loss of my own honour as by the shameful and grave danger to which the souls of my people are exposed. Once blinded by this soot of suspicions, they are easily driven headlong into any abrupt and atrocious deed. Far from recognising their sin and peril, they will even claim their zeal for themselves, while I am meanwhile shown to deserve to perish, so that they themselves seek out those who would chiefly destroy me. They think they fear God most when they have cast off all reverence for the King.

units.la: Nunquam tamen propter hæc (Laus Deo) iracundia mihi major, quàm miseratio suborta est: nec in me usque invalescebat ulla animi perturbatio, ut interdiceret pro illis vel cùm tenerrimo affectu precari, quos non sua malitia, sed honestus error in piam hanc ( ut putabant ) Rebellionem prodiderat.
units.tr: Yet on account of these things (thanks be to God) anger has never risen in me more than compassion, nor did any disturbance of mind ever grow so strong in me as to forbid me to pray for them with the tenderest feeling: those whom not their own malice but an honourable error had betrayed into this pious (as they thought) Rebellion.

units.la: Quâ enim eram in Illos charitate, credebam, eorum plerosque non in Me, sed in meos ( ut putabant) errores pugnâsse, nec eo animo ut perderent, sed ut emendarent. Spero, Dei misericordiam veniam huic errori dedisse, & eo usque bonum animum eorum acceptâsse simul & exaudivisse, ut, quemadmodum me hactenus conservavit, ita per hæc adversa præparaverit, ut illi melius in posterum serviam, & fiam populi mei commodis, quàm superius fueram, attentior.
units.tr: For from the charity I bore them, I believed that most of them were fighting not against me but against my errors (as they thought), and not with the intent to destroy but to amend. I hope that God's mercy has pardoned this error, and has accepted and heard their good intentions, so that, just as He has hitherto preserved me, so through these adversities He may have prepared me to serve them better in future, and to be more attentive to the welfare of my people than I was before.

units.la: Nec libentius ignosco in errorem seductis, qui sic Fidem suam præposterè per injurias declarant, quàm verè expeto & enitar in posterum, omni bene merendi occasione arrepta, injustas Suspiciones eximere, & quæ bene cogitârint, remunerare.
units.tr: Nor do I pardon more readily those led into error who thus wrongly declare their loyalty through injuries, than I truly desire, and will strive in future, to seize every opportunity of doing good, to remove unjust Suspicions, and to reward those who have thought well.

units.la: Nimis enim sum affectus mei in populum conscius, ut in Illorum de Me, mutuò, suspicionem adducar, nec ulla hostium malitia eo me solatio fraudabit, quod ex hac fiducia percipio. Nunquam ita indulgebo paucorum livori, ut, quod Illi exoptant maxime, omnes inter Obsequii desertores annumerem, quos piæ hæ fraudes deluserunt: quicquid prava quorundam Ambitio moliatur, haud maligniùs hinc subditos meos in universum æstimabo, qui errare forsan possunt, Hæretici esse non possunt.
units.tr: For I am too conscious of my affection for the people to be drawn, in return, into suspicion of them concerning me, and no malice of enemies will deprive me of the consolation I derive from this confidence. I will never so indulge the envy of a few that I count all as deserters of obedience, whom these pious frauds have deluded. Whatever the wicked ambition of some may attempt, I will not judge my subjects in general any more spitefully on that account: they may perhaps err, but they cannot be heretics.

units.la: Juxta mihi sunt acerbæ illæ subditis meis factæ injuriæ, ac quas ipse graves pertulerim, cùm seorsim bene habere non possumus: in hoc deterior eorum conditio, quod seductoribus istis nimis creduli & Mihi & Sibiipsis fiant injurii.
units.tr: Those injuries done to my subjects are as bitter to me as those I myself have suffered, since we cannot fare well apart. Their condition is worse in this, that they, too credulous of those seducers, become unjust both to me and to themselves.

units.la: Parum enim videtur Inimicorum malitiæ ut me reddant miserrimum, nisi id iis instrumentis efficiant, ut sit ipsa calamitate calamitosius, quod ab iis hæc demum perpetiar, quos felices esse maximè exopto, & deceptis serio illachrymor.
units.tr: It seems too little for my enemies' malice to make me most wretched, unless they achieve it by such means that I am made more miserable by the calamity itself: that I must suffer these things from those whom I most desire to be happy, and I weep sincerely for the deceived.

units.la: Hoc si Hostes mihi aperti & exteri fecissent, tolerari utique potuerat, haud verò perinde levia sunt à subditis meis propriis inflicta, quos à liberis meis proximè caros habeo, quibus ut tranquillitas reddatur, libenter Jonas forem, qui me in undas exponerem; nisi id satis prospicerem divulsis magis postea, & distractis eorum studiis (qui mihi pariter & illis hostes) tanquam toe[?] ventis contrariis, procellam calamitatum sævam multo potiùs quàm pacatam futuram.
units.tr: If open and foreign enemies had done this to me, it could certainly have been endured. But things inflicted by my own subjects, whom I hold dearest after my children, are by no means so light. For their tranquillity I would gladly be Jonah and cast myself into the waves, unless I foresaw clearly that, once their pursuits were torn apart and distracted (they who are enemies to me and to themselves alike), like contrary winds, the storm of calamities would be far fiercer than any calm.

units.la: Mihi quidem si optio daretur, multò malim Ruinæ populi obstare, quàm gaudere Imperio: cujus nunquam ita cupidus fui (licet jure mihi debiti) ut non potior esset longè subditorum fœlicitas, modo his unquam tanta esse possit, quæ tam improbis subditorum in Regem facinoribus comparari omninò mereatur.
units.tr: For my part, if the choice were given me, I would much rather stand in the way of the people's ruin than rejoice in rule. I was never so desirous of it (though it is due to me by right) that the happiness of my subjects was not far more important, provided it could ever be so great as to be deserved by such wicked crimes of subjects against the King.

units.la: Idem tamen malo omnes vitæ ærumnas, & multas mortes obire, quàm Justa mea Iura Dominii vel unquam cum pudore disfercre, vel cum infamiâ prodere: ut, vel sic gratam rem faciam, ambitioni, vel malitiam Hostium justificem, inter quam, & aliorum errores non inferius discrimen agnosco, quàm à Febre distat pestilentia; à prurigine Novitatis, lepra perfidiæ.
units.tr: Yet I would rather endure all the troubles of life and many deaths than either yield my just rights of dominion with shame, or betray them with infamy, so that I might thus gratify ambition or justify the malice of enemies. Between this and the errors of others I recognise no less difference than between fever and plague, or between the itch of novelty and the leprosy of treachery.

units.la: Quemadmodum verò mentientibus necessarium est benè reminisci, ita his non minùs, benè comminisci; ut ad diversas hominum Phantasias calumniæ suæ aptentur, & quod deest veritatis, numero saltem & specie suppleant.
units.tr: Just as liars must remember well, so they must no less invent well, so that their calumnies may be fitted to the varied fancies of men, and so that they may supply, at least in number and appearance, what is lacking in truth.

units.la: Plus mihi interim (Deo gratia) ad ferendum patientiæ, & ad ignoscendum charitatis, quàm est otii quo respondeam ad plurimas hasce calumnias, queis nonnulli me falsò resperserunt, & , nisi multo magis subditis meis satis factum cuperem, quàm meipsum vindicatum, minimè hanc voluptatem dedissem aliorum malitiæ, ut omninò, quid dixerint vel quid objecerint, me sollicitum viderent, aut memorem.
units.tr: Meanwhile I have (by God's grace) enough patience to bear and enough charity to forgive, but not enough leisure to answer the many calumnies with which some have falsely besmirched me. Unless I wished far more to satisfy my subjects than to clear myself, I would by no means have granted this pleasure to others' malice, that they should see me anxious about, or even mindful of, whatever they have said or objected.

units.la: Reliquissem eorum Authores, suâ olim Improbitate & Cauteriatis Conscientiis puniendos, quæ nigra illa & falsa quæ in me jecerunt Scandala satis ipsæ refellent & ulciscentur, atque id Orbi tandem perspicuum facient, juxta parùm verè excogitata, & indignissimè sparsa, quàm nulla curâ humanitatis (quid enim dicam Officii?) ab iis minime coërcita, quorum fides (credo) & existimatio, brevi futurum, ut apud ipsum hunc populum, eodem halitu nigrescat, ex eadem maledicentiæ fornace prodeunte, quam ita omnibus modis accenderunt, ut Famam meam & Honorem injecta pe-nitus absumerent.
units.tr: I would have left their authors to be punished by their own wickedness and cauterised consciences. Those black and false scandals which they have cast against me will refute and avenge themselves, and will at last make it plain to the world that they were devised with little truth and spread most unworthily, with no restraint of humanity (for what shall I call it, duty?). Those whose good faith (I believe) and reputation will soon, among this very people, grow black, breathing the same fumes that come from the same furnace of slander, which they have kindled in every way, so that, by casting it in, they might utterly consume my reputation and honour.

units.la: Magna mihi causa erat (fateor) suspicandi innocentiam meam, & accuratius in illam inquirendi, cum tot singularem pietatem professos, ita promptos in diversum à Me ire perspicerem: Id enim vulgi animos tam sinistra de Me, & causa Mea opinione imbuerat, ut vix fieri posse existimarent, ut quis Parti Mee adhæreret, & non à Deo simul discederet: immo & idem prorsus illis sonabat de Me bene loqui, & Deum blasphemare: adeo haec inter se invicem pugnare videbantur, in me Fides, & in Deum Religio.
units.tr: I had great reason (I admit) to suspect my own innocence and to inquire into it more carefully, when I saw so many who professed singular piety so readily going over to the opposite side from me. For this had so imbued the minds of the crowd with such sinister opinions about me and my cause that they thought it scarcely possible for anyone to adhere to my side without at the same time departing from God. Indeed, to speak well of me and to blaspheme God sounded exactly the same to them: so mutually opposed did these seem, faith in me and religion toward God.

units.la: Erant tamen (laus Deo) ex mea parte complures,docti pariter & pii, (idque multis parasangis ultra vulgarem illam Magnitudinem & mensuram scientiæ, quâ nonnulli ita gloriantur) quibus tàm integre probatur Victa[?] Causa, ut mecum pati potius vellent, quam in malis deferere.
units.tr: Yet there were (thanks be to God) on my side many, both learned and pious (and that many leagues beyond the common measure and extent of the knowledge in which some boast), to whom my cause was so thoroughly proved that they preferred to suffer with me rather than abandon me in misfortune.

units.la: Haud interim mirandum, si tot pii prætextus contra Me usurpati, homines alioqui non malos vehementer percellerent, & in partem adversam simul traherent: accedente præterea populari Concionatorum facundiâ, quibus nullum erat flagitium pro Deo mentiri, (vel quod ipsi Dei Causam appellare libuerat) diris omnibus devoventes, qui secum pariter devovere noluerant, & tam vehementer plaudentes Bono Fini, & in eum ita unicè intenti, ut nec, quàm illicita essent media, attenderent, nec in sceleris profundum (quod revera Finis erat præcipuus) omnino penetrarent.
units.tr: Nor is it surprising that so many pious pretexts, employed against me, greatly unsettled men who were otherwise not wicked and drew them to the opposite side, especially with the popular eloquence of the preachers added. To these no crime was forbidden in lying for God (or for what they had chosen to call the cause of God). They cursed with every dire curse those who refused to curse with them, and applauded so vehemently the good end, and were so intent upon it alone, that they neither considered how unlawful the means were nor penetrated at all into the depth of the wickedness (which was in truth the chief aim).

units.la: Homines imbecilli judicio, qui quod illis hic deest, clamore improbo, & fedulitate farciunt, quorum magna pars Religionis, Me & Meos infamare, ut, qui alias suam afferere non possent, nisi Meam tanquam falsam impugnarent.
units.tr: Weak-minded men, who fill with wicked clamour and busy effort what their judgement lacks, a large part of them aim to defame Religion, Me and Mine, since they could not assert their own unless they attacked mine as false.

units.la: Deo gratias habeo: quanquam domi forisque lacessitus fuerim, experimentum majus habeo Divinæ assistentiæ quâ firmus maneam Protestantium Doctrinæ quatenus in Ecclesia Anglicana agnoscitur, quàm (opinor) illis unquam suturum.
units.tr: I thank God that, although I have been assailed at home and abroad, I have greater proof of divine assistance in remaining firm in the Protestant Doctrine, insofar as it is acknowledged in the Anglican Church, than they (I think) will ever have.

units.la: Neque ulli me ita Crimini obnoxium scio (si eorum Sententiæ staretur) quàm quòd nimis videar pertinaciter Religioni illi adhærere, quæ summo Judicio & Fundamentis solidis in Scriptura & Antiquitate stabilita, haud me unquam vel probare, vel consentire permittet in illas plenas periculi, & inter se discordes Novitates, quas audax quorundam Ignorantia Mihi voluit, & Populo obtrudere.
units.tr: I know of no charge to which I am so liable (if their opinion were to stand) as that I seem too stubbornly to cling to religion, which, established by the highest judgement and on solid foundations in Scripture and Antiquity, will never allow me to approve of or consent to those dangerous and mutually discordant Novelties which the bold ignorance of some has tried to force on me and on the people.

units.la: Quæ cùm penitus adversentur exploratis fundamentis Veritatis & Ordinis, quæ multo illis Doctrina præstantiores, & puriori zelo accensi in Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ Confessione, & Constitutione sanciverant, quæque Superiora Parlamenta (in sedatis maximè temporibus & nullo Partium studio corruptis) crebro etiam firmaverant, in his semper (Deo juvante) perseverabo, ut qui hic credam maximè Primitivam Veritatem & Ordinem inesse.
units.tr: Since these utterly oppose the established foundations of Truth and Order, which, far superior in doctrine and kindled with a purer zeal, the Church of Anglican Confession and Constitution has sanctioned, and which the higher Parliaments (especially in calm times and uncorrupted by party spirit) have often confirmed, I shall always persevere in these (God helping), since I believe that the most primitive Truth and Order are present here.

units.la: Quod verò auxiliis quorundam è Religione Pontificia Subditorum meorum usus [?] fuerim pugnat nullo modo cum hac meâ Profesione, quod nonnulli perverse colligunt; ii praesertim, quibus minimè omnium pensi fuerat, qualium hominum operâ uterentur, vel omnino quid dicerent aut facerent, modo quâcunque ratione pollerent.
units.tr: That I have used the help of some of my subjects of the Popish religion is in no way inconsistent with this my Profession, as some perversely infer; especially those to whom it mattered least of all what kind of men they employed, or what they said or did at all, so long as they prevailed by any means.

units.la: Mirum sanè, homines eô (quo videri volunt isti) acumine, id non facile animadvertere, posse in re Religionis discrepare, eodem aliàs Officio, obsequio, Fidelitate conjunctos: Illam enim Deo ut Christiani, hanc mihi ut Regi in commune debent; cum diversæ Religionis professio haud magis quam diversa artificia, communem illam Relationem vel ad Parentes, vel Principes, tollat. Ecqua vero tanta uspiam Religionum Farrago, quàm in istorum Castris, & Satellitio? cum quod in me reprehendunt ipsi facile in seipsis admittunt, nullo habito Sectarum aut Opinionum discrimine.
units.tr: It is truly remarkable that men with that acuteness (in which they wish to be seen) do not readily notice that people may differ in religion while otherwise bound together by the same Office, obedience, Fidelity. For they owe the former to God as Christians, and the latter to me as King, in common; since a profession of a different religion removes that common relation no more than different trades remove it from parents or princes. Yet is there anywhere such a medley of religions as in their camps and retinues? For what they blame in me they readily admit in themselves, with no distinction made between Sects or Opinions.

units.la: Ingens vero probrum, & macula non eluenda, illos Ipsos Professantes (ita enim se haberi volunt) me Regem suum & Dominum, Professantem manifestum, ad necessaria adigere Papistarum auxilia, qui hîc suum duntaxat officium fecerunt, opem mihi ad Me tuendum ferentes, nec ego quicquam aliud, quàm, quòd licet Principibus in eadem conditione versantibus, ut subditorum cujusvis opeutantur.
units.tr: It is a great reproach, and a stain that cannot be washed away, that these very Professors (for so they wish to be called) should drive me, their King and Lord, a manifest Professor, to the necessary aid of the Papists. These men merely did their duty here, bringing help to defend me; and I did nothing other than what is allowed to princes in the same condition: to seek help from any of their subjects.

units.la: Dolet mihi vehementer, majori sensu officii fui tactos Papistas, quàm permultos ejusmodi Protestantes, qui mihi sanè videntur à Romanæ Ecclesiæ deterrimis, dogmata omnium deterrima hausisse? ita enim omninò fe gerunt.
units.tr: I grieve greatly that the Papists were moved by a greater sense of duty than so many Protestants of this kind, who seem to me to have drawn from the most wicked of the Roman Church the most wicked of all doctrines. For so they altogether behave.

units.la: Præposterus certe fuisset, & importunus conscientiæ scrupulus, & voluptátem proculdubio hostibus meis facturus, tunc, cum Illi mecum disputarent gladiis, cum ceteris meis subditis controverfias de Fide agitaffe; quorum non folùm auxiliis ut hominum, sed ut Christianorum precibus indigui.
units.tr: It would certainly have been a preposterous and troublesome scruple of conscience, and one that would undoubtedly have pleased my enemies, if, while they were disputing with me by the sword, I had been raising controversies about faith with my other subjects, whose prayers, as men and as Christians, I need, not merely their aid.

units.la: Clamor ille in Pravos Consiliarios aliud erat Commentum perutile, iis nimirum qui ægre admodum ferebant cujufquam alterius consilio, quàm suo obtemperari: qui ita valde fe finabant meliora consulere, ut, nec libertate eâ, quæ hominem decet, nedum eâ honorificentiâ quâ Princi-pem, paterentur accipere, cùm effent potiùs ejusmodi, quæ violenter insufa, necessario protinus absorbenda effent quàm velut salubris potio, quam lentè pitissando exhaurirem.
units.tr: That outcry against wicked counsellors was another very useful invention, namely for those who could hardly bear that anyone's advice should be followed rather than their own. They allowed themselves so greatly to advise better things that they would suffer neither the freedom which befits a man, much less the honour due to a Prince, to be accepted; for they were rather such that, forced in violently, they would have to be swallowed at once, rather than like a wholesome draught which I might drain by sipping slowly.

units.la: Haud me eximam vel ipsum, vel Confiliarios meos humanis erroribus: poterant quidem aliqua in deterius consuli, non tamen ita gravi incommodo, ut non fecundis & melioribus cogitatis reparari possent multo facilius, quàm illa valde insana & portentosa, quæ non cladem solum Regno & Ecclesiæ, sed excidium pene attulerunt.
units.tr: I shall not exempt either myself or my counsellors from human errors. Some things indeed could have been decided for the worse, yet not with so grave an inconvenience that they could not be repaired, with fertile and better thoughts, far more easily than those very mad and monstrous things which brought not only ruin to the Kingdom and Church, but almost destruction.

units.la: Exitus aliquando docebit Subditos meos, quòd etiamsi vel pessimus Confiliis, vel quæ pessimi omnium Consiliarii mihi audebant proponere, vel in quæ Ipse forsan propensior forem, obsequutus fuissem, haud ita celeriter in Tribus Regnis Florentissimis Ecclesiam pariter & Rempublicam in illud Chaos confusionum & ærumnarum Gehennam (quod nonnullorum consiliis effectum est) conscii unquam potuisse: è quibus nec jam possunt, vel certè nolunt quanquàm viribus ad id satis pollentes, Me aut Subditos meos redimere.
units.tr: Time will one day teach my subjects that even if I had yielded to the worst counsels, or to those which the worst of all counsellors dared to propose, or to those toward which I myself might perhaps have been more inclined, the Church and the Commonwealth would not so quickly have been plunged, in the three most flourishing kingdoms, into that chaos of confusions and miseries, a Gehenna (as has been brought about by the counsels of some). From this they now neither can nor, at any rate, will rescue me or my subjects, though strong enough to do so.

units.la: Nemo unquam libentiùs querelam instituit, quàm ego cupidus eram corrigendi, quod Rationi meæ apparuit dictum vel consultum perperam: quod quidem me fecisse putabam, atque id paulò prolixius quàm modesti homines exspectabant, quibus molestum erat, me nimio in subditos[?] Zelo ita facilè in meipsum extitisse injurium.
units.tr: No one ever made a complaint more willingly than I was eager to correct whatever my reason showed had been said or advised amiss; which I thought I had done somewhat more lengthily than modest men expected, who were troubled that I, through excessive zeal toward my subjects, had so readily become injurious to myself.

units.la: Sed illa vindictæ cupido insatiabilis, quâ in Me simul & Aulam, & Clerum Meum ruebant nonnulli, lusit penitus & fraudavit Ecclesiam pariter & Rempublicam usu omni eorum & beneficio, quæ à Me concessa vel revocata. Quin nec Ipsis cessit admodùm fœliciter, qui (nunc Zelo licet persequutores) nuper suas perpessiones apud vulgus jactabant, quarum omnium solatiis & præmiis destituuntur. Quas quidem si verè passi suissent, humilitas Christiana haud tanta duceret, ut non mallet vel nunquam succurri, quàm eo modo vindicari, ut periret sibi Christianæ patientiæ corona, quæ humilibus afflictis præparatur.
units.tr: But that insatiable desire for revenge, by which some rushed against me together with my Court and my Clergy, mocked and cheated the Church and the Commonwealth alike of all the use and benefit of those things granted or revoked by me. Nor did it turn out very happily even for those who, though now persecutors out of zeal, lately boasted to the common people of their sufferings, of which they are deprived of all comforts and rewards. If they had truly suffered them, Christian humility would not think it so great a thing that it would not rather wish never to be helped than to be avenged in such a way that the crown of Christian patience, which is prepared for humble sufferers, should perish for them.

units.la: Aliud jam porrò artificium, quo suffurari mihi Populi affectus, & ad se pellicere volebant, erat Libertatis ostentatio & strepitus: cujus haud naturâ magis avidi homines, quàm ferendo impares, sic eo sensu vulgari accipiatur Libertas, ut sit, id prorsus facere, quod cuique libuerit.
units.tr: Another trick, by which they wanted to steal the affections of the people and draw them to themselves, was the display and clamour of Liberty. Men are no more eager for it by nature than they are unable to bear it, when Liberty is taken in that vulgar sense: to do absolutely whatever one pleases.

units.la: Sin verò ea fit Libertas sanctissima, velle homines quod debent, & quod sic velint, facere, prout Rationi, Legibus, Religioni consentaneum, haud invideo subditis meis
units.tr: But if, on the other hand, it is the most holy Liberty, to wish to do what men ought, and to do it because they so wish, as is consistent with reason, laws and religion, I do not begrudge my subjects that liberty.

units.la: [The leftover text runs into the catchword line: the final word "eam" is the catchword, not body text.] eam Libertatem, quâ nec Ipse ampliore frui postulo, nedum aliorum opprimere[?]. Neque reverà credendum est, Proceres illos, cæterosquë (qui in Partibus meis erant) splendidis plurimos Familiis ita prodigos suæ Libertatis fuisse, ut servitutem sibi & Posteris, fortunis suis & sanguine procuratam voluerint.
units.tr: That Liberty, which I myself do not demand to enjoy in any greater measure, much less to use to oppress others. Nor indeed must it be believed that those nobles, and the rest who were on my side (many of them from splendid families), were so lavish of their liberty as to have wanted slavery procured for themselves and their posterity by their fortunes and blood.

units.la: Quod ad Civiles Immunitates attinet, nemo (pauculis tantum exceptis, obstinatis ambitiosa sua & avara consilia quaquaversum agere & ferre per ruinas Ecclefiæ, Status, Principis, Procerum Populi) vel majorem Libertatem optaret, quàm quæ à Lege[?] permittitur: cuius Iustos limites Boni Viri Ornamento sibi ducunt & Præsidio, cæteri Compedes appellant, & Gravamina.
units.tr: As for civil immunities, no one (except a few obstinate men who pursue their ambitious and avaricious schemes in every direction, through the ruin of Church, State, Prince, nobles and people) would wish for greater liberty than that which is permitted by Law. Good men regard its just limits as an ornament and a protection to themselves, while others call them fetters and grievances.

units.la: Haud interim æquum censendum est, ut quis Legis beneficia & præmia exspectet, illam Normam sibi, & Moderatricem aspernatus; merito enim fraudatur Patrocinio Legis, qui dissolutam anhelat Libertatem.
units.tr: Nor is it fair to think that anyone should expect the benefits and rewards of the Law, having scorned it as his rule and moderator; for he is rightly deprived of the protection of the Law who longs for a loose liberty.

units.la: Tempus melius erudiet Subditos Meos, illos optimè veram Libertatem conservare,qui sibi minimam licentiam vel contra Leges, vel extra illas indulgent.
units.tr: Time will better teach my subjects to preserve true liberty, which they keep best who indulge themselves the least licence, either against the Laws or outside them.

units.la: Sentient aliquando damno suo, quicquid simulant hi homines) omnino fieri ncn[?] posse, ut ullo molli & tenero affectu Concivium libertatem prosequantur, qui me Regem suum ausi sunt tanta asperitate coercere, contra omnes Divinas & Humanas Leges: qui tamen vel sic perire malim, quàm apud illos plangere, quibus nil aā consummandum suum Triumphum deest, quàm ut sic flebili voce accinatur.
units.tr: They will one day feel to their cost (whatever these men pretend) that it is altogether impossible for them to pursue the liberty of their fellow citizens with any gentle and tender affection, since they have dared to coerce their King with such harshness, against all divine and human laws. Yet I would rather perish thus than lament among those for whom nothing remains to complete their Triumph except that it be sung in such a mournful voice.

units.la: Quod ad conscientias verè teneras attinet (quæ ex sua humilitate & lenitate æstimantur, non ex improba illa & sedula arrogantiâ, quâ ovum quodque diversæ Opinionis in Schisma protinùs & Factionem extruditur) sæpè antea profeffusfum, me id minime expetere, ut Leges meæ, aut Sceptrum ullam Dei conscientiarum Domini prærogativam invaderent: cum id interim constet, itaà Deo ipso homines astringi, utprœcipiantur Subditi e/fe conscientiæ Causa, nulla aliâ licentiâ indultâ in quamcunque constitutam Legem committendi, nisi eo duntaxat animo, ut sint pœnas annexas subituri potius, quàm quicquam Publicæ Pacis perturbetur.
units.tr: As for consciences that are truly tender (which are judged by their own humility and gentleness, not by that shameless and busy arrogance by which every egg of a differing opinion is straightway hatched into schism and faction), I have often declared before now that I by no means desire my laws or my sceptre to invade any prerogative of God, the Lord of consciences. Yet it is clear that men are bound by God himself to be ordered to be subjects for conscience's sake, with no licence granted to break any law whatsoever, except only with the intention of being ready to undergo the penalties attached, rather than that anything of the public peace be disturbed.

units.la: Omnino sic fe res habet. Aliis rerum Novarum cupiditas, aliis, qui afflictæ suæ fortunæ mederi aut importunæ Ambitioni satisfacere volebant, utriusque in Pace desperatio (cùm Divinæ Providentiæ non minùs quàm meritis suis dissiderent.) occultæ quidem fuerunt sed præcipuæ Causæ, quæ has Turbas Civiles concitarunt, in quibus, credulum populum eousque perpulerant, ut multi rem lautam suam (quam pacatis Temporibus sub meo regimine & comparabant facile, & fœliciter gaudebant) hîc maximam partem dissiparent, me interim probris illis exposito, summâ omnium virulentiâ excogitatis, queis Majestas Regia maximè lædeRetur, & ingrati Populi infolentia accresceret.
units.tr: It is entirely so. Some, through a lust for revolution; others, who wished to remedy their afflicted fortunes or satisfy their unseasonable ambition, and who were in despair of peace (since they were at odds no less with the providence of God than with their own deserts): these, though hidden, were the principal causes that stirred up these civil disturbances. By them the credulous populace was driven so far that many of them squandered, here, for the most part, their own comfortable wealth (which in peaceful times under my rule they had easily acquired and happily enjoyed), while meanwhile I was exposed to those reproaches, devised with the utmost virulence, by which the majesty of the king would be most injured, and the insolence of an ungrateful people would be increased.

units.la: Quod ad Honorem meum spectat: persuasum habeo quôd (quemadmodum jam purus & innocens horum omnium quæ calumniantur, coram Deo appareo ita &) famæ mea aliquando instar solis (postquam noctis parumper & tenebrarum licentiâ, Vespertiliones isti & Striges abusi fuerint) exoritura fit denuò, & ascensura in eum splendorem, quem ferales istæ volucres & intueri doleant, & sustinere non posint. Nulli enim tantâ cluent gloriâ Principes, quàm quos Deus in ærumnarum chalybe per injurias subditorum explorari permisit.
units.tr: As for my honour: I am persuaded that, just as I now appear before God pure and innocent of all these things with which I am slandered, so my fame will at some time rise again like the sun (after night and darkness have been abused for a little while by these bats and screech-owls), and will ascend to that splendour which those deadly birds grieve to behold and cannot endure. For no princes are rendered so famous as those whom God has allowed to be tested in the furnace of afflictions through the injuries of their subjects.

units.la: Et quis scit, an Justus Ille & misericors Deus bonum mihi aliquando redditurus sit, propter falsas eorum & acerbas maledicentias, qui loquuntur quæ optant potiùs, quàm quæ vel credunt vel sciunt.
units.tr: And who knows whether that just and merciful God will at some time repay me with good, on account of their false and bitter slanders, who speak what they wish rather than what they either believe or know?

units.la: Sed nec isti spurci adeo & infames Libelli (velut Ignis in magna conflagratione susque deque volitantes, ut omnia inflamment) mihi magis in probrum quam ipsis cedent, qui eximiam pietatem professi, ita parum se memores ostendunt vel in Deum vel in Me, officii, ut nec tantillum curaverint Majestatem Regis sui vindicare ab eorum calumniis, qui & Dei praecepto & Angelorum exemplo contrarii, dignitates probris lacessunt, & maledicti notam iis impingunt qui Deorum nomine honorantur.
units.tr: But neither will these foul and infamous libels (flying about like fire in a great conflagration, upside down, so that they set everything alight) bring more disgrace upon me than upon themselves, who, professing exceptional piety, show themselves so little mindful of their duty either towards God or towards me that they have not cared in the slightest to vindicate the majesty of their king from the calumnies of those men who, contrary both to the precept of God and to the example of the angels, assail dignities with reproaches and fix the stain of slander on those who are honoured with the name of gods.

units.la: At haud mirum, si, qui Deum non metuant, nec Regem suum revereantur.
units.tr: But it is no wonder, if those who do not fear God do not revere their king.

units.la: Facilè enim contemnent has Umbras Dei, & Imagines, qui Supremæ Illius & Adorandæ Majestatis reverentiam exuerint, cui collata omnis hominum & Angelorum gloria sordes duntaxat & tenebrae: qui tamen (tanto licet intervallo disjunctis) eos Regibus Divinæ Authoritatis & Sacrosanctæ Potestatis Characteras impressit, qui sine gravi peccato obliterari non possunt. Quicquid nigri hic veli oppositerint, non abscondetur lumen vultus mei, dum mihi Deus cor dederit ad frequenter & humiliter cum illo versandum, à quo vera omnis Gloria & Majestas derivatur.
units.tr: For they will easily scorn these shadows and images of God, those who have cast off reverence for that Supreme and Adorable Majesty, compared with which all the glory of men and angels is only filth and darkness. Yet He has impressed on those He has set as kings the marks of Divine Authority and sacred Power, which cannot be erased without grave sin, though they are separated by so great an interval. Whatever dark veil they may have placed over it, the light of my countenance will not be hidden, as long as God gives me a heart to dwell frequently and humbly with Him, from whom all true glory and majesty is derived.

units.la: Deus Tu scis Improperium meum, & consusionem meam, in conspectu tuo sunt omnes qui tri-bulant Me,
units.tr: O God, thou knowest my reproach and my shame; all who trouble me are before thee.

units.la: Anima mea est in medio Leonum inter filios hominum qui flammis exurunt, quorum dentes lanceæ, & sagittæ, & lingua eorum gladius acutus.
units.tr: My soul is among lions, among the sons of men, who burn with flames, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and whose tongue is a sharp sword.

units.la: Tota die exprobrabant mihi Inimici mei, & insanientes in Me adversum Me jurabant.
units.tr: All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who were raging against me swore against me.

units.la: Filii hominum usque quo (Domine) gloriam meam ad ignominiam? quousque diligent vanitatem, & quærent mendacium?
units.tr: O sons of men, how long (Lord) will you turn my glory into shame? How long will you love vanity and seek after lies?

units.la: Audisti opprobria Inimicorum undique. Ne taceas, ne quando dicat Inimicus meus prævalui adversus eum, & gloriam meam in pulverem deducat.
units.tr: Thou hast heard the reproaches of my enemies on every side. Do not be silent, lest my enemy say, I have prevailed against him, and bring my glory down to the dust.

units.la: [illegible, ~10 letters] Tu Domine perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendacium, virum sanguinum, & dolosum abomi-naberis.
units.tr: [illegible] Thou, O Lord, wilt destroy all who speak lies; the bloody and deceitful man thou wilt abhor.

units.la: Educ quasi lumen Iustitiam meam, & Innocentiam meam tanquam meridiem.
units.tr: Bring forth my righteousness as the light, and my innocence as the noonday.

units.la: Fac ut nec silens prodam' Innocentiam meam, nec patientiam iratus: ut servatoris mei exemplo maledictis appetitus non maledicam, & execrationibus devotus non contra referam.
units.tr: Grant that I neither betray my innocence by silence, nor my patience by anger: that, after the example of my Saviour, I, who was assailed with reproaches, may not revile, and, devoted to curses, may not retort.

units.la: Tu qui linguam illam virulentam Shimei impunè[?] illi esse non permisisti, cum tua in Davidem judicia viderentur haec probra vera facere, câ Me donec gratiâ, ut apud Misericordiam tuam intercedam pro Inimicis meis, ne dentur his linguis dolosis cai bones[?] juniperorum inflammati à Gehenna. Sint preces meæ & patientia velut aqua offusa quâ mitescant vel extinguantur linguæ Igneæ, quæ à Gehenna jam diu accendi videntur, & inter malitiosas illas flammas æstuare.
units.tr: Thou who didst not permit that venomous tongue of Shimei to go unpunished, when, in thy judgments against David, those reproaches seemed to be true, grant me grace now, that I may intercede before thy mercy for my enemies, lest these deceitful tongues be given the coals of juniper kindled from Gehenna. Let my prayers and my patience be like water poured over them, by which those fiery tongues, which seem to have been kindled from Gehenna for a long time now, may be softened or extinguished, and may seethe amid those malicious flames.

units.la: Des eorum maledicta benefaciendo[?] vel refellere omnino, vel silentium imponere. Ne gaudeant fructu labiorum suorum, sed Orationis meæ potius pœnitentiam illis & veniam precantis.
units.tr: Grant that they either wholly refute their slanders by doing good, or impose silence upon them. Let them not rejoice in the fruit of their lips, but rather let my prayer seek repentance and pardon for them.

units.la: Instrue me Davidis patientiâ & pietate Hezekiæ, ut per eorum virulentiam misericordiam tuam perspiciam & in eorum peccato Iustitiam.
units.tr: Teach me the patience and piety of David and of Hezekiah, so that through their virulence I may perceive thy mercy, and in their sin thy justice.

units.la: Ille Turbidæ Shebæ conciones, illa Rabshekah opprobria, & execratio Shimei, preces meas humiles lacessant, & repetitas Tuas in Me benedictiones.
units.tr: Let those seditious sermons of Sheba, those reproaches of Rabshakeh, and the curse of Shimei, provoke my humble prayers, and thy repeated blessings upon me.

units.la: Licet illi maledicant, tu benedicas, & benedictus ero[?], & benedictio fiam populo meo.
units.tr: Though they curse, do thou bless; and I shall be blessed, and I shall become a blessing to my people.

units.la: Et Lapis quem reprobaverunt ædificantes, factus erit in Caput Anguli.
units.tr: And the stone which the builders rejected will be made the head of the corner.

units.la: Prospice me de excelso Sancto tuo, & libera me ab iis qui me absorbere cupiunt.
units.tr: Look down upon me from thy holy height, and deliver me from those who long to swallow me up.

units.la: Absconde me in conspectu tuo à superbia hominum malorum, & à contradictione linguarum serva me.
units.tr: Hide me in thy sight from the pride of evil men, and keep me from the contradiction of tongues.

units.la: 16. De Decreto Parla- mentario contra Litur- giam Anglicanam, seu Librum Precum Solennium.
units.tr: 16. On the Parliamentary Decree against the English Liturgy, or the Book of Solemn Prayers.

units.la: Familiare hoc cunctis fere Novitatibus, ut Reformationis Nomine in Ecclesia & Statu, inducantur, idque ab iis plerumque, qui famam apud vulgus captantes pietatis & ingenii singularis, irrita omnia facere conantur, quae rectissimè & prudentissimè constituta.
units.tr: Nearly all novelties share this familiar trait: they are introduced in the name of Reformation, in both Church and State. This is usually done by men who, seeking a reputation for piety and singular talent among the common people, try to nullify everything that was established most rightly and most wisely.

units.la: Ita ægrè impetratur à Novatorum superbia, ut in superioribus se seculis quidquam omninò prudentiæ aut pietatis agnoscant.
units.tr: So reluctantly does the pride of the innovators allow that anything of prudence or piety existed in earlier ages.

units.la: Quoniam vero Preces & Cultus Dei Publicus magna Religionis momenta sunt, ut, quibus Animæ hominum cum Divina Majestate propiore commercio fruuntur, haud alias gratiosius se jactant Populo quàm id serio monentes, Deum malè in hac parte coli.
units.tr: Since public prayers and the public worship of God are matters of great weight in religion, because through them men's souls enjoy closer fellowship with the Divine Majesty, they boast of nothing more gratifying to the people than seriously warning that God is ill worshipped in this respect.

units.la: Hinc Publica Liturgia & Solennes Precum Formulæ non corrigendæ solum ( si quæ, liberâ priùs & publicâ consultatione habitâ, vel in re, vel modo minùs commodè habere viderentur, cui sane haud quaquam repugnâssem ) sed antiquanda penitus & abolenda, & post plurima demum ludibria in Librum ipsum & Libro utentes, prout Conscientia & Leges exigebant, ad extremum Decreto crucifiguntur, ut iis nimirum gratum fiat, qui extemporanea sua facultate & divite vena gloriantur; vel iis saltem, qui malè sibi conscii perfunctoriè nimis in hac parte egisse, expiatam jam sibi hanc culpam ducerent: illius convitio, quasi litera mortua effet, merito repudianda, ut sic Corda sua mortua melius excusent.
units.tr: Hence the public liturgy and the solemn forms of prayer are not merely to be corrected (if any of them, after free and public consultation, seemed less suitable in content or in manner, a point to which I would by no means have objected), but are to be utterly antiquated and abolished. After very many mockeries aimed at the Book itself and at those who use it, as conscience and the laws demanded, it is at last crucified by decree. This pleases those who glory in their extemporary faculty and rich vein, or at least those who, conscious of their own fault, had acted too perfunctorily in this matter and now reckon this fault expiated. Under the reproach that the Liturgy is a dead letter, it is rightly rejected, so that they may better excuse their dead hearts.

units.la: Quod ad Argumentum hujus Libri: Satis jam diù docti & cordati homines ab eorum cavillis & stricturis vindicârunt, quorum magna pars pietatis in hoc sita est, ut profanè illum criminentur, Papisti, inprimis, & Superstitionis nomine: cùm proculdubiò Liturgia ad Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ Doctrinam exactè formata fuerit, eam scilicet, quæ ab omnibus Reformatis Ecclesiis sana maximè & Orthodoxa agnoscitur.
units.tr: As for the content of this Book, learned and sensible men have long since sufficiently defended it against their cavils and censures. A large part of their piety consists in accusing it of profanity, the Papists above all, and in the name of superstition. Yet the Liturgy was without doubt framed exactly in accordance with the doctrine of the Church of England, namely that doctrine which all the Reformed Churches acknowledge as most sound and orthodox.

units.la: Quod vero ad certas & præscriptas pre-
units.tr: As for the certain and prescribed

units.la: cum Formulas: haud dubitandum est, quin verba sana, & Nota, & intellectui hominum accommodata, cum facillime in corda recipiantur, tum affectus prudenter fervidos, sint excitare & promovere aptissima.
units.tr: forms: there is no doubt that sound words, known and adapted to the understanding of men, are most easily received into the heart, and are therefore most apt to arouse and promote affections that are prudently fervent.

units.la: Neque ullam omninò causam video, cur fastidium magis daret Christianis bene formata & composita (qualem hanc existimo) Liturgia, quâm res aliæ complurimæ, quibus ob perpetuam consuetudinem, nilde[?] fructu aut excellentia decedit: vel, quâ tandem ratione suadeatur Christiano, ut aspernetur has easdem Precum Formulas, vel interdici sibi hunc morem æquum censeat, qui eundem semper Deum precatur, in eundem Servatorem credit, veritates easdem profitetur, eandem legit Scripturam, eisdem obligatur, & eosdem plerunque in se defectus, (tam externos quàm internos) toti scilicet Ecclesiæ communes, agnoscit.
units.tr: Nor do I see any cause at all why a liturgy well formed and composed (as I judge this one to be) should cause Christians more distaste than many other things which, through constant custom, lose nothing of their fruit or excellence. Or on what reasoning could it be urged on a Christian that he should spurn these same forms of prayer? Or how could it be deemed fair to forbid this custom to one who always prays to the same God, believes in the same Saviour, professes the same truths, reads the same Scripture, is bound by the same obligations, and acknowledges in himself the same defects, both external and internal, which are of course common to the whole Church?

units.la: Rogo, cur non liceat perinde praecognitum habere quid precamur, ac Illum quem precamur? cur non æque verba, ac sensum? Cum eadem omnes expectimus, quid obstat quo minus iisdem ipsis voculis? certe panis noster quotidianus haud ideo sapit deterius, quod quotidie (ut precamur) manducatur. Est tamen genus quoddam hominum ita impatiens coarctari, vel in quacunque precatione Doni sui usu, id est propria inventione interdici, ut ipsâ etiam Oratione Dominica non solùm (quod plerique) raro admodum utantur, sed eam penitus repudient & aspernentur, cujus id quoque grande crimen est, quod fit praescriptum quoddam & Archetypon omnium Liturgiarum in Christiana Ecclesia.
units.tr: I ask, why should it not be permitted to know beforehand what we pray for, just as we know whom we pray to? Why should the words not be as known as the sense? Since we all look for the same things, what stands in the way of using the very same little words? Surely our daily bread does not taste the worse because it is eaten every day, as we pray for it to be. Yet there is a certain kind of men so impatient of being confined, or of being forbidden to use their own gift in any prayer, that is, their own invention, that not only do most of them use the Lord's Prayer very rarely, but they utterly reject and scorn it. Its great crime, in their eyes, is that it is a prescribed form and the archetype of all liturgies in the Christian Church.

units.la: Equidem semper arbitrabar, superbam hanc ingenii ostentationem, & affectatam verborum redundantiam in Precibus Publicis, vel in Sacris Officiis quibufcunque, majus multo in fe crimen habere, quàm quod Frigus appellant, & sterilitatem. Porrò, in his Novationibus haud rarius, quàm in Perpetuae Formae usu contingit, ut eâdem prorsus supinitate & oscitantiâ (animi saltem) peragantur, cum, si quid fit ejusmodi, cordi potiùs quàm verbis fit imputandum.
units.tr: Indeed, I have always thought that this proud display of talent, and this affected redundancy of words in public prayers or in any sacred offices whatever, is a far greater fault than what they call coldness and barrenness. Moreover, in these novelties it happens no less often than in the use of a fixed form that things are performed with exactly the same listlessness and drowsiness, at least of mind. Yet if anything of this kind happens, it should be imputed to the heart rather than to the words.

units.la: Alii, oratione multiplici, & extemporaneâ se effusione jactantes, formam tantum habent pietatis, alii, intra certas verborum & consuetas formulas, vim optimè illius, & fervorem retinent. Neque est Deus magis diversitatis Deus, quam constantiæ; nec omninò majus periculum est, ne consuetâ Precum Formula [?] obstipetur & torpeat Spiritus precum & Devotionis, quàm, ne confusa & immeditata varietas distrahat illum penitus, vel excludat.
units.tr: Some, boasting of a manifold speech and an extemporary outpouring, have only the form of piety. Others, within certain words and customary formulas, preserve its power and fervour very well. God is no more the God of variety than of constancy. Nor is there any greater danger that the spirit of prayer and devotion be dulled and benumbed by a customary form of prayer than that a confused and unpremeditated variety should tear it apart utterly or exclude it.

units.la: Quamquam verò haud repugnem exerceri à Ministris dona sua, etiam in publico, dum id graviter fiat & humiliter, & eâ quâ decet prudentia, quo, & sua forsan magis & Populi studia excitari possint, & in præsens negotium præparari; nulla suadet propterea necessitas, ut quantacunque visingenii, & eximiæ dotes privatorum hominum, pellant penitus ab Ecclesia, vel illi fraude eripiant conjunctas facultates & confspirantia dona tot Doctrinæ & pietatis laude præstantium, quales erant, qui nostram illam Formam Publicam composuerunt, qui sanè merito existimentur ampliori fuisse Gratiâ & Donis instructi, quò maturâ deliberatione, & consociatis consiliis, eas Formas precum componerent, quæ communibus Ecclesiæ indigentiis optimè possent competere, tum Auditorum intellectus informare, & eam denique fiduciam & fervidam mentis intentionem (vitam scilicet Precum & Animam, verumque Illum quem sic crebro jactant Spiritum) fœlicius multo excitare, quàm sperandum sit ab uno homine, quantácunque seorsim facultate pollenti. Quæ, quanta sit in istorum plærisque (etiam in quo se ostentant maximè) illa passim eorum affectationes, illa inania, insulsa, rustica, confusa, illud exsangue, putidum, obscurum, vanæ & ridiculæ repetitiones, sensu vacuæ expressiones, & sæpè etiam blasphemiæ, tædio denique omnia, & prolixitate immensa, satis omnibus demonstrant, nisi qui eodem Pharisaismo gloriantur.
units.tr: Although I would by no means object that ministers exercise their gifts, even in public, provided it is done gravely and humbly and with the prudence that befits it, whereby perhaps both their own zeal and the people's may be stirred up and prepared for the business at hand, no necessity therefore urges that, however great the talent and outstanding gifts of private men, they should be driven entirely from the Church, or be robbed by stealth of the combined faculties and harmonious gifts of so many men eminent for doctrine and piety. Such were those who composed our public Form, who are rightly thought to have been endowed with greater grace and gifts, so that by mature deliberation and united counsel they might compose forms of prayer that could best suit the common needs of the Church, inform the understanding of the hearers, and, far more happily than can be hoped from one man however powerful in his own faculty, stir up that trust and fervent intention of mind (namely the life and soul of prayer, and that true Spirit which they so often boast of). What great affectations are found everywhere in most of these men, even in those things in which they most display themselves: those inanities, insipidities, rusticities, confusions, that bloodlessness, foulness, obscurity, vain and ridiculous repetitions, expressions empty of sense, and often even blasphemies, and in short tedium and immense prolixity. All of this sufficiently shows everyone, except those who glory in the same Pharisaism.

units.la: In quo frontem eorum demiror, & cœcam sui adulationem, haud pudere, hoc modo agentes in rebus Sacris coram Deo & mundo tam ridiculos confpici, ne dicam prophanos.
units.tr: At this I marvel at their brazenness and blind self-flattery, that they are not ashamed, acting in this way in sacred matters, to appear before God and the world so ridiculous, not to say profane.

units.la: Nec revera vitari potest, quin, in solennibus & crebris officiis (quales sunt Sacramentales Celebrationes, quæ eodem semper modo fiunt) vel suas Formas peculiares perpetuò sint usurpaturi (quas certè, haud tàm sanas futuras credibile est, & naturam officii complectentes, quàm has in publicum usum compositas) vel ut singulis vicibus varietur, cùm argumentum semper sit idem: in quo sanè sperari non debet (sint quantumvis aliàs instructissimi) ut non aliquid saltem desideretur in gravitate, ordine, perfectione, quæ in hujusmodi Officiis requiritur, quæ hoc tandem modo celebrata fiunt omnium Ministrorum erroribus, tum infirmitatibus plærunque & perturbationibus, tum judicii & eloquentiæ mancamentis obnoxia.
units.tr: Nor indeed can it be avoided that, in solemn and frequent offices (such as the sacramental celebrations, which are always performed in the same way), they will either always be using their own peculiar forms (which surely are not believed to be so sound, nor to embrace the nature of the office, as those composed for public use), or else they will vary them on each occasion although the subject is always the same. In this one should not hope (however well equipped they are otherwise) that something will not be lacking in the gravity, order and perfection required in such offices. Celebrated in this way, these offices are liable to the errors of all ministers, to their infirmities and disturbances, and to deficiencies of judgement and eloquence.

units.la: Quæ incommoda necessarió fequuntura diversos Celebrandi modos, cùm vehementer ferió perpenderet sapientia & pietas Antiquarum Ecclesiarum, occafionem hinc arripuerunt (quâ mederentur huic malo) instituendi perpetuas Liturgias, easque publicè priùs componendas.
units.tr: Since the wisdom and piety of the ancient Churches weighed seriously the inconveniences that necessarily follow from diverse ways of celebrating, they seized the occasion to remedy this evil by instituting fixed liturgies, to be composed publicly beforehand.

units.la: Quarum defectum aliquando sentiet (credo) hæc Ecclesia, cùm effrenis in posterum ignorantiæ, & imbecillium ingeniorum præsidentiæ fructus indies calamitosi, in omne genus erroribus, consusionibus, Schismatis, & alienis charitate diffidiis, (quæ jam nimis malo nostro experti fuimus) magis magisque detegentur.
units.tr: This Church, I believe, will one day feel the lack of them, when the fruits of unbridled ignorance and the rule of feeble minds, daily more calamitous, are increasingly revealed in every kind of error, confusion and schism, and in divisions alien to charity. We have already experienced these too much to our harm.

units.la: Sin vero ita obstinati sint, (ne omninò nil agere videantur) has suas Novitates invehere, quas & Lex & Ratio & Religio prohibet, (saltim ita per vim obtrudi, ut Liturgia publica extrudatur) nullo tamen colore excusatur iniquissima horum hominum severitas, qui (cum Ipsi non ita pridem, pars maxima subsignarent, usurparent quoque hunc Librum, & asserent, vel, qui id recusarant, vehementer in Legum & Episcoporum truculentiam inveherentur, qui libertatem conscientiarum hac in parte negabant) ita jam derepente alii facti sunt, ut non solum Liturgiam in Directorium commutaverint, quasi subsidiis inventionis egeret Spiritus, expressione utcunque non necessariâ, vel, quasi non æquè angustaretur præstitutâ[?] & stata materiâ, quam intra certas verborum formas inclusus, ita facilè vulgo imponitur) sed cà porro severitate hîc agant, ut nec usum Liturgiæ cuivis amplius permittant, licet utrinque obligati, pietate in Deum, * & in Leges obsequio.
units.tr: But if they are so obstinate that (lest they seem to accomplish nothing) they introduce these novelties of theirs, which law, reason and religion forbid, and at least force them through by violence so that the public liturgy is thrust out, still no pretext excuses the most unjust severity of these men. Not long ago most of them had subscribed to it, used this Book too, and asserted it; or, if they had refused, they inveighed vehemently against the harshness of the laws and bishops, who denied liberty of conscience in this matter. Yet now they have suddenly become so changed that they have not only turned the Liturgy into a Directory, as if the Spirit needed aids of invention, in some expression however unnecessary, or as if a fixed and settled matter were not equally narrow (enclosed within certain forms of words, it is so easily imposed on the crowd). They also act here with such severity that they no longer permit anyone the use of the Liturgy at all, although they are bound on both sides, by piety towards God and by obedience to the laws.

units.la: Unde constat nullos magis Tyrannidem moliri nec rigidiùs ab aliis exacturos ut illicitis suis Novationibus obtemperent, quàm, qui Ipsi ( qua erant superbia ) ad parendum legitimæ sanctitis[?] minime omnium fuerunt proclives ; qui enim suæ[?] haud ita dudum ut indulgeretur licentiæ, libertatem Conscientiæ crepabant, hanc mihi, & meis Sacellanis si quando Copia eorum data fuerit, vix & ægrè permittunt ; quos quidem, non dubito, etiam in illa suâ exemporanea facultate minime illis concedere, modestiavero & doctrinâ longè præstare.
units.tr: Hence it is clear that no one plots tyranny more, or demands more rigidly that others obey their unlawful innovations, than those who were themselves (such was their pride) least inclined to obey lawful sanctity. For those who, not long ago, while license was granted to them, cried out for liberty of conscience, now scarcely and grudgingly permit this to me and to my chaplains, if ever an opportunity is given them. Yet these men, I do not doubt, in their own extemporaneous faculty yield to no one in modesty and learning, and far surpass them.

units.la: Hæc verò ita merè popularia sunt, & ad vulgi sensum, ut satis ipsi animadvertant, eruditam disputationem non latura: ne rationum evidentiâ non minùs, quàm apertâ Lege convicti, vel jam magis contra scientiam suam peccarent sublatâ Liturgiâ, vel permissâ illius consuetudine Factioni suæ & Parti displicerent. Quanquam multò plures hîc offensos crediderim, eosque majoris pretii homines, nec numeris solùm & opibus, sed judicio pietate pollentiores, quorum longè & alia ratio habenda, quàm nonnullorum imbecilli & fluxo ingenio, quibus gratam rem secerunt hæc abrogando.
units.tr: But these things are so merely popular, and suited to the understanding of the crowd, that they themselves plainly perceive they would not bear learned debate. They fear that, convicted by the evidence of reasons no less than by the plain law, they would sin even more against their own conscience if they abolished the Liturgy, or would displease their faction and party if they permitted its custom. Yet I believe far more are offended here, and these men of greater worth, more powerful not only in numbers and wealth but in judgment and piety. Their case must be considered far differently from that of some feeble and fickle minds, to whom they have made a welcome gift by abrogating these things.

units.la: Illùd maximum (opinor) apud homines ejusmodi in Communis Precum Formulæ crimen valere, quod pro me totiens orare instituit, cùm his Fides desit quæ respondeat AMEN, & multò magis Charitas in illis suis Orationibus, quæ Precum vice, probra, & maledicta in me omnia effundunt.
units.tr: That, I think, is the greatest crime among men of this sort in regard to the common forms of prayer: that they have so often undertaken to pray for me, when they lack the faith to answer AMEN, and much more charity; and in those prayers of theirs, which take the place of prayer, they pour out every reproach and curse upon me.

units.la: Nullam aliam his pœnam opto præter suam pœnitentiam, ut advertentes mala jam indicta Publicarum Liturgiarum desuetudine, eam denuo illis-exiflimationem, usum porrò & reverentiam restituant, quæ certis Formis sanorum & salubrium verborum ob antiqua Ecclesia habebantur.
units.tr: I wish them no other punishment than their own repentance: that, recognising the evils already brought on by the disuse of the public liturgies, they may restore that esteem, use and reverence which the Church of old held for certain forms of sound and wholesome words.

units.la: Et Tu Domine qui es semper idem Deus in æternum benedictus, cujus variæ Misericordiæ, & constantes tamen; Tu veteres nostros & quotidianos defectus, nova usque & recenti benignitate restauras, nec renovatos affectus aspernaris, iisdem licet verbis prolatos.
units.tr: And you, Lord, who are always the same God, blessed for ever, whose mercies are various yet constant; you restore our old and daily defects with ever new and fresh kindness, and you do not despise renewed affections, though they are uttered in the same words.

units.la: Ne destituamur beneficio orationum, quas recte prius meditatas unita Tua fundit Ecclesia.
units.tr: Lest we be deprived of the benefit of the prayers which your united Church pours forth, rightly meditated beforehand.

units.la: Sit Precum nostrarum Argumentum voluntati tuæ conforme, quæ semper eadem, & suggestionibus tui Sancti Spiritus, animorum fervor-
units.tr: Let the subject of our prayers be conformed to your will, which is always the same, and to the promptings of your Holy Spirit, the fervour of our minds-

units.la: Et jam nulli dubitamus, Te qui tota es Spiritualis perfectio nec affectata Novitate delectarnec iisdem sæpe repetitis, piis modo precibus of-i fenai.
units.tr: And now we doubt not that you, who are all spiritual perfection, take no delight in affected novelty, nor are offended by the same things often repeated, provided they are pious prayers.

units.la: Has enim varias esse, vel easdem, nullibi à Te vel præceptum vel vetitum: sed relictum pictati & prudentiæ Ecclesiæ, cui utrisque harum uti licet, neutram spernere.
units.tr: For nowhere have you commanded or forbidden these prayers to be various or the same; but this is left to the piety and prudence of the Church, to which it is lawful to use either form, and to reject neither.

units.la: Fac ut in Re Religionis ita discant homines judicia sua pie moderari, ut nec aliis ignorantia sua noceant, nec facultatem suarum præsidentia iis omnibus quærant privare, quæ rite simul & pie in Infirmitatis subsidium adhibentur.
units.tr: Grant that in matters of religion men may learn so to moderate their judgments piously, that they neither harm others through their ignorance, nor seek by their presumption to deprive of their use all those things which are rightly and piously employed as help for our weakness.

units.la: Et cum Errores fere inducant Novitas & Diversitas, Veritas contra in unione, & Constantia servatur, Ne Ecclesiam tuam sineris vel corrumpi erroribus, vel indecoris in te colendo ritibus deformari à diversa & nova invehentibus [?]: sed nec etiam fraudari veritate, unione & ordine, hac fallaci sententia deceptos, statas nempe has Formas Formam tantum Religionis generare.
units.tr: And since novelty and diversity usually induce errors, while truth is kept in unity and constancy, do not allow your Church either to be corrupted by errors, or to be disfigured in your worship by rites unbecoming, introduced by those who bring in different and new things; nor let her be defrauded of truth, unity and order, deceived by this fallacious opinion, namely that these set forms generate only the form of religion.

units.la: Integra nobis corda custodi ab Hypocriseos larva, nec jam eadem precantibus, aut Te laudantibus voce illa Davidica aut aliorum sanctorum, quicquam nobis deterius evenit.
units.tr: Keep our hearts whole, free from the mask of hypocrisy; nor let anything worse befall us while we pray the same things, or praise you with that voice of David or of other saints.

units.la: Da nobis Sapientiam, ut quae intus sint prava corrigamus, minus erit jam extra emendandum.
units.tr: Give us wisdom, so that we may correct what is depraved within; there will then be less left to amend outside.

units.la: Libera semper Ecclesiam tuam, & immunem præsta his malis quæ cæcitatem zeli & audacem pietatem consequuntur.
units.tr: Always free your Church, and grant that she be immune from those evils which follow the blindness of zeal and bold piety.

units.la: 17. De controversiis in- ter Regem & utram- que Domum Parla- menti in Disciplina Ecclesiastica.
units.tr: 17. On the controversies in Parliament between the King and both Houses concerning ecclesiastical discipline.

units.la: REgimen Ecclesiæ per Episcopos quòd eâ semper pertinaciâ defenderim, ea erat plurimorum suspicio me non vera pietate id facere, sed Politicis rationibus adductum.
units.tr: That I have always defended government of the Church by bishops with such stubbornness has given many people the suspicion that I do this not from true piety but moved by political reasons.

units.la: Nec sanè diffiteor, eousque apud me valere Rationes Politicas, ut hoc Regimen aliis anteponam, quatenus mihi jam diu exploratum est Regi esse omninò impossibile Regnum suum in pace servare, nisi eam in Ecclesiasticos vim habeat, & ij vicissim ita ab Illo dependeant, ut sit frœnum aliquod positum Ministrorum linguis nimis alias proclivibus in seditiosam licentiam evagari: cum enim Claves cœlorum tenere existimantur, ita tenent plærunque Cordium claves (plebis præsertim hominum) ut (prout varia oratione placuerit) pacem sæpe & obsequium in principem vel intromittere possint vel excludere.
units.tr: I do not deny that political reasons weigh so heavily with me that I prefer this government to others. For it has long been clear to me that the King can by no means keep his kingdom in peace unless he has power over the ecclesiastics, and they in turn depend on him, so that there is some bridle placed on the tongues of ministers, which are otherwise too prone to wander into seditious licence. For since they are thought to hold the keys of heaven, they generally hold the keys of hearts (especially those of the common people), so that, as their varied speech may please them, they can either admit peace and obedience toward the prince or exclude them.

units.la: Atque adeò (mea quidem sententia) cùm Mihi ut Regi tum à Deo & Legibus salus Regni & Ecclesiæ commendatur, nulli erat rationi consentaneum, ut quacunque in diversum mutatione vim illam meam & influentiam (qua omni jure & ratione in utramque pollere debeo) infirmarem ullo modo, aut defererem.
units.tr: And so, in my opinion, since the safety of the kingdom and the Church is committed to me both as King, by God and by the laws, there was no reason consistent with reason that I should in any way weaken or give up that power of mine and my influence, which by every right and reason I ought to hold over both, through whatever change to the contrary.

units.la: Exclusio Episcoporum è Domo Parium satis erat excludendæ etiam illi suspicioni me Illis ideo favisse, quo mihi commodè vicissim in rebus Regni sententiis suis obsequerentur. Cum revera indignum Illo consessu Episcopum arbitrror, qui secundum Conscientiam suam suffragari non audet.
units.tr: The exclusion of the bishops from the House of Lords was enough to exclude even that suspicion that I favoured them for this reason, that they would in turn comply with my views in the affairs of the kingdom. Indeed I judge a bishop unworthy of that assembly if he does not dare to vote according to his conscience.

units.la: Impetrare tandem liceat ab istorum charitate, ut hac solum causa existimer Ordinem Illum confervandi cupidus, uti primò institutus fuerat, quatenus Rem Religiosam & Sacram agnosco, quæque argumentis perspicuis (quibus [?] judicium meum confirmatur) probat se tum solidissimis Scripturæ fundamentis inmiti, tum Christianarum Ecclesiarum perpetuæ Praxi, usque ad paucos admodum abhinc annos: cum, vel Turbæ populares, vel Presbyterorum Factiones & Arrogantia, vel etiam Principum ipsorum & Statuum Avaritia, occasionem dederunt nonnullorum ingeniis, Novas has suas Formas excogitandi, atque eas demum proponendi sub speciosis istis Titulis, Christi nimirum Gubernationis, Sceptri Ipsius & Regni, quò commodius opus suum agerent, quibus utile erat, res sic mutari.
units.tr: May I finally obtain from their charity that I be thought to desire to preserve that Order for this reason alone, as it was first instituted, inasmuch as I acknowledge it to be a religious and sacred matter, and one which by clear arguments (by which my judgment is confirmed [?]) proves itself to rest both on the most solid foundations of Scripture and on the perpetual practice of the Christian Churches, right down to a very few years ago. Since then, either popular mobs, or the factions and arrogance of elders, or even the avarice of the princes themselves and of the estates, have given some men of talent the occasion to devise these new forms of theirs, and to propose them at last under those specious titles, namely of Christ's government, of his sceptre and kingdom, so that they might carry out their work more conveniently, since it suited them that things be changed in this way.

units.la: Veniam interim mihi dabunt, si nullis hujusmodi tentamentis illectus ad movendos gradu Episcopos (quo fortunas eorum tanto melius invadam) parum etiam fidei adhibeam prætensis Novandi rationibus, quæ ita omnium Historiarum constanti & perpetuo testimonio repugnant, quo certe sanis hominibus, & nullo partium studio actis facile fiet exploratum, quòd, quemadmodum Primitivæ Ecclesiæ proculdubio ab Apostolis Regebantur, & eorum Immediatis successoribus primis illis & optimis Episcopis, ita nulla ratio vel Charitas existimabit omnes totius Orbis Ecclesias, vel ignorasse Regulam ab illis præscriptam, vel à sacro & divino exemplari tam cito deviasse; cum, à primo usque sæculo, ad mille quingentos annos, ne unum quidem exemplum prodeat stabilitæ cujusquam Ecclesiæ (in quo plurimi Ministri & Cætus erant) ubi non aliquis præsidebat Episcopus, cujus cæ-teri teri Regimini & Jurisdictioni parebant.
units.tr: Meanwhile they will pardon me if, not being enticed by any such attempts to move the Episcopos from their rank (so that I might the more easily seize their fortunes), I put little faith in the pretended reasons for Novandi innovation. These conflict so much with the constant and perpetual testimony of all histories that it will easily be made clear to sane men, and to those acting with no partisan zeal, that just as the Primitive Church was undoubtedly governed by the Apostles and their immediate successors, those first and best Episcopis bishops, so no reason or charity will judge that all the Churches of the whole world either were ignorant of the rule prescribed by them, or so quickly deviated from the sacred and divine pattern. For from the first century down to fifteen hundred years, not even one example appears of any established church (in which there were many ministers and assemblies) where some bishop did not preside, whom the others obeyed in government and jurisdiction.

units.la: Harum autem perpetua & Universa praxis tot perspicuis & amplis in Scriptura Regulis pariter & Exemplis consona, cum satis oftendatur in Epistolis ad Timotheum & Titum co consilio scriptis, ad stabiliendum hoc maximè Regimen, non in personis duntaxat Timothei & Titi, sed in eorum etiam successoribus (cùm Disciplina & Regimine haud magis poflit Ecclesia quoad suum bene esse, quàm verbo, & Sacramentis quoad Esse, destitui) Miror illos, qui sic jus Episcopale & Authoritatem maligne intuentur, ita penitus livore occæcari, ut nec tantillum animadvertant, vel quis usus horum in Ecclesiâ, vel quàm fit Ἀποστολικὴ [?] constitutio, quod utrumque in his Epistolis videtur haud minus perspicuè explicari, (tanquam scopus earum esset & finis Principalis, ut peculiare quoddamMunus, Jus & Authoritas instituatur & delegetur certis hominibus, qui Præsidentes Episcopi, cæteris in Ordinatione, Censuris, & reliquis porrò Ecclesiasticæ Disciplinæ actibus praesent) quam breviores illæ notæ Qualitatum & Munerum ad Presbyteros, Episcopos, & Diaconos pertinentium, alibi in eadem Epistola describuntur. In latiori enim sensu & promiscuo usu Nominis, utrosque horum mos erat, (& fortasse nunc licet) appellare Episcopos, quatenus Curam quandam ipsi, & Inspectionem obtineant in Privatos suos Greges, quos illis Apostoli, vel Ἀποστολικοὶ [?] illi Episcopi demandarant, ij nimirum qui ( non secus ac Timotheus ac Titus ) succedebant in ordinariam potestatem in ampliori aliqua parte Ecclesiæ & jam plures Presbyteros complectente.
units.tr: But this perpetual and universal practice agrees equally with so many clear and ample rules and examples in Scripture.
