Since it is sufficiently shown in the Epistles to Timothy and Titus, written with this very purpose, namely to establish this government above all, not only in the persons of Timothy and Titus but also in their successors (since the Church can no more be deprived of discipline and government for its well-being than of the word and sacraments for its being), I marvel that those who look so malevolently on episcopal right and authority are so thoroughly blinded by envy that they notice not even the slightest thing, either what use these have in the Church, or how Apostolic [ἀποστολικὴ] the institution is. Both of these seem to be explained no less clearly in these Epistles, as if their aim and principal end were that a peculiar office, right and authority be instituted and delegated to certain men, who as presiding bishops preside over ordination, censures and the other acts of ecclesiastical discipline. The briefer marks of the qualities and offices pertaining to presbyters, bishops and deacons are described elsewhere in the same Epistle. For in a wider sense and promiscuous use of the name, both of these were customarily (and perhaps may still be) called bishops, insofar as they hold some care and oversight over their own private flocks, which the Apostles, or those Apostolic [ἀποστολικοὶ] bishops, had entrusted to them. These men, no differently from Timothy and Titus, succeeded into ordinary power over some larger part of the Church, already embracing several presbyters.

units.la: Ea vero humilitate erant Primi Illi Episcopi, ut declinantes eximium Apostolorum nomen (quod jam stylus Ecclesiæ à communi illa sua acceptione (qua Nuncium vel Missum significat) ad specialem Illam dignitatem traduxerat, quæ Extraordinariam suam Vocationem, Missionem, Dona & Potestatem immediate à Christo acceperat) sat haberent fe Episcopos vel Presbyteros vocari; donec tandem consuetudo (magna verborum arbitratrix & loquendi norma) cum justa causa videretur peculiari aliquo Nomine distinguendi quorum Jus & officium in Ecclesia non diversum solum à cæteris, sed Illis omnibus erat superius (cum Apostolorum essent succedanei in Ordinaria illa & perpetua potestate administrandi Ecclesias, utcunque Nominis Illius Honore, modestè sed laudabili more abstinentes) his Nomen Episcopi appropriandum vellet: quod sanè fieri potuit absque ulla vel minima Arrogantiæ nota in Eos, qui propagine quadam Apostolica recta serie ab illis descendentes, excelsissima & Amplissima Potestate induebantur gubernandi purissimas & Primitivas Ecclesias, quæ proculdubio multos habebant sanctos Episcopos ad exemplum Titi & Timothei, quorum peculiaris potestas haud magis clare innotescit ex præfatis Epistolis[?], quæ sunt quasi Fundamenta & limites Illius quod ex Iure Divino sibi vendicant Epifcopi) quàm expresse notantur periculosa hæc Tempora, & qui Illis hæc pericula creârunt: qui Sanam Doctrinam non ferentes & clarissimis Testimoniis Ecclesiarum Praxeos adversantes ita præfractè disputant & arroganter usurpant in verum Episcopatum, qui si minus Proditores & Gloriosi appellandi sint, at videntur quidem Illi ipsi esse cupidi, præcipites, inflati, intemperantes, immites, voluptatum amantes potius quàm amantes Dei, habentes formam pietatis, sed qui vim ejus abnegârint.
units.tr: Those first bishops were, however, so humble that, avoiding the distinguished name of Apostles (which the usage of the Church had already transferred from its common meaning of messenger or Missum to that special dignity which had received its extraordinary calling, mission, gifts and power immediately from Christ), they were content to be called bishops or presbyters. Until at last custom, the great arbiter of words and the norm of speech, seemed for a just cause to call for a special name to distinguish those whose right and office in the Church was not only different from the rest but superior to all of them. For they were successors of the Apostles in that ordinary and perpetual power of governing the churches, while modestly and laudably abstaining, in a becoming manner, from the honour of that name. Custom wished the name Episcopi to be appropriated to these men. This could certainly be done without any even the slightest mark of arrogance towards those who, descending from them in a straight succession by a certain Apostolic lineage, were invested with the most exalted and ample power of governing the purest and primitive churches. These churches without doubt had many holy bishops after the example of Titus and Timothy, whose peculiar power is not more clearly known from the aforesaid Epistles, which are as it were the foundations and limits of what bishops claim for themselves by divine right, than these perilous times, and those who created these perils, are expressly noted. These men, not bearing sound doctrine and opposing the clearest testimonies of the practice of the Churches, so stubbornly dispute and arrogantly usurp the true Episcopate. If they are not to be called traitors and glorious, yet they themselves seem indeed to be lovers of self, covetous, boastful, proud, abusive, disobedient, unholy, implacable, incontinent, fierce, despisers of the good, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God, having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof [2 Tim. 3.].

units.la: Hi vero cum nil aliud habeant, cumulo quodam futilium, leviculorum, & nullius eruditionis Doctorum quasi mole congestâ opprimere quærunt penitus & obrucere Claritatem simul & Authoritatem Episcopalis Regiminis, quæ citra omnem Æquivocationem aut ambigui Nominis fallaciam evidentissimè in Scriptura demonstratur, tum in omnibus Ecclesiæ Historiis.
units.tr: These men, however, having nothing else, seek to crush and bury, as if under a heap of trifles, light things and teachers of no learning, the Episcopal Government's clarity and authority. That authority is most evidently demonstrated, without any equivocation or fallacy of an ambiguous name, in Scripture, and then in all the histories of the Church.

units.la: Hæc Theologi potius more, quàm Principis scribo, ut Posteritati saltem liqueat (si in publicum prodierint hæ chartæ) quibus tandem fundamentis Judicium meum tum ex Scripturæ Canonibus, tum Ecclesiasticis Exemplis de Episcopali Regimine confirmatur: cui profecto nec Ratione ulla Politica, nec obstinatæ voluntatis pervicacia, nec ullo vel in Homines ipsos, vel in Ordinem peculiari studio indulsi: Nulli enim horum tanti mihi esse possunt (saltem quoad seculum) ut injurias, & detrimenta ullo modo compensent, quæ Mihi, & Meorum charissimis, tum & Regnis quoque hæc potissimum controversia creavit.
units.tr: I write these things more as a theologian than as a Prince, so that at least posterity may understand (if these papers come out in public) on what foundations my judgment about Episcopal Government is at last confirmed, both from the canons of Scripture and from ecclesiastical examples. To this judgment surely no Political reason, nor the obstinacy of a stubborn will, nor any peculiar zeal indulged toward the Men themselves or toward the Order, has contributed. For none of these can be so great to me (at least as to my age) that they compensate for the injuries and losses which this controversy above all has created for me and my dearest ones, and for the kingdoms as well.

units.la: Quinimò non solum quoad Religionem (cujus optimus Canon Scriptura est, & universæ Ecclesiæ Praxis optimus Commentarius (sed fi quis recta ratione naturam Gubernationis expenderit, omninò credi non potest, benè inftitutam fubordinationem inter Presbyteros vel Ministros ullo modo Christianitati magis repugnare, quàm sæculari & civili Regimini, ubi plerunque è paritate Confusio & Factiones oriuntur.
units.tr: Indeed, this holds not only for religion, whose best canon is Scripture and whose best commentary is the practice of the whole Church. Anyone who weighs the nature of government by right reason will find it utterly incredible that a well-ordered subordination among presbyters or ministers should be any more repugnant to Christianity than it is to secular and civil government, where equality usually gives rise to confusion and factions.

units.la: Mihi sane, qui negaverit hæc posse cum vera Religione consistere, perinde est ac fi dixerit, nec cum Harmonia Numeros, nec bona lineamenta cum bona forma constare.
units.tr: To me, whoever denies that these things can coexist with true religion is as if he had said that numbers cannot agree with harmony, or good outlines with good form.

units.la: Sed nec credibile est, Deum, qui distinctos Ordines & Præsulatum[?] ad gubernandam illam primam Ecclesiam in Judacio[?] Sacerdotio inftituerat, eandem inter Christianos ministros vetare voluisse aut respuere, cum in his, non secus ac aliis subsint etiam seditionum & Schismatum femina: quæ, ut anticiparet, vel mature reftinguerat, prudentia Apostolica (quæ certè Divina erat) crescente in multiplices Congregationes (in quibus singulis erant Presbyteri) Christianorum Numero, hanc Gubernandi rationem instituit, quæ unitatem optimè & ordinem cum Authoritate confervaret. Unde satis perspicuum est, nec Principum Gratiæ nec Presbyterorum ambitioni institutionem Episcoporum in Ecclesia deberi, qui hoc iure suo gaudebant, & exercebant perpetuo, iis maximè temporibus, queis Religio purissima erat, persequutiones asperrimæ.
units.tr: Nor is it credible that God, who had established distinct orders and a presidency in the Jewish priesthood to govern that first Church, wished to forbid or reject the same among Christian ministers, since seeds of sedition and schism lie in these no less than in other bodies. Apostolic prudence, which was certainly divine, either anticipated these or quickly extinguished them, as the number of Christians grew into many congregations, each of which had presbyters. It instituted this manner of governing, which best preserved unity and order with authority. Hence it is clear enough that the institution of bishops in the Church is owed neither to the favour of princes nor to the ambition of presbyters. Bishops enjoyed and exercised this right continually, and especially in those times when religion was purest and persecutions were most severe.

units.la: Nec tamen repugno, hanc unius Præsidentiam & Authoritatem eo modo administrari, ut commune Multorum Presbyterorum Consilium & Consensus adhibeatur (quod etiam ultra largiebar) ut medium prorsus non inutile ad vitandos errores, cæterasque corruptelas impotentis præsertim studii & Gratiæ, quibus unus aliquis esset magis forsan obnoxius, tum autem ad cavendam Tyrannidem, quæ, ut minimè Christianos, ita minimè omnium Ecclesiasticos decet. Accedebat hoc insuper commodum, quod levare aliquo modo videretur onera illa & odia, quæ unius viri humeris nimis graviter incubuissent: quod & opinor, Episcopis meis accidisse.
units.tr: Nor do I object to this presidency and authority of one man being administered in such a way that the common counsel and consent of many presbyters is employed. I even went further in granting this. It is a means by no means useless for avoiding errors and other corruptions, especially those of an unbridled zeal and of favour, to which one man might perhaps be more prone. It also guards against tyranny, which is as unbefitting to churchmen as it is to Christians. There was the further advantage that it seemed to relieve in some way those burdens and hatreds which had weighed too heavily on the shoulders of one man. I think this happened to my bishops as well.

units.la: Quid jam magis Rationi aut Religioni consonum[?], quàm ejusmodi forma Gubernationis, qua Parentem quis magis quàm Dominum referat? & qua non solum ad vitandas Factiones, Confusiones, Æmulationes & Contemptus (quæ facile omnia inter pares nascuntur) maximè valet, verum etiam (cum sint aliqua in Donis Ministrorum discrimina, & diversa Gubernandi capacitas) hic utique videtur necessaria, ut, qui cæteris sint præstantiores, diversiori[?] aliquo Munere fungantur: Sed neque hæc præoccupato Iudicio, & contradici non ferente pronuncio. Satis constat, me conatum sedulò, ut mihi integrè fieret exploratum, quid diversæ Partis Patroni præcipui vel contra hanc obiicere, vel pro sua allegare potuissent: id verò ferio tandem deprehendi, non Scriptura solum & ratione multum infra nostros caufâ [?] cadere, sed exemplis Ecclesiarum, & Praxis, & Historiarum Testimoniis plane destitui, ita toto flumine in Episcopatum ruente, ut nec tenuissimus illis rivulus relinquatur.
units.tr: What is more in accord with reason or religion than a form of government by which one might liken a man more to a father than to a lord? It is most effective not only for avoiding factions, confusions, rivalries and contempt, which easily arise among equals, but also because there are differences in the gifts of ministers and in their capacity to govern. Here it seems especially necessary that those who are more outstanding than others should discharge some different office. But I pronounce this not as a prejudged judgment that tolerates no contradiction. It is well established that I diligently tried to learn fully what the chief patrons of the opposite party could either object against this or allege in favour of their own. At length I discovered in earnest that they fall far short of our cause in Scripture and reason, and are wholly destitute of examples from churches, of practice, and of testimonies from history. The whole torrent rushes towards episcopacy, and not even the slightest rivulet is left to them.

units.la: Quod ad exempla illa (nimis importuna) Ecclesiarum quarundam nuperæ Reformationis, (omnes enim non carent Episcopis) quas Rerum & Temporum necessitas excusat potius, quàm absolvit ab Antiquitate diversas, nullam sane causam video, cur Ecclesiæ rectè reformatæ, & ab Episcopis administratæ ad paucorum hominum exemplar componi potius adiungantur, quàm ad Antiquarum [?] Ecclesiarum Catholica (quæ nullâ prorsus Reformatione egenerunt) vel ad illas jam extantes Ecclesias, quarum plures sunt in Christiano orbe ab Epifcopis administratæ, quàm vel omnium Prefbyterianorum & Independentium simul, quas quidem omnes (opinor) ipsas in Tribus Meis Regnis ab Episcopis rectas Ecclesias æquare saltem numero fi non excedere.
units.tr: As for those examples (very inopportune) of certain churches of recent reformation, for not all of them lack bishops, which the necessity of affairs and times excuses rather than absolves from differing from antiquity: I certainly see no reason why churches rightly reformed and governed by bishops should be joined to the pattern of a few men, rather than to the Catholic churches of antiquity, which suffered no reformation at all, or to those churches still existing. Of these, more in the Christian world are governed by bishops than by all Presbyterians and Independents together. I think that in my three kingdoms alone, the churches rightly ruled by bishops equal those others in number, if they do not exceed them.

units.la: Minimum interim prudentiæ aut Charitatis sapere videatur in hac Christianorum difcrepantia (qui plus nimis in cæteris discordant) latius plagam diducere, & toti orbi Christiano (præ(præter aliquem Protestantium manipulum) tantum scandalum objicere in Administratione Ecclesiastica: quos, etiamsi in nonnullis Doctrinalibus manifesti erroris convincendos nunquam eò perduces, ad ut consu[?]mandam Reformationem deserant illam penitus & repudient Institutionem, quam cum omnibus retrò seculis Catholicam, Primitivam, Apostolicam adeo tenuerunt, ut nulli unquam Schismatici cætera vel Hæretici (unis illis Aerianis exceptis) ab unitate Ecclesiæ, & conformitate in hac parte deviarint, inter quos semper Episcopi Presbyteris superiores.
units.tr: Meanwhile, in this discord of Christians, who already disagree too much on other matters, it would seem the least sign of prudence or charity to widen the breach further and to cast such great scandal on the whole Christian world in ecclesiastical administration, except for some handful of Protestants. Even if these could never be convicted of manifest error in some doctrinal matters, would they abandon and wholly reject that institution to complete the reformation? That institution all ages past have held to be Catholic, Primitive and Apostolic. No schismatics or other heretics, apart from those Aerians alone, ever departed from the unity of the Church and conformity on this point. Among these, bishops were always superior to presbyters.

units.la: Nec eo parùm argumento judicium meum confirmatur, quòd Regimen istud Episcopale haud ita dudum Universo Consensu probaverint, & se illi submisserint non Laici solum sed ipsi etiam in his Regnis Clerici, quorum tanta levitas & inconstantia in præjudicium cedit Novitatis: cùm enim (quâ sum Charitate) doctrinam eorum & probitatem cousque suspicari non possim, quasi aut ignorassent quid fecerint, vel adversus Conscientias subscripsiffent[?], nunquam certè excusabo facilitatem hanc illis & mobilitatem ingenii, qui priusquam liberè & æquè controversia hæc fuisset disceptata, contra Juramenta sua superiora & Praxim, contra obedientiam in Leges jam valentes, me denique repugnante, non solum Regimen Episcopale exploserunt, sed plausum etiam & stimulos illis addiderunt qui Episcopos cæterosque Ecclesiasticos tam nefario & crudeli modo fpoliarunt, ut ipsas ctiam Terras Ecclesiæ venales habuerint, & ab omni Sacro usu in perpetuum abalienandas; Eam vim habent fluxus temporum, & præpotentia Partium in nonnullorum hominum judicia, qui ut sic jam repente & penitus mutarentur, nullam aliam possunt causam afferre, quàm, quòd Scotorum Exercitus jam in Anglium ve-niffet.
units.tr: My judgment is not confirmed to a small degree by the fact that not so long ago, with universal consent, they approved this episcopal government and submitted themselves to it. Not only the laity did so, but the clergy themselves in these kingdoms. Their great levity and inconstancy redounds to the prejudice of novelty. Since I cannot, in my charity, suspect their learning and probity so far as to think that they did not know what they were doing, or that they subscribed against their consciences, I will never excuse this facility and fickleness of mind in those who, before this controversy had been freely and fairly debated, cast out episcopal government. They did so against their earlier oaths and practice, against obedience to laws now in force, and finally against my opposition. Not only that, they gave applause and spurs to those who despoiled bishops and other churchmen in so wicked and cruel a manner that they even put the lands of the Church up for sale, to be alienated from all sacred use for ever. Such is the force of the flux of times and the overbearing power of parties over the judgments of some men, that they could be changed so suddenly and completely. They can assign no other cause than that the Scottish army had now come into England.

units.la: At fe olim castigabit horum hominum fultitia, & desertores Episcopatus sibi ipsis non minus inimici, & rem suam prodidisse deprehendentur: nunquam enim vel ipse Presbyteratus vim illam aut pretium seorsum obtinebit, ac fuisset Episcopatui conjuncto & eodem quafi coronato: Ut vero fecundior fit Ministris aura populi, quàm Principis Gratiæ[?], æquè parum sperari debet, ac, ut crescant fælicius plantæ manu rigatę illis rore cęlesti dulci & liberali perfusis. Quin inopia & contemptus cleri ostendent, quale jam cadaver supererunt, cùm à Capitis Iilius[?] influentia, in cujus Primatum jurárunt, dimoventur.
units.tr: But in time the folly of these men will chastise itself, and the deserters of episcopacy will be found no less enemies to themselves, having betrayed their own cause. For presbyterate itself will never obtain that power or worth on its own, as it would have had if conjoined to episcopacy and, as it were, crowned by it. Just as the breath of popular favour is no more likely to make ministers more fruitful than the grace of the Prince, so little ought it to be hoped that plants watered by hand will grow more happily when bathed in sweet and liberal heavenly dew. Indeed, the want and contempt of the clergy will show what kind of corpse they will then be, when they are removed from the influence of that Head to whose primacy they swore.

units.la: Modico interea temperamento adhibito, occurri forsan potuisset magnis malis. Id interim fixum est mihi, Epi scopatum illum Primitivum quantum in Me est extirpandum non pati: facile reformabit Prudentia affectibus incorrupta, quicquid temporum ærugo, vel indulgentia Legum, vel corruptela Morum induxit: vitia Personarum aut Temporum toti ordini imputare, vel propterea in poenam depof-cere, cere, crassus vulgi error, & inter eas seditionum Maximas, à quibus omnes Cordati homines merito abhorrent.
units.tr: With a moderate remedy applied, perhaps great evils could have been averted. Meanwhile this is fixed in my mind: as far as in me lies, I will not allow that primitive episcopacy to be uprooted. Prudence, uncorrupted by passions, will easily reform whatever the rust of the times, the indulgence of laws, or the corruption of morals has introduced. To impute the faults of persons or of times to the whole order, or to demand it in punishment on that account, is the crude error of the crowd, and among the greatest of seditions, from which all sensible men rightly shrink.

units.la: Secularia vero illa additamenta Authoritatis & Honoris Civilis, & Fortunæ ornamenta, quæ Majores mei & alii Christiani Principes Episcopis cæterisque Ecclesiasticis annectanda censuerant, haud alia semper existimavi, quàm justa eruditionis & pietatis præmia iis maximè debita qui Ecclesiasticæ Administrationi aliquo modo immisceri mereantur; Accedit, quod sic melius ad Charitatis opera, & Hospitalem beneficentiam instruantur, tum Authoritatem etiam habeant munitiorem quoad externum respectum & observantiam (quæ vix unquam in pacatis temporibus, ita ex Virtutis dimenso, ac Fortunæ persoluitur) cum tenuitate haud dubio & inopia ipsi simul & Munus evilescerent in hac morum dissoluta & animorum licentia, quam dura illa Tempora castigabant.
units.tr: As for those secular additions of civil authority and honour, and the ornaments of fortune, which my ancestors and other Christian princes resolved to annex to bishops and other churchmen, I have always thought them nothing other than just rewards of learning and piety. These are due above all to those who deserve to take part in ecclesiastical administration in any way. Besides, thus they are better equipped for works of charity and hospitable beneficence, and their authority is more fortified as to external respect and observance. Such respect is hardly ever paid in peaceful times in proportion to virtue, but rather to fortune. Without these supports, both they and their office would grow feeble through poverty and want, in this dissolute morality and licence of minds that those harsh times were chastising.

units.la: Tales semper exopto Episcopor fieri qui sint his incitamentis dignissimi, & in optimum usum conversuri: Si quid judicio erravero, bono saltem animo excusabor. Erant mihi (sat scio) nonnulli hujusmodi, quos eruditos, graves, & pios homines fuisse nemo certè inficietur cui vel mica Judicii aut frontis inest; Illud fateor me summopere expetisse ut Ecclesiastici præ cæteris (maximè ij qui præsunt) ab illo vulgi contemptu securi viveRent, qui (præter id quod fere omnibus innatum estiis potissimum adversari qui reprehendere aut coercere videantur) necessario debet comitari vel Presbyterorum paritatem quâ o-mnes æquantur, vel Independentium disparitatem, quâ infra Populum collocantur Pastores.
units.tr: I always wish for such bishops as are most worthy of these incentives and will put them to the best use. If I have erred in judgment, I shall at least be excused by good intent. There were, I am well aware, several such men: learned, grave and pious, whom no one with a grain of judgment or shame could deny. I confess that I have earnestly desired that churchmen, and especially those who preside, should live secure from that contempt of the common people. Such contempt, besides the fact that almost all men are naturally inclined to oppose those who seem to rebuke or restrain them, must necessarily accompany either the parity of the Presbyters, by which all are made equal, or the disparity of the Independents, by which the ministers are placed beneath the people.

units.la: Hæc mea de Episcopatu sententia est, in qua (Deum testor) nullo affectu privato aut studio vel tantillum à veritate deflexi.
units.tr: This is my opinion concerning episcopacy, and in it (I call God to witness) I have not swerved a hair from the truth through any private affection or partisan zeal.

units.la: Deum jam appello & orbem Christianum, an sit subditis, vel Christianis pium, vi merâ & injuriis in servilem modum coercentes me Regem suum eo velle subigere (quod nonnulli fecerunt) ut, reluctante judicio ita solidis fundamentis subnixo, in infirmas istius- modi & inter se distractas Novitates consentiam.
units.tr: I now call God and the Christian world to witness whether it is pious for subjects, or for Christians, that a king should try, by mere force and injuries, to subdue me in a servile manner (as some have done), so that, though my judgment resists, a judgment resting on such solid foundations, I should consent to such weak and mutually conflicting novelties.

units.la: Nemo prorsus eorum est, etiam qui optime affecti videntur, qui vehementius quàm ego exoptat ut administretur Ecclesia secundum ipsum Christi institutum, prout recta Ratione è Scriptura colligitur, ubi nullum adhuc video Argumenti simulachrum cur hæc nova potiora crederentur, nisi id satis habeant afferre nonnullarum Ecclesiarum exempla in Infantia illa Prima & solitudine, (cum jam raro adhuc Christianismo, uni forsan in Civitate vel Regione cætui unus facile Presbyter sufficeret) vel hanc velint perspicuam veritatem negare, exercuisse scilicet Apostolos Episcopatum æque in eos quos Presbyteros instituerant, quàm, in quas plantaverant Ecclesias; & (cum hoc effet imprimis necessarium ad bene csse Ecclesiæ aucta postea, & in multiplices cætus abeuntis, formam aliquam Regiminis institui) hunc etiam necessario ab Apostolis derivatum ad exemplar Potestatis illius & Authoritatis, quæ ab Ipsis in alios exercita usu adhuc & fine Gubernationis manente, cum ipsis finire non poterat.
units.tr: No one at all among those who seem best disposed wishes more earnestly than I that the Church be governed according to Christ's own institution, as it is gathered from Scripture by sound Reason. Yet I see no shadow of an argument why these new forms should be believed superior, unless they are content to bring forward the examples of some churches in that first infancy and solitude of Christianity, when, as Christianity was still rare, a single presbyter might perhaps suffice for one assembly in a city or region. Or else they must deny this plain truth: that the Apostles exercised episcopacy over those whom they had ordained presbyters just as over the churches they had planted. And since this was above all necessary for the well-being of the Church, which later grew and spread into many assemblies, some form of government had to be instituted. This too was derived necessarily from the Apostles, after the pattern of that power and authority which they exercised over others. It remained in use, and its purpose of governing remained, and it could not end with the Apostles themselves.

units.la: Constat eas quæ Purissimæ, Primitivæ & Optimæ Ecclesiæ audiebant sub Episcopis omnes floruisse, quod etiamnum fieri posset, ni ignorantia, superstitio, avaritia, ultionis porro cupiditas aliique inordinati & perversi affectus ita animos quorundam contra illos concitassent, ut, quod deest Rationum & Primitivorum Exemplarium, vi & Animis perficere conentur: dum nonnulli magno zelo (proculdubio) Episcoporum Agris, Ædibus, & vectigalibus inhiantes, propter hæc multo promptius Episcopatum deglutiunt. quod meo quidem judicio, quicquid illi existimant, nihilo levius crimen sacrilegio est, cum Deum omnium datorem fraudent illa portione, quam olim pio animo Ecclesiæ & Prophetis donantes Ipsi grate vicissim retribuerunt, qui per manus hujusmodi Calicem frigidæ libamentum sibi esset accepturus.
units.tr: It is agreed that all the churches which heard the most pure, primitive and best teaching flourished under bishops. This could still be the case, were it not that ignorance, superstition, avarice, a continuing desire for revenge and other disordered and perverse passions have so stirred the minds of some against them that they try to achieve by force and by violence what they lack in reasons and in primitive examples. Some, with great zeal (no doubt), gape after the fields, houses and revenues of the bishops, and for these reasons swallow up episcopacy all the more readily. In my judgment, whatever they may think, this is no lesser crime than sacrilege, since they defraud God, the giver of all things, of that portion which the Church and the prophets once devoutly gave, and which God in turn gratefully repaid, promising that whoever received such a one through their hands would not lose his reward, even the cup of cold water.

units.la: Porro aliud est mihi vinculum particulare, Iuramentum judicio meo consonum, quo me conceptis verbis obligavi ad tutandum hoc Regimen & Iura Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Furthermore, I am bound by another particular tie, an oath agreeing with my judgment, by which I have obliged myself in express words to uphold this government and the rights of the Church.

units.la: Quo tamen Juramento haud difficulter forsan exolvi poteram (ut, errore, suscepto) si mihi plane constaret cffe ordinem illicitum vel (quæ audax quorundam sed infirma calumnia est) Antichriftianum. Cùm verò exquisitissima veritatis exploratione habita magis indics magisque confirmor in æ[?]quitate & pietate eorum in quæ juraverim, certè nemo, nisi qui animæ meæ perniciem struit, in hæc duo tam atrocia scelera, Sacrilegium nempe & Perjurium se hîc invicem trahentia impellat: mitto hîc personales injurias in plurimos de me optimè meritos, qui haud minore Iure suis gaudent fortunis, quàm, qui Illos privare student propriis suis patrimoniis, quinque nulla adhuc lege convicti sunt eorum criminum, ob quæ prædiis suis & Bonis cæteris mulctari merentur.
units.tr: Yet perhaps I could, not with much difficulty, be released from that oath, as if I had sworn in error, if it were plainly established to me that this order was unlawful or (which is the bold but weak calumny of some) Antichristian. But since I have reached this view after the most careful search for truth, and am daily more confirmed in the equity and piety of those things I have sworn to, surely no one except him who plots the ruin of my soul would drive me here to these two atrocious crimes, sacrilege and perjury, which drag each other along. I pass over here the personal injuries done to many who have deserved well of me, and who have no less right to enjoy their fortunes than those who strive to strip them of their own patrimonies, though they have not yet been convicted under any law of those crimes for which they deserve to be fined in their lands and other goods.

units.la: Sæpe equidem demiratus sum istos homines magnam Conscientiæ teneritudinem & Reformandi studium præ se ferentes, id mihi velle persuadere, me Iuramento Coronationis meæ obstrictum in quæcunque ab illis proposita consentire debere (quod vehementer urgent) utcunque Rationis & Religionis libertati contraria, (quam certè tueri omnes debent, & de qua Ipsi in suffragiis suis tam impensè cavent) eodem simul tempore affirmantes irritum me facere oportere, & aperte violare illam partem Iuramenti, qua, secundum optimum Rationis & Religionis lumen, Regimen Ecclesiæ, & Legitima ejus Iura tueri obstringor. Mirum sane, in hæc solum valere Iuramentum quæ mihi & cæteris in eadem conditione versantibus iniqua prorsus & injuria videntur (cum animarum essentiali libertati directe repugnent irritum tantum in illa Clausula & invalidum futurum, quâ me Deo & Hominibus jure obligatum existimo.
units.tr: Often indeed I have marvelled that those men, who make a great show of tenderness of conscience and zeal for reforming, want to persuade me that, being bound by my Coronation oath, I ought to consent to whatever they propose (which they press most vehemently), however contrary it is to the liberty of Reason and Religion (which surely everyone ought to defend, and about which they themselves are so anxious in their votes). At the same time they assert that I ought to make that oath void and openly violate that part of it by which, according to the best light of Reason and Religion, I am bound to uphold the government of the Church and its lawful rights. It is indeed remarkable that the oath is held valid only in those matters which seem wholly unfair and unjust to me and to others in the same position, and which directly oppose the essential liberty of souls; whereas it would be void and invalid only in that clause by which I consider myself rightfully bound to God and men.

units.la: In hoc tamen equuleo jam diu versor, quid ambitiosâ illorum avaritiâ, quid Sacrilegâ aliorum crudelitate distentus qui Me & Regnum & Ecclesiam cousque civilibus dissidiis lacerare certi, dùm me in ea assentiri cogant & palam comprobare, quæ (Deus novit) improbo maxime, & ex animo detestor (ut multimodis Religioni tum Rationi etiam & Iustitiæ adversantia) quibus tamen etiamsi cum pudore meo & infamia consentirem, haud utique illis satisfacerem, qui Consiliis & opinione diversi non contra me magis & Episcopatum, quàm intra se invicem pugnant..
units.tr: Yet I have long been stretched on this rack, pulled between the ambitious avarice of some and the sacrilegious cruelty of others. These men are resolved to tear apart the kingdom and the Church by civil discord to such a degree that they force me to agree to and openly approve things which (God knows) I most wickedly and from my heart detest, as being contrary in many ways to religion, to reason and to justice. Yet even if I consented to them with shame and disgrace, I would by no means satisfy those men who, divided among themselves in counsels and opinions, do not fight less against each other than against me and against episcopacy.

units.la: Quod verò Scotis haud ita pridem in Ecclesiastico Regimine morem gesserim, nullo modo rectè urgetur, ut in Regnis meis cæteris id propterea admitterem. Hoc enim debent cogitare, haud ita altas unquam radices egisse, vel stabilitum in Scotia Episcopatum fuisse, prout fuerat in Anglia, atque adeò me neutiquam obligari ad hunc pariter in utrinque Regnis tuendum; Quod enim meâ sententiâ optimum est, haudquaquam omni loco & tempore absolutè necessarium existimandum est.
units.tr: As for the fact that I recently yielded to the Scots in ecclesiastical government, it is wrongly urged that I should therefore allow the same in my other kingdoms. For they ought to consider that episcopacy never took such deep roots in Scotland, nor was it established there as it was in England, and so I am by no means bound to uphold this equally in both kingdoms. For what I judge to be best must not be thought absolutely necessary in every place and at every time.

units.la: Hanc autem in Illos indulgentiam si quis errorem meum aut peccatum dixerit, facilè agnoscam: pessimè verò hinc argumenta colligunt, idem iterum faciendum, vel potius multo deterius, cùm de his forsàn quam antea exploratiùs jam constet, quin nec illa ipsa concessio ita cessit fæliciter, ut animum mihi addiderit porrò aliis concedere.
units.tr: If anyone calls this indulgence towards them an error or sin of mine, I will readily admit it. But they draw a very bad argument from it, that the same concession should be made again, or rather a much worse one, since these matters are now perhaps better understood than before. Indeed, that earlier concession did not turn out so happily as to encourage me to grant more to others in future.

units.la: Si quid hîc magis Christi in his Novos Modos affectantibus lenitatis scilicet & Justitiæ, si quid ordinis magis aut Charitatis, autobedientiæ conspiceretur, suspicari forsàn poteram judicium meum affectu aliquo prœoccupatum aut diversum sentiendi consuetudine inflexum: Cum verò justis ita causis adducar ut de his longè credam contraria, haud sperate possunt his moribus Novæ suæ Regiminis Formæ existimationem acquirere.
units.tr: If anything more of Christ's gentleness, namely, and justice, anything more of order or charity, or of obedience, were visible in those who aspire to these New Models, I might perhaps suspect that my judgment was prejudiced by some feeling, or bent by a habit of thinking otherwise. But since I am led by such just reasons to believe quite the contrary, they cannot hope to win a reputation for their new form of government by these manners.

units.la: Sed nec in aliis etiam quibuscunque Ecclesiis (quarum exemplo sic plauditur, quodque in illas à Me regnatas omni vi importare contendunt) quicquam adhuc compertum est vel doctrinæ uberius, vel Religionis, imo nec ulla pietatis aut Charitatis opera ita eximia præ nostris sub Episcopatu agentibus (quibus Dei benedictio in hac parte non defuit) ut ex his omnino adducat credere vel Presbyterifmum vel Independentiam benignius in corda & vitas hominum, quam Episcopatum rite habitum influcere.
units.tr: But in no other churches whatever (by whose example they applaud themselves, and which they strive to force upon the churches I rule by every kind of violence) has anything yet been found either more abundant in learning or in religion, or indeed any works of piety or charity so outstanding, as those of our churches under episcopacy, to which God's blessing in this respect has not been lacking. So from these facts there is no reason at all to believe that either Presbyterianism or Independency flows more beneficially into the hearts and lives of men than episcopacy, when it is rightly maintained.

units.la: In quem si abusus forte aliqui irrepserint, horum fiat exterminatio, si adhuc Illius retento. Multo enim satius duco Primitivæ & uniformi Antiquitatis vestigiis iusistere, quàm distrahe Novitati manus præbere.
units.tr: If some abuses have perhaps crept into it, let them be removed, provided the thing itself is kept. For I think it far better to stand by the footsteps of primitive and uniform antiquity than to lend a hand to distracting novelty.

units.la: Rectus certè Episcopatus justis omnium desideriis satisfaceret, quicquid boni Episcopi, vel Presbyteri humiles, vel modestia populi exoptet, ut sic Re Ecclesiastica nec per Tyrannidem, nec Paritatem, nec populares Tumultus administrata evitentur haec maxime periculae, ut vel ejiciantur Episcopi, vel fpernantur Presbyteri, vel fit populus vexationibus obnoxius.
units.tr: Certainly a right episcopacy would satisfy the just desires of all, whatever good bishops, humble presbyters, or the modesty of the people may wish, so that the Church's affairs might be administered neither by tyranny, nor by parity, nor by popular tumults; the most dangerous of these being that bishops are cast out, presbyters despised, or the people made liable to vexations.

units.la: Et in hac Judicii & Conscientiae meae Integritate Deus me (ut spero) custodiet.
units.tr: And in this integrity of my judgment and conscience, God (as I hope) will keep me.

units.la: Tu enim Domine, nosti Integritatem meam & teneritudinem, qui cum me Fidei Defensorem & Ecclesiae Tutorem posueris, ne me ulla violentia patiaris adversus Conscientiam impelli.
units.tr: For you, Lord, know my integrity and tenderness, you who have placed me as defender of the faith and guardian of the Church, and who will not suffer me to be driven by any violence against my conscience.

units.la: Exurge, Domine, protege causam tuam, ne deformetur tua Ecclesia manca facta illo Regimine, quod ab Apostolis [?] derivatum primitiva & purissima tempora conservarunt, nec proventus Ecclesiae fiant saeculari invidiae obnoxii, quae jam omnia illi quaerit eripere Doctrinae & pietatis incitamenta.
units.tr: Arise, Lord, protect your cause, lest your Church be deformed, made maimed by that government which the primitive and most pure ages preserved, derived from the Apostles [?], and lest the revenues of the Church become liable to secular envy, which now seeks to snatch away from her all the incentives of teaching and piety.

units.la: Me vero cum bono illo Samaritano misericordem efficias, & afflictae tuae Ecclesiae subvenire promtum, quam a nonnullis vulneratam & spoliatam ceteri negligenter praeterierunt, nulla omnino miseratione aut ope adhibita.
units.tr: Make me, with that good Samaritan, merciful, and ready to help your afflicted Church, which others have wounded and despoiled and, with no pity or help at all, have negligently passed by.

units.la: Potestas mea a Te derivata, si (tua Gratia juvante) ut pro te maxime exerceatur; & quam cetera mea Iura Regia amplius mihi in praesens non permittantur, usque tamen custodias in illa Rationis libertate & Religionis amore, & in Ecclesiam Studio, quæ in Conscientia mihi ut Christiano altè insidunt.
units.tr: My power is derived from you; if (with your grace helping) it may be exercised chiefly for you; and although my other royal rights are not for the present permitted to me, yet keep in me that freedom of reason and love of religion, and that zeal for the Church, which lie deep in my conscience as a Christian.

units.la: Custodi à sacrilega depredatione benedictionis illas temporales, quas Ecclesiæ Tuæ providentia in Gloriam Tuam dispensavit.
units.tr: Guard those temporal blessings, which by your providence you have dispensed to your Church for your glory, from sacrilegious plunder.

units.la: Ignosce qui flagitiis suis & erroribus hanc sunt maximè pœnam commeriti, ut sic Aprum de Silva, & astutos vulpes exterminare patiaris vincam tuam dextera plantatam, & diu rore cœlesti in felicem fœcunditatem irriguam.
units.tr: Pardon those who by their crimes and errors have most deserved this punishment, so that you may suffer the boar out of the forest and the crafty foxes to be destroyed, and may water your vineyard, planted by your right hand, with heavenly dew for a happy fruitfulness.

units.la: One illa infami nota in æternum maculer, primum me Regem Christianum hujus Regni extitisse, qui in Ecclesiam opprimendam, & una Patres Ecclesiæ consenserim, quorum omnium errores malucrim Constantini illius exemplo silentio velare, aut lenitate corrigere, quam personas eorum & sacrum Munus ludibriis vulgi exponere.
units.tr: May I not be stained forever with that infamous mark, that I, the first Christian king of this kingdom, consented to oppressing the Church, and together with the Fathers of the Church, whose errors I would rather have veiled in silence, after the example of that Constantine, or corrected with gentleness, than exposed their persons and sacred office to the mockery of the crowd.

units.la: Vides (Domine) quid pro Tua Ecclesia, & quid una cum Illa passus fuerim, ne tardaveris Domine Illam simul & me liberare, à perversis hominibus quorum & pepererunt Consilia, & jam usque parturiunt confusiones, cum antiquos illos limites intra quos stetit pax Ecclesiæ ita omnes vesano impetu dirimant, omne genus erroribus, Schismatis, & dissolutione introductâ.
units.tr: You see, Lord, what I have suffered for your Church, and what I have suffered together with her. Do not delay, Lord, to set her and me free at once from perverse men, whose counsels have conceived and now bring forth confusions, while they so with mad impetus tear apart those ancient boundaries within which the peace of the Church stood, introducing every kind of error, schism and dissolution.

units.la: Tu vero Deus veritatis & ordinis, hanc in bono tempore tuo compescere malitiam, furorem mitiga, & confunde celeratas eorum machinationes, qui & tibi & Mihi, & Ecclesiæ Tuæ juxta inimici.
units.tr: But you, O God of truth and order, restrain this malice in your good time, mitigate the fury, and confound the wicked machinations of those who are enemies both to you and to me, and to your Church.

units.la: Ut & ipse, & qui amant Ecclesiam Tuam Psallamus tibi, & magnificemus salutare tuum coram filiis hominum.
units.tr: So that both I myself, and those who love your Church, may sing to you, and magnify your salvation before the sons of men.

units.la: 18. De Tractatu Vxbri- gensi, & Conditioni- bus à Rege latis..
units.tr: 18. Of the Treaty of Uxbridge, and the Conditions offered by the King.

units.la: PErinde mihi videntur Tractatus, ac, si qui missò ferarum ritu pugnare, jam disceptare incipiant ut homines, quorum robur certè plus in ingeniis esse oportet, quam in Membris situm.
units.tr: Such treaties seem to me like wild beasts that have fought with their teeth and claws and now begin to argue like men, whose strength ought surely to lie in their wits rather than in their limbs.

units.la: Quanquam rarae sic agenti oportunitates adfuerint, nunquam tamen defuit vel. assectus vel studium, ut qui semper minus Gladio meo quam Rationi confisus, ita hic penitus cedere potiori statueram, ut nil opus illo postea arbitrarer, modo nos invicem cognoscendi & perspiciendi copia daretur.
units.tr: Although such opportunities as this have rarely come my way, I never lacked either inclination or zeal. I have always trusted my reason more than my sword, and I had resolved to yield entirely to the stronger side, thinking nothing more would be needed once we were given the chance to know and understand one another.

units.la: Quod autem studium meum in hac parte palam fecerim;atque illos aliquoties de Tractatu interpellaverim, haud me quicquam exinde imminutum credidi, cùm non magis sit Hominis Ratione potius quàm vi agere, quàm pacem quaerere & consectari, Christiani.
units.tr: Yet I do not think I lost anything by making my zeal in this matter plain, or by having several times pressed them about the treaty. It is no less the mark of a Christian to seek peace than of a man to act by reason rather than by force.

units.la: Cum enim Arma perinvitus in defensionem meam tantùm sumpserim, omnia ad pacem facientia libenter amplectar: Omnes Belli eventus tristes, Civilis tristissimi, fine vix compensante & sero reparante Mediorum mala.
units.tr: For although I have taken up arms only very reluctantly, in my own defence, I will gladly embrace everything that tends toward peace. Every outcome of war is sad, and that of civil war is the saddest, since its end scarcely makes up for the evils of the means, and repairs them only late.

units.la: Nullo unquam successu inflatus carius ideò pacem destinabam, quam vehementius omnibus concupivi, licet à me carissimè redimendam: Honorem meum tantum & Conscientiam peculiares mihi volui servare, cum illum quidem Regi, hanc Christiano nefas esset deserere.
units.tr: Never puffed up by any success, I have always valued peace the more dearly, and desired it more eagerly than anyone, though I would have bought it at a high price. I wished to keep only my honour and my conscience, which are peculiarly my own: for it would be wrong for a king to abandon the former, and for a Christian to abandon the latter.

units.la: Tractatus vero iste Vxbrigensis[?] spem mihi maximam fecit faelicioris eventus, ad quem si alii eandem mecum moderationem attulissent, proculdubio finis Bello fuisset impositus.
units.tr: That Uxbridge [?] treaty, however, gave me the greatest hope of a happier outcome. If others had brought the same moderation to it that I did, an end would undoubtedly have been put to the war.

units.la: Eousque enim cedere volebam, quoad Ra-tio, Honor, Conscientia permitteret, nec quae restabant controversiae tanti erant, vel in Rem Populi tam necessariae, ut securitati subditorum meorum aut felicitati obstarent, quorum utraque multo melius gavisi fuerant annos ante complures quam haec omnino postulata nascerentur, è quibus nonnulla repudiando, & mihi Ipsi jus facere, & subditis meis gratum arbitrabar.
units.tr: For I was willing to yield as far as reason, honour and conscience would allow. The remaining disputes were not of such weight, nor so necessary to the public good, as to stand in the way of the security of my subjects or their happiness. Both of these they would have enjoyed much better several years earlier, before these demands arose at all. By rejecting some of them, I thought I would both do justice to myself and please my subjects.

units.la: Nimis vero constat, haud ita facile mitigari suspiciones ac primo excitantur. Major enim nonnullis timor est, ne à violentis foedérationibus quibus jam sunt impliciti discedant, quam erat olim ne se his implicarent: quod deest aequitatis pertinaciâ supplent; Ipsi videlicet quibus modica admodum res fuit, quâ vel in pace gauderent, vel Bello perderent, illud sedulo agebant ut ipsum Nomen Pacis suspicioni & odiis obnoxium redderetur.
units.tr: It is quite clear that suspicions are not so easily calmed, and that they are first aroused. For some men fear more that they will withdraw from the violent alliances in which they are now entangled than they once feared becoming entangled in them. What they lack in fairness they make up for in obstinacy. Those very men, for whom the matter was of small moment, by which they might either rejoice in peace or lose in war, took care to make the very name of peace liable to suspicion and hatred.

units.la: In rebus Ecclesiasticis, ubi tot ligaminibus Conscientiæ astrictæ minima erat deliberandi libertas, eo modo sancire placuerat, quo abundè esset omnibus satisfactum, quos non Factio aut Avaritia, aut Superstitio denique, quam Zeli fervor aut charitas aut Reformationis studium impulerat.
units.tr: In ecclesiastical matters, where the conscience is bound by so many ties and there was the least freedom to deliberate, I had been willing to settle things in such a way that everyone was fully satisfied, all those whom faction, avarice or superstition, or the fervour of zeal, charity or the desire for reformation, had not driven on.

units.la: Promptus eram omnia largiri quæ synceram[?] pietatem promovere viderentur, ea solum retinendi cupidus quæ in ordinem præsidium & Authoritatem Ecclesiastici Regiminis necessaria, & quæ persuasissima habeo ( prout alibi me uberius explicui ) veris omnis Politiæ principiis, etiam quæ consummatissimæ sunt) consentire, tum Primitivo imprimis & Apostolico Exemplari & Primitivæ Ecclesiæ Praxi.
units.tr: I was ready to grant everything that seemed to promote sincere piety. I wished to retain only those things necessary for the order, protection and authority of the ecclesiastical government, which I hold most firmly (as I have explained more fully elsewhere) to agree with the true principles of every polity, even the most perfected, and above all with the primitive and apostolic pattern and the practice of the primitive Church.

units.la: A quâ ut penitus discedatur, in eorum tantum gratiam qui nec quicquam probabile pro suis afferre, nec vel uni objectioni respondere valent (sed perversa voluntate acti, nec inter se fere aliâ re concordant quàm quòd utrique eradicandum Episcopatum, & contra me pugnandum simul censeant) eam animi mollitiem & imbecillitatem arguet, quæ à Dei veritate potius quàm à pace humana depelli voluit, & Ecclesiastici Honoris naufragium facere, quàm factiosis quorundam studiis adversari.
units.tr: If one were to depart entirely from this, in favour only of those who can neither offer anything probable on their own side nor answer even a single objection (but who, driven by a perverse will, hardly agree among themselves on anything except that both think episcopacy must be uprooted and both want to fight against me), this would show a softness and weakness of spirit. It would be a spirit that preferred to be driven from God's truth rather than from human peace, and to suffer the shipwreck of ecclesiastical honour rather than oppose the factious designs of certain men.

units.la: Quorum interim vitio ita male successit hic Tractatus & qui sequentium calamitatum crimen maximè sustinent, Deus novit, & Tempus patefaciet: Me (credo) coram Deo & in corruptis hominibus ( qui hæc ferió expenderint) liberari, qui non minori studio adlaboravi pacem Populo meo restituere, quàm ipsas meas Coronas Posteris meis incolumes servare.
units.tr: God knows, and time will reveal, what ill success this treaty met through the fault of these men, and who bears most of the blame for the calamities that followed. I believe that before God, and among corrupt men who will weigh these things fairly, I am cleared, since I have laboured with no less zeal to restore peace to my people than to keep my own Crowns intact for my posterity.

units.la: Eâ sunt arrogantiâ nonnulli, ut omnes hujusmodi Concessiones in Imbecillitatis argumentum statim trahant, & tunc se rigidos maximè & pervicaces ostendunt, cum alios flecti faciles, & de suo remittentes, invenerint.
units.tr: Some are so arrogant that they at once take all such concessions as a sign of weakness, and then show themselves most stiff and obstinate when they find others easy to bend and giving up their own claims.

units.la: Hæc Illis pars magnà Prudentiæ, aliquid semper ultrà exposcere, quam Æquitatis aut Honoris Ratio concedat, ut isto saltem colore alia omnia Concessa repudient; tam iniquis plærunque pacis conditionibus ut præ his leve fit quod in bello deterrimum. Cum id unicè semper egerunt, ut inhonestis Concessionibus me primùm jugularem, quò minus Ipsis restaret conficiendum.
units.tr: It is the great prudence of these men always to demand something beyond what the reason of equity or honour would grant, so that under this pretext they may reject all the other concessions made. Their conditions of peace are usually so unfair that, compared with them, what is worst in war seems slight. For they have always aimed solely at this: first to cut my throat with dishonourable concessions, so that less would remain for them to finish off.

units.la: Prorsus nihil amplius vel in hoc Tractatu vel in alio quovis effectum est, quàm ut Orbi constaret, quo utrique animo essemus in Pacem Publicam: Ipse, nihil sere negare promptus, Illi nihil concedere.
units.tr: Nothing more at all was achieved, either in this treaty or in any other, than that it became clear to the world with what spirit each of us stood toward public peace: I, ready to deny almost nothing; they, to concede nothing.

units.la: Duriores hinc factos nonnullos, pravis eorum ingeniis imputandum est, haud, à Me tunc Concessis, vel Negatis. Me nunquam pigebit conditionum quas detuli, culpa eorum sit & pudor qui recusaverant.
units.tr: That some have become harder is to be imputed to their own perverse minds, not to the conditions I then conceded or refused. I shall never regret the conditions I offered. The fault and the shame lie with those who refused them.

units.la: Haud evexit me unquam secundissimus Fortunæ cursus ne Tractatui auscultarem, nec ita hactenus reciprocaverat, ut non possem Armis contendere, licet nunquam id veræ fortitudinis duxerim vitas hominū malle prodigere,quā, collatis utrinq; rationibus, si opus effet alienis subscribere.
units.tr: The most favourable course of fortune never lifted me so high that I was unwilling to listen to a treaty, nor has it so far turned against me that I could not contend by arms. Yet I have never considered it true courage to prefer squandering men's lives to weighing the reasons on both sides and, if need be, subscribing to the views of others.

units.la: Quod verò de plærisque Tractatibus pessimè ominarer, inde erat, quod tam inviti ad illos trahebantur, quo tacitè licet indicabant, quædam gladio esse impetranda, de quorum iniquitate disputatum nollent, quæque inter Milites agitati, quàm Consilij aptiora.
units.tr: What I feared most about most treaties was this: men were drawn to them so reluctantly. This tacitly indicated that certain matters were to be obtained by the sword, matters whose iniquity they would not wish to dispute, and which were more suited to the debate of soldiers than to the counsel of statesmen.

units.la: Deus illis ignoscat, qui dissoluti hujus Tractatus rei fuerant: & id gratiâ suâ in iis efficiat, ut jam Bello potiores fortunæ suæ opportunitate ad moderatius agendum utantur, ut quæ hactenus ob peccata nostra Pax merito dilata est, feliciter tandem procuretur, dum, quod Tractatu non licuit, precibus saltem consequamur.
units.tr: May God forgive those who were the cause of this treaty being broken off. May He by His grace bring it about that they, now stronger in the opportunity of their fortune than in the war, use it to act more moderately, so that the peace which has hitherto been justly deferred on account of our sins may at last be happily secured. And since we could not obtain it by the treaty, may we at least obtain it by prayers.

units.la: Tu O Deus Rationis & Pacis qui nec Ipse dedignaris cum Peccatoribus agere, ultro pace oblata præveniens, & ut velint tecum in gratiam redire obtestans, quos & potes, & juste potes perdere, ni misericordia in salutem abundaveris, emollias corda nostra Redemptoris nostri sanguine, quo & pacem tuam accipiamus, eamque rursum inter nos invicem (quod Christianos decet & homines) procuremus simul & conservemus. Quoties pacem obsecravi? Sed cum loquor de pace, ipsi ad bellum parati sunt.
units.tr: O God of reason and peace, who does not disdain to deal with sinners Yourself, anticipating them with peace freely offered, and beseeching them to be reconciled with You, whom You both can and justly could destroy, unless Your mercy abounds unto salvation: soften our hearts with the blood of our Redeemer, so that we may receive Your peace, and procure and preserve it again among ourselves, as becomes Christians and men. How often have I begged for peace? But while I speak of peace, they are ready for war.

units.la: Ne dedas nos Impot entiæ affectuum, & no-bis, & aliis exitiosæ.
units.tr: Do not give us up to the impotence of our passions, hurtful both to us and to others.

units.la: Purga nostros Intellectus, ut veritatem tuam videant, tum Rationis ut homines, tum Religionis ut Christiani: & sic omnium corda inclines, ut servemus unitatem Spiritus in vinculo pacis.
units.tr: Purge our understandings, that they may see Your truth, both of reason as men and of religion as Christians; and so incline the hearts of all, that we may keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

units.la: Tolle illam in te Inimicitiam, cordibus nostris nimis insitam, & illam indas charitatem, quam exercere mutuo debemus.
units.tr: Take away that enmity toward You, too deeply planted in our hearts, and give us that charity, which we ought to exercise toward one another.

units.la: Remove quæ ita valde commeriti sumus Belli mala, & illam Pacem Largiaris, quam Ille noster Pacificus Christus unice potest mereri.
units.tr: Remove the evils of war which we have so greatly deserved, and grant that peace, which our Pacifying Christ alone can merit.

units.la: 19. De vario Belli suc- cessu ,· Victoriis & Cladibus.
units.tr: 19. Of the varied success of the War, Victories and Defeats.

units.la: VArii huius Belli Infœlicissimi Eventus occasionem suggesserunt varia meditandi. Placuit Deo nōnunquam experiri me victoriis, fusis hostibus & profligatis, eo fine, ut discerem simul gratè agnoscere & moderatè uti ea Ipsius Potentia, qui est vere Dominus exercitum, potens (ubi collibuisset) repri-mere mere fiduciam contra me pugnantium, Numero ita & Viribus superiorum.
units.tr: The varied outcomes of this most unhappy War gave me occasion for various reflections. God has sometimes been pleased to let me experience victories, with the enemy routed and overthrown, so that I might learn both to acknowledge gratefully and to use with moderation that power of His, who is truly the Lord of hosts, and who can (when He chooses) restrain the confidence of those who fight against me, however much they surpass me in numbers and strength.

units.la: Ab exiguis admodum initiis aucto, satis ostendit, me non penitus ita populi mei amore, & Illius præsidio destitui.
units.tr: That my cause has grown from very small beginnings shows plainly that I have not been wholly abandoned, either by the love of my people or by His protection.

units.la: Alibi exercebat Patientiam meam, & docebat non in bracchio Carnis, sed in Deo vivente confidere.
units.tr: At other times He tested my patience and taught me to trust not in the arm of flesh, but in the living God.

units.la: Valuerunt aliquoties peccata mea contra causæ Iustitiam, & qui mecum tunc erant, argumentum abunde & occasionem subministrabant severè utrosque castigandi. Pœna interim hostibus non minor, qui secundis rebus indurati, magis hanc suæ causæ iniquitatem asseruerunt, & (quam licentia Tumultuum Parlamentis indigna inchoaverat) jam apertius Armis promoverunt.
units.tr: At times my own sins have prevailed against the justice of my cause, and those who were with me then gave ample reason and occasion to rebuke both them and me severely. Meanwhile the enemy has not been punished less; hardened by their successes, they have defended the wickedness of their cause all the more, and (what the licence of tumults, unworthy of Parliaments, had begun) have now pushed forward more openly with arms.

units.la: Nocent sæpe Publicæ Causæ Privatæ flagitia, nec qui vulgo generosi & fortes audiunt, idonei semper à Deo habiti qui Iustam Causam Bello propugnent: Quo enim proclivior quisque est suæ Arti, Consilio, aut Virtuti tribuere, eò minùs (in suam Gloriam) Deus per Illos operatur.
units.tr: The crimes of individuals often harm the public cause, and those whom the common people hear as noble and brave have not always been judged by God as fit to defend a just cause in war. For the more readily each man attributes his success to his own skill, counsel or virtue, the less God works through him for His own glory.

units.la: Illud constat malè admodum ex evertu[?] æstimari vel Iustitiam Causarum, vel Conscientiæ Pacem, vel in quem statum Animæ nostræ in futurum mittuntur.
units.tr: It is clear that it is very wrong to judge from the outcome either the justice of causes, or the peace of conscience, or the state into which our souls are sent in the future.

units.la: Quià Mea Parte stabant, clarè (crëdo) & indubiè Dei Verbum, & Leges Regni, tùm Iuramenta sua porpria omnia à fe conjunctim stantia habuerunt: his enim omnibus præcipitur justis meis Imperiis parere ; nemini certe concediditur extra meum Consensum, nedum contra me, arma fumere.
units.tr: For on my side stood the Word of God, clearly and undoubtedly (I believe), and the laws of the realm, and their own oaths, all holding together in harmony; for all of these command obedience to my just commands. Certainly no one is allowed to take up arms without my consent, much less against me.

units.la: . Illi ex parte adversâ, ad nescio quas confugiunt prætenfas formidines, & diffolutiffima Statut ( ut vocant ) Fundamentalia, ea scilicet quæ præfentem Statum Ecclesiæ & Regni evertunt ; quædam porro hic afferunt Sui in defensionem argumenta futilia & imaginaria, quæ etiamsi vera effent, minime omnium ab illis urgenda, qui cum mei Subditi effent, Me & Leges meas primi impugnabant, turbas illas initio non coercentes, mox etiam conscripto Exercitu; Ejusmodi certe argumentis, cuicunque Factioni licebit (vires modò adsint & fiducia) quæcunque contra Leges exantes & Magistratus postulant, ea Gladio demùm expugnare. Nunquam enim tàm commodè erunt res constitutæ; ut non aliqui saltem offendantur, & quod Ipsis reformandum videbitur ad Rebellionem usque prosequi incitentur, accedentibus præsertim parasitastris Concionatoribus, quales hi qui Martyres appellare audent, qui contra Me & Leges, nec minùs Iuramenta sua Religionémque pugnantes occubuerunt.
units.tr: The others on the opposing side flee to I know not what pretended fears and to what they call the most loose Fundamentals, namely those that overthrow the present state of the Church and Kingdom. Further, they bring forward here certain frivolous and imaginary arguments in their own defence, which, even if they were true, ought least of all to be urged by those who, while they were my subjects, first attacked me and my laws, not checking those disturbances at the start, and soon afterwards even raising an army. Certainly by arguments of this kind any faction whatever will be free (provided it has the strength and the confidence) to force by the sword whatever it demands against the existing laws and magistrates. For affairs will never be arranged so well that some people at least are not offended, and that what they think ought to be reformed does not stir them on to rebellion. This is especially so when parasitical preachers join them, such as those who dare to call martyrs those who fell fighting against me and the laws, and no less against their own oaths and religion.

units.la: Probè verò intelligunt Boni Christiani, iis duntaxat inclytum hoc Nomen tribui, qui Dei veritatem & quæ speciatim hîc debent officia vitâ suâ habent potiora, cæterisque in Mundo charissimis; qui nil sibi privatim è rebus novis quærentes id solum piè cogitabant, quibus animarum vinculis, Deo, Mihi, & Ecclesiæ, obligati erant in obsequium fimul, & auxilium.
units.tr: Good Christians, however, rightly understand that this glorious name belongs only to those who value the truth of God and the duties especially required here above their own lives and all things most dear to them in the world; who, seeking nothing for themselves privately from the new affairs, thought only of this, how they might be dutifully bound to God, to me and to the Church by the bonds of souls, both in obedience and in help.

units.la: Deus suâ misericordiâ potuit donare, & donavit procul dubio multos vitâ æternâ qui in justa causa obierunt. ipso illo corporum interitu in Salutem Animarum Sanctificato, vulneribusque & clade temporali viam quasi ad æternam felicitatem siernente[?]; dum certa mortis approximatio ita corda eorum in eam fidei disponeret humilitatis, pœnitentiæ capacitatem, quæ justissimæ causæ conjuncta in meliorem multo vitâ præpararet, quàm vel nefarii illis hostes adimere, vel sibi ipsis sine pœnitentia sperare potuerant.
units.tr: God, in His mercy, could give, and undoubtedly has given, eternal life to many who died in a just cause, the very destruction of their bodies being sanctified for the salvation of their souls, and their wounds and temporal calamity making, as it were, a way toward eternal happiness. For the near approach of certain death so disposed their hearts to that humility of faith and capacity for repentance which, joined with a most just cause, prepared them for a far better life than either the wicked enemy could take from them or they themselves could have hoped for without repentance.

units.la: Sæpe (fateor) in prælio superiores fuere nostris partibus; nunquam ita apud Dei Tribunal, & conscientias suas futuri, ubi certe haud eâdem fiduciâ cominus ibunt tot perspicuis rationibus, (à Lege Iuramento Fidelitatis & Christianæ Re-ligionis fundamentis contra cunctis militantibus (quibus intùs jam agitantur, & fe in corde suo accusant) quâ olim actì vecordiâ, in quas Deus mihi dederat copias impetum fecerunt.
units.tr: Often (I confess) the other side has been superior in battle to our party; but never before the tribunal of God, and of their own consciences, which they must face. There they will certainly not go with the same confidence to meet so many clear reasons, drawn from the law, the oath of allegiance and the foundations of the Christian religion, against all who fight, by which they are already being troubled inwardly and accuse themselves in their hearts. With that madness by which they once rushed upon the forces God had given me,

units.la: Horum fors utcunque ærumnosa, oppressis plærifque aut extinctis, (haud dubito) longè optabilior est pio homini, & mentis bene sanæ (cui officium suum & salus Animæ præfentaneæ hujus vitæ oblectamentis potiora) quam omnes Hostium nostrorum Triumphi & Gloria, qui vix fieri potest ut effugiant quotidianos illos horrores, quibus (semper ambiguæ, nunc vero palam convictæ) conscientiæ Illos persequuntur, præsertim postquam Orbi jam factis constet, quàm falsi penitùs & ab animis Ipsorum alienifimi illi primò sparsi Prætextus fuere, quibus forfan speciosum aliquid inerat, nil, quod justè excusaret vel hæc ἔργα[?] moveri, velin illis tam diù perstari, contra Me & Leges fancitas, in quorum utriusque conservatione omnes probi arbitrantur publicam maximè salutem consistere atque adeo propter simul & cum illis honeftius multo & fœlicius ducunt occumbere, quam per Ruinas has crescere & extolli.
units.tr: the lot of these men, however wretched it may be, with most of them overcome or killed (I do not doubt), is far more desirable to a godly man, and to a mind well and sound, for whom duty and the salvation of the soul outweigh the pleasures of this present life, than all the triumphs and glory of our enemies. For it can hardly be that they escape those daily terrors with which their consciences (always uncertain, and now plainly convicted) pursue them. This is especially so now that it is already clear to the world how utterly false, and how wholly alien to their own minds, were the pretexts first spread abroad, which perhaps had something plausible about them. Nothing was there that could justly excuse these deeds, or justify persisting in them for so long against me and the laws sanctioned by God, in the preservation of which all good men judge that the public safety chiefly consists. Therefore they judge it far more honourable and happy to perish along with those laws, and with them, than to grow and be exalted through these ruins.

units.la: Sæpe id precibus à Deo expetivi, ut qui mearum partium essent, veram pietatem cum obsequii sensu conjungerent & in Deum æque atque animas suas extarent ac in Me fideles, ne quæ hic deliquissent, cæteros illos conatus prorsus irritos efficerent.
units.tr: Often I have asked God in prayer that those of my party might join true piety with a sense of obedience, and might stand in God and for their own souls as well as faithful to me, so that whatever wrongs they have committed here might not render all those other efforts entirely vain.

units.la: Nunquam tamen existimabo ullam in parte adversa non prætensam modo, sed veram (si fuisset) pietatem, vel excusare omnino, vel compensare posse illa Obsequii & Fidei dispendia quæ mihi penitus deberi ita manifestè evincuntur conscientiæ hominum, ut hac sola permoti homines (alias prophani satis) vitas suas mei causa periculo objecerint.
units.tr: Yet I shall never think that any piety on the opposing side, not merely pretended but true (if it had existed), could wholly excuse, or make up for, those losses of obedience and faith which are so clearly owed to me, as shown to men's consciences, that men otherwise quite profane have exposed their lives to danger on my account for this reason alone.

units.la: Nulla mihi unquam victoria sine dolore meo obtigit, nempe in Subditos meos parta, quorum plurimi nimis vereor cum Absalone in peccatis suis perierunt. Nec vero fusus unquam proelio de Misericordia Divina, & præsidio desperavi.
units.tr: No victory has ever come to me without my grief, namely those won against my own subjects, of whom I greatly fear that many have perished with Absalom in their sins. Nor, indeed, have I ever been beaten in battle and despaired of the divine mercy and protection.

units.la: Nunquam certe ejusmodi victoriam optavi, qua Leges & Libertates Populi Mei vincerem magis quàm restituerem: has enim utrasque simul cum Jure meo vehementer oppressas videbam ab iis ipsis hominibus, quibus Justa omnis coercio gravis erat. Dante interim vel negante victoriam Divinâ Providentiâ, id unicè duxi cavendum ne vel de viribus meis gloriarer, vel Deum stulte aspergerem, quem credebam etiam aliquando in bonum omnia conversurum.
units.tr: I never wished for a victory of such a kind that I would conquer the laws and liberties of my people rather than restore them. For I saw both of these, together with my right, grievously oppressed by the very men to whom every just restraint was burdensome. Meanwhile, whether Divine Providence granted or denied victory, I judged this one thing alone must be guarded against: that I should not boast of my own strength, or foolishly cast reproach upon God, whom I believed would at some time turn all things to good.

units.la: Nihil aliud mihi è Bello insuper aecedere optabam, quàm ut Hostibus meis modum imponerem, Amicis pacem darem.
units.tr: Beyond this, I wished nothing else to come to me from the War than to set a limit to my enemies and to give peace to my friends.

units.la: Expavi tentationem integrae nimis victoriae: nec id magis sum à Deo precatus, ut Hostes meos, quàm ut Meipsum [?] vincerem. Illud Deus negavit, hoc dedit, quod mihi optimè vidit expedire.
units.tr: I feared the temptation of a too complete victory. Nor did I pray to God so much that I might conquer my enemies as that I might conquer myself. He refused the one and gave the other, which He saw to be most profitable for me.

units.la: Varii Rerum Successus erant diversæ Methodi Divinæ Iustitiæ [?], his quasi ventis contrariis excutere nos volentis & repurgare, ut puniendo peccata nostra, puros simul illis præstaret, & ita animos nostros erudiret, ut futuras benedictiones & estimare melius possemus, & rectius uti.
units.tr: The varied successes of events were different methods of divine justice, which, as it were, wished to shake us and cleanse us with contrary winds, so that by punishing our sins it might at the same time make us pure, and so instruct our minds that we might better value future blessings and use them more rightly.

units.la: Cùm illos toties de Pace interpellaverim, satis patet Bellum mihi haud quaquam voluptati fuisse; quemadmodum & Superiores meæ Concessiones indicabant quàm libenter illi obviassem, & sic ab omnibus esse imparatum, erat illius qui nec de Bello cogitâsset.
units.tr: Since I so often pleaded for peace, it is plain enough that war was by no means a pleasure to me; and as my concessions to my superiors showed how gladly I would have met them, so it was the mark of one who had not even thought about war that everyone found him unprepared.

units.la: Vetuit Me Conscientia Innocentiæ meæ quicquam à Bello metuere; sed amor Populi exegit, ut quanquam fas effet de-fugerem.
units.tr: Conscience of my innocence forbade me to fear anything from the war; but the love of the people required that, although it would have been lawful, I should flee.

units.la: Ea mihi in hoc Bello culpa præcipua est, quod nonnullis plus nimio indulferim, confirmando hanc illis poteftatem, quâ, eâ modestia & gratitudine uti nolebant, quæ eorum tum fidem, tùm fiduciam meam decuisset.
units.tr: The chief fault I find in myself in this war is that I indulged some men too much, confirming in them this power, which they were unwilling to use with that moderation and gratitude which would have become their loyalty and my trust.

units.la: Si parciùs dedissem, parciùs forsan oppugnaffent: si plus negassem, plùs fuisset obsequii.
units.tr: If I had given more sparingly, they would perhaps have attacked more sparingly; if I had refused more, there would have been more of obedience.

units.la: Serò jam recensemus causas Belli. Illud unice exopto, ut fit fœlix tandem exitus infœlicium cœptorum. Ea fors Inevitabilis peccata nostra exfpeftabat, ut non ampliùs quiesceret Divina Justitia: victa primò Dei patientia in ea nos supplicia damnavit, ut alternantibus victoriis mutuò colliderentur: utriusque enim Partis prospera, Publico adversa.
units.tr: Late now we recount the causes of the war. I desire only this, that the unhappy beginnings may at length have a happy outcome. Perhaps the inevitable fate awaited our sins, so that the Divine Justice should rest no longer: God's patience, once exhausted, condemned us to such punishments that we should be struck against each other by alternating victories; for the successes of each party were the misfortunes of the public.

units.la: Miseræ vero omnes Victoriæ quæ peccata adhuc relinquunt indomita, queis ef-fertur insolentius superbia, & ad cumulandas injurias animatur.
units.tr: Wretched indeed are all victories which leave sins unsubdued, by which pride is carried away more insolently and is spurred on to heap up injuries.

units.la: Quin nec Pax Ipsa expetenda est, dum nos in Illam pœnitentia præparaverit.
units.tr: Nor is peace itself to be desired, unless it shall have prepared us for it by repentance.

units.la: Cum adversus Nos Ipsos magis, & in Deum minus pugnare didicerimus, his invicem pugnis abstinebitur. Sanæ has utinam cogitationes in cordibus nostris coeant, ut melius satagatur Belli huius Infœlicis periodus: & discamus utrimque, Ego Deo obtemperare, & Populum regere, Illi & Deo & Mihi parere; nec Mihi amplius pareri postulo quam Deo simul pareatur.
units.tr: Since we have learned to fight more against ourselves and less against God, these mutual fights will be abstained from. Would that sound thoughts might meet in our hearts, so that the course of this unhappy war might be better brought to an end: and let us learn on both sides, I to obey God and to rule the people, they to obey both God and me; nor do I demand to be obeyed by them any more than God is obeyed at the same time.

units.la: O Deus Meus, fac ut æquo animo vincar, cùm sic Tibi placuerit.
units.tr: O my God, grant that I may be conquered with an even mind, since it has so pleased you.

units.la: Doce Me (quæ pulcherrima omnium victoria est) meipsum vincere, & Hostes meos patientia. Sic enim Christus vicit, atque adeò nec Regę Christiano indignum.
units.tr: Teach me (which is the most beautiful of all victories) to conquer myself, and my enemies by patience. For so Christ conquered, and this is not unworthy of a Christian king.

units.la: Inter utramque Manum tuam, sublevantem dexteram & prementem sinistram, in illam formes pietatem quæ tibi maximè grata est futura.
units.tr: Between your two hands, the one raising up and the other pressing down, shape me into that piety which will be most pleasing to you.

units.la: Ignosce secundarum rerum comiti arrogantiæ, & in adversis non minus, querimoniis & stomacho, quoties in fiducia virium nostrarum incendentibus tu vim tuam merito subtrahis, nec inter opias [?] nostras unà egrederis.
units.tr: Pardon in me the arrogance that accompanies prosperity, and likewise in adversity the complaints and bitterness, whenever, in the confidence of our own strength, you rightly withdraw your power and do not go out with our [?] forces.

units.la: Esto Tu Omnia, sive Nos aliquid, seu nihil simus, & seu victores seu victi tibi Gloriam tri-buemus.
units.tr: Be you all things, whether we are something or nothing, and whether victors or vanquished, we shall ascribe the glory to you.

units.la: Tu Domine nosti quantâ animi molestia hæc à Subditis meis mala perpetior, quibus optima semper concupivi, & ob hanc causam, maxime sentio quæ me cogunt sibi mala facere, dum eorum luam supplicia. Cùm ergo victor simul & victus utrinque plectar, dones me geminata Spiritus tui[?] portione, & ea gratiæ mensura quæ mihi sola sufficiat.
